atomic-structure: Valence electrons are the outermost shell’s electrons — the ones involved in bonding.
Carbon’s configuration is 1s² 2s² 2p² — the 2nd shell holds 4 electrons, all valence.
The number of protons (atomic number) defines which element an atom is.
Neutrons are electrically neutral, unlike protons (+1) and electrons (−1); they add mass but no charge to the nucleus.
Isotopes share the same number of protons (same element) but differ in neutron count, which changes the mass number.
Neutral atoms have no net charge, so the negative electrons exactly balance the positive protons.
Electrons contribute negligible mass, so mass number counts only protons plus neutrons in the nucleus.
Adding an electron gives the atom one more negative charge than positive, making it a negatively charged anion.
Modern quantum theory describes electrons as occupying probability clouds (orbitals), not fixed circular paths — the old planetary picture is an oversimplification.
Atomic number is defined as the number of protons, so atomic number 7 means 7 protons (and, when neutral, 7 electrons).
Charge equals protons minus electrons: 8 − 10 = −2, consistent with the oxide ion O²⁻ that oxygen commonly forms.
Atoms of the same element can have different neutron counts — these variants are isotopes, and they still behave identically in chemical reactions.
Protons and neutrons, both much heavier than electrons, reside in the tiny nucleus, which is why it holds almost all the atom's mass.
Every electron must be uniquely described by its quantum numbers; two electrons can share an orbital only if their spins differ.
Hund's rule minimizes electron-electron repulsion by spreading electrons into separate same-energy orbitals before any pairing happens.
The second shell contains one 2s and three 2p orbitals (4 orbitals total), each holding 2 electrons, for a maximum of 8.
Valence (outermost) electrons are the ones available to be shared or transferred in bonds, so they govern how an atom reacts chemically.
Both have 6 protons (defining them as carbon), but carbon-14 has 2 extra neutrons, giving it a higher mass number.
Neutrons are neutral (no charge); protons are the positively charged nuclear particles.
Nitrogen is in group 15, and for main-group elements the group number corresponds to 5 valence electrons.
Oxygen sits in group 16, so it has 6 valence electrons — which is why it typically forms 2 bonds to complete an octet.
For main-group elements, the group number (17, or 7A) gives 7 valence electrons, explaining why chlorine needs just one more electron for a full octet.
Elements are ordered by increasing atomic number (proton count), which also roughly tracks increasing mass for most elements.
Only protons and neutrons occupy the nucleus; electrons exist in surrounding orbitals/shells outside the nucleus.
Chemical behavior is driven by valence electrons, and elements in a group share the same valence electron count, giving them similar reactivity.
An electron has roughly 1/1800th the mass of a proton or neutron, so electrons contribute almost nothing to an atom's total mass.
The spin quantum number (m_s = +1/2 or −1/2) distinguishes the two electrons that can occupy the same orbital.
Being one electron short of an octet, fluorine strongly favors gaining an electron to form the stable F⁻ ion rather than losing one.
Atomic number is fixed by proton count; this is what defines which element an atom is, regardless of isotope or ionic charge.
Sodium (group 1) has just 1 valence electron; losing it leaves sodium with the same stable electron configuration as neon, a noble gas.
orbitals: p orbitals have two lobes on either side of the nucleus along one axis; s orbitals are spherical.
The Pauli exclusion principle allows at most 2 electrons per orbital, and they must have opposite spins.
By the (n+l) filling order, 4s (4+0=4) fills before 3d (3+2=5).
The s orbital is the only orbital type with a simple spherical shape centered on the nucleus.
A p subshell consists of three orbitals (px, py, pz), oriented along the three perpendicular axes.
An s subshell has just one spherical orbital, regardless of which energy level it belongs to.
The d subshell has five distinct orbitals, each able to hold up to 2 electrons, for a maximum of 10 electrons.
Each of the 3 p orbitals holds up to 2 electrons, so 3 orbitals × 2 electrons = 6 electrons maximum.
Like any p subshell, 2p has three orbitals that each hold 2 electrons, giving a maximum of 6 electrons.
Two electrons can occupy one orbital only if their spins are opposite; a third electron would necessarily duplicate a full set of quantum numbers, which the Pauli exclusion principle forbids.
Orbitals are regions of space describing the probability of finding an electron, not fixed trajectories — this is a key distinction from the outdated Bohr model.
Sigma bonds result from orbitals overlapping end-to-end directly along the axis connecting the two nuclei, giving strong, rotation-tolerant bonding.
Pi bonds arise when two parallel, unhybridized p orbitals overlap side-by-side above and below the bond axis, creating electron density off the direct line between nuclei.
Sigma bonds are symmetric around the bond axis, so rotating one end doesn't disrupt the overlap, unlike pi bonds whose parallel-p-orbital overlap would be destroyed by rotation.
Hybridization combines an atom's own s and p orbitals into new, equivalent hybrid orbitals (sp, sp2, or sp3) better suited for bonding geometry.
The n=2 shell has one 2s orbital plus three 2p orbitals, totaling 4 orbitals (which can hold up to 8 electrons).
Electron-electron shielding changes the relative energies of orbitals in multi-electron atoms, making 4s slightly lower in energy than 3d, so it fills first according to the Aufbau principle.
Unlike the spherical s orbital, a p orbital has a dumbbell shape with two lobes separated by a node right at the nucleus.
A node is a location where the probability of finding the electron drops to zero, separating regions (lobes) of the orbital.
The s designation corresponds to orbitals with zero orbital angular momentum, which are spherically symmetric.
The three p orbitals point along the x, y, and z axes, perpendicular to one another, minimizing their mutual overlap.
1s, 2s, 3s, etc. are all spherically symmetric; higher-energy s orbitals are simply larger (with additional internal nodes) but keep the overall spherical shape.
Even p orbitals can form a sigma bond if they overlap directly along the internuclear axis, concentrating electron density between the nuclei.
Side-by-side, parallel overlap of p orbitals places electron density above and below the bond axis, which is the defining feature of a pi bond.
Quantum mechanics describes orbitals as three-dimensional probability distributions for where an electron is likely to be found, not fixed paths.
The f subshell contains seven orbitals, each capable of holding 2 electrons, for a maximum of 14 electrons.
The n=3 shell has 1 s-orbital, 3 p-orbitals, and 5 d-orbitals (9 orbitals total), each holding 2 electrons, for a maximum of 18.
The Pauli exclusion principle requires that the two electrons sharing an orbital differ in their spin quantum number, since all their other quantum numbers are identical.
A sigma bond's defining feature is head-on overlap along the axis connecting the nuclei, giving the strongest, most direct electron density between them.
Subshell orbital counts follow 2l+1: s=1, p=3, d=5, f=7, g=9 — each subsequent subshell type has 2 more orbitals than the last.
hybridization: Three regions of electron density (trigonal planar) come from mixing one s and two p orbitals — sp².
sp hybridization gives 2 regions of electron density arranged linearly, 180° apart.
2 regions of electron density (linear) come from mixing one s and one p orbital — sp, leaving 2 unhybridized p orbitals for the 2 pi bonds.
sp3 hybrid orbitals point toward the corners of a tetrahedron, giving the characteristic 109.5° bond angle.
sp3 hybridization uses all of the atom's s and p orbitals (one s and all three p's), leaving none available for pi bonding.
The three sp2 hybrid orbitals spread out evenly in a plane, 120° apart, to minimize electron repulsion.
With 4 sigma bonds and 0 lone pairs (steric number 4), the carbon mixes one s and three p orbitals into four sp3 hybrid orbitals.
Counting 3 sigma bonds plus 1 lone pair gives a steric number of 4, corresponding to sp3 hybridization, even though one 'position' is a lone pair rather than a bond.
Adding 2 sigma bonds and 2 lone pairs gives a steric number of 4, so oxygen is sp3 hybridized despite forming only 2 visible bonds.
Steric number 2 gives sp, 3 gives sp2, and 4 gives sp3 — this simple count is the standard shortcut for assigning hybridization.
The carbonyl carbon has 3 sigma bonds total (the double bond counts once for sigma purposes) and 0 lone pairs, giving a steric number of 3 and sp2 hybridization.
sp hybridization mixes only one s and one p orbital, leaving 2 p orbitals unhybridized and available to form two pi bonds.
sp2 hybridization mixes one s orbital with two p orbitals, leaving exactly 1 p orbital unhybridized for pi bonding.
Hybridization combines one s and two p orbitals into three sp2 orbitals; the one remaining, un-mixed p orbital is what allows sp2 carbons to form a pi bond.
Higher s-character (50% in sp vs 25% in sp3) pulls electron density closer to the carbon nucleus, which better stabilizes the negative charge left behind when that C–H bond's proton is removed.
More s-character spreads the hybrid orbitals further apart in angle — from 109.5° (sp3) to 120° (sp2) to 180° (sp).
Greater s-character pulls the bonding electron pair closer to the carbon nucleus, making sp C–H bonds shorter (and stronger) than sp2 or sp3 C–H bonds.
A steric number of 4 with no lone pairs always corresponds to sp3 hybridization and a tetrahedral arrangement of bonds.
Counting 2 sigma bonds plus 1 lone pair gives a steric number of 3, so the imine nitrogen is sp2 hybridized, just like the carbon it's double-bonded to.
With 3 sigma bonds and no lone pairs, boron has a steric number of 3, giving sp2 hybridization and a trigonal planar shape, even though boron lacks a full octet.
The central carbon has only 2 sigma bonds (one to each neighboring carbon, with each double bond contributing one sigma and one pi bond), giving a steric number of 2 and sp hybridization.
sp hybrids are formed from one s and one p orbital (50% s-character), more than sp2 (about 33%) or sp3 (25%), making sp orbitals hold electrons closest to the nucleus.
Trigonal planar geometry is the direct geometric consequence of mixing one s and two p orbitals into three equivalent sp2 hybrids.
With only 3 sigma bonds and no lone pair, the carbocation's steric number is 3, giving sp2 hybridization and a trigonal planar shape with an empty, unhybridized p orbital.
Counting 1 sigma bond plus 2 lone pairs gives a steric number of 3, so the carbonyl oxygen is sp2 hybridized, matching its planar carbon partner.
A steric number of 4 means the atom mixes one s and all three p orbitals together, producing four sp3 hybrid orbitals.
A steric number of 2 means only one s and one p orbital are mixed, leaving two p orbitals unhybridized and giving a linear sp arrangement.
Hybridization reflects the current bonding situation, not a fixed property, so it shifts as bonds break and form — here losing a sigma bond drops the steric number from 4 to 3.
sp hybrid orbitals point exactly 180° apart from each other, producing a linear arrangement around that atom.
Combining one s and one p orbital mathematically yields two equivalent hybrid orbitals oriented oppositely (180° apart), which is the geometric root of every linear sp center.
bonding: A triple bond is 1 sigma bond plus 2 pi bonds — 3 total.
Twisting misaligns the parallel p orbitals that form the pi bond, breaking that overlap — sigma bonds alone allow free rotation.
More bonds between the same two atoms pulls the nuclei closer together, so C=C (~134 pm) is shorter than C–C (~154 pm).
A single bond is exactly one sigma bond; no pi bonds are involved.
A double bond is always composed of exactly one sigma bond plus one pi bond, never two sigma bonds.
Pi bonds form from side-by-side p-orbital overlap, which is generally less effective than the direct head-on overlap of a sigma bond, making pi bonds typically weaker.
Sigma bonds are defined by overlap directly along the internuclear axis, concentrating electron density right between the two nuclei.
Pi bonds arise specifically from parallel p orbitals overlapping off to the sides of the bond axis, not along it.
Each additional bond (sigma or pi) increases the electron density held between the two nuclei, which pulls them closer together and shortens the bond.
Ionic bonds form when there's a large electronegativity difference, typically between a metal (low electronegativity) and a nonmetal (high electronegativity), not between two similar nonmetals.
Covalent bonding involves two atoms sharing a pair of electrons, as opposed to ionic bonding's complete electron transfer.
Ionic bonding occurs when electrons are essentially transferred rather than shared, producing a cation and an anion held together by electrostatic attraction.
Bonds within a molecule connecting atoms like O and H, where electrons are shared, are covalent bonds (here, polar covalent).
Head-on sigma overlap is more efficient than the side-by-side overlap of a pi bond, so sigma bonds are typically stronger per bond.
The pi bond depends on two p orbitals staying parallel to overlap; rotating one end of the double bond twists the orbitals out of alignment, breaking the pi bond's overlap.
Because a sigma bond's overlap is symmetric around the bond axis, rotating the atoms at either end doesn't disrupt the bonding — unlike a pi bond.
With 4 valence electrons and a strong drive to complete an octet, neutral carbon almost always forms exactly 4 total bonds (counting each bond in a double or triple bond separately).
Bond order simply counts the number of shared electron pairs between two atoms; a single bond has exactly one.
A triple bond consists of 1 sigma plus 2 pi bonds, for a total bond order of 3.
More shared electron pairs pull the two nuclei closer together, so higher bond order consistently means shorter bond length.
More shared electron pairs create a stronger overall attraction holding the atoms together, so higher bond order means more energy is needed to break the bond.
The opposite is true: as bond order increases, bond length decreases while bond strength increases — both trends move together, not apart.
Polar covalent bonds occur when the bonded atoms differ enough in electronegativity that the shared electrons spend more time near the more electronegative atom.
When two bonded atoms have essentially the same electronegativity, the shared electrons are distributed evenly, producing a nonpolar bond.
A bond between two identical carbon atoms has zero electronegativity difference, making it essentially nonpolar, unlike bonds to more electronegative heteroatoms.
The sigma bond holds the two atoms at the right distance and orientation; without it, there would be no stable framework for the p orbitals to align and form a pi bond.
A carbon-carbon triple bond is made of one sigma bond plus two perpendicular pi bonds, totaling three bonds overall.
The pi bond's electrons are held less tightly (weaker, more exposed overlap above and below the bond axis), making it the part of the double bond that typically reacts first in addition reactions.

The key distinction between bonding types is the behavior of the valence electrons — transferred in ionic bonds, shared between specific atoms in covalent bonds, and delocalized across many atoms in metallic bonds.
A double bond is one sigma bond plus one pi bond — these are fundamentally different types of overlap, not two sigma bonds.
electronegativity: Nuclear charge increases across a period while shielding stays roughly constant, pulling electrons in more tightly.
Fluorine is the most electronegative element on the periodic table.
Atomic radius increases down a group, so the valence electrons are farther from the nucleus and less tightly held — electronegativity decreases.
Electronegativity is specifically about how strongly an atom pulls on the electrons it is sharing in a covalent bond.
Oxygen (electronegativity ≈ 3.5) is significantly more electronegative than carbon (≈ 2.5), reflecting oxygen's position further right on the periodic table.
Electronegativity specifically describes an atom's behavior within a bond, pulling on shared electrons — it's meaningless for a truly isolated, unbonded atom.
Electronegativity decreases down a group, so nitrogen (higher up, smaller atom) is more electronegative than phosphorus below it.
Electronegativity decreases going down a group, and fluorine, chlorine, and bromine appear in that order from top to bottom, so F is most electronegative and Br is least.
With zero electronegativity difference between identical atoms, the shared electrons are distributed perfectly evenly, making the bond nonpolar.
Fluorine's small size means its nucleus is close to the bonding electrons, and its high effective nuclear charge gives it an especially strong pull on those shared electrons.
Metals tend to lose electrons easily (low electronegativity), while nonmetals tend to attract electrons strongly (high electronegativity) — this split underlies much of ionic bonding.
Alkali metals sit at the far left of the periodic table, where atoms are large and electronegativity is at its lowest for that period.
The small electronegativity difference (about 0.4) between carbon and hydrogen makes C–H bonds only weakly polar, often treated as essentially nonpolar in practice.
Fluorine (≈4.0) is more electronegative than chlorine (≈3.0), giving the C–F bond a larger electronegativity difference and therefore greater polarity.
Moving left to right across a period, increasing nuclear charge with similar shielding pulls electrons more strongly, so electronegativity rises steadily from Li to F.
Electronegativity increases across a period (left to right) and decreases down a group (top to bottom), so the highest values cluster in the upper right, with fluorine as the extreme.

Even though nuclear charge increases down a group, the valence electrons are farther from the nucleus and more shielded by inner electrons, so the net attraction on bonding electrons actually weakens.
Oxygen sits one position to the right of nitrogen in period 2, and electronegativity increases across a period, so oxygen is more electronegative.
Within the same period, electronegativity increases moving rightward, and chlorine sits to the right of sulfur, making it more electronegative.
Linus Pauling developed the widely used electronegativity scale, assigning fluorine the highest value (about 4.0).
A small or zero electronegativity difference gives a nonpolar bond, while a moderate difference gives a polar covalent bond — this difference is the key diagnostic.
Very large electronegativity differences pull shared electrons so strongly toward one atom that the bond behaves more like a full electron transfer — approaching ionic character.
Electronegativity decreases down a group, so carbon, sitting above silicon, is more electronegative.
A smaller atomic radius means the nucleus is closer to the bonding electrons, strengthening its pull on them and increasing electronegativity across the period.
Within the same period, a shorter distance between the nucleus and the outer (bonding) electrons lets the nucleus attract those electrons more strongly, raising electronegativity.
Fluorine has the highest electronegativity of the three, giving the C–F bond the largest electronegativity difference and therefore the greatest polarity.
Electronegativity increases from left to right across a period, so the leftmost element (an alkali metal) has the lowest electronegativity in that row.
Electronegativity decreases down a group, and iodine is the lowest (largest, furthest down) of these four common halogens.

Being higher up the group, oxygen is smaller than sulfur, so its bonding electrons sit closer to the nucleus and experience a stronger pull, despite both elements sharing the same valence electron count.
The C-H electronegativity difference is small enough that chemists commonly treat it as nonpolar for most practical purposes, even though a slight polarity technically exists.
formal-charge: Formal charge = valence e⁻ − nonbonding e⁻ − ½(bonding e⁻), since each atom "owns" half of each shared bond.
N normally has 5 valence e⁻; with 4 bonds (8 shared e⁻, 4 "owned") and 0 lone pairs: 5 − 0 − 4 = +1.
O normally has 6 valence e⁻; with 1 bond (1 "owned" electron) and 3 lone pairs (6 nonbonding e⁻): 6 − 6 − 1 = −1.
Formal charge subtracts an atom's nonbonding electrons and half of its bonding (shared) electrons from its normal number of valence electrons.
4 valence electrons − 0 nonbonding − 1/2(8 bonding) = 4 − 0 − 4 = 0, matching carbon's normal, neutral bonding pattern.
Formal charges are a bookkeeping device, and for consistency they must sum to the molecule's actual overall charge — zero for any neutral molecule.
4 valence electrons − 0 nonbonding − 1/2(6 bonding) = 4 − 0 − 3 = +1, consistent with the positive charge of a carbocation.
4 valence electrons − 2 nonbonding − 1/2(6 bonding) = 4 − 2 − 3 = -1, consistent with a carbanion.
6 valence electrons − 4 nonbonding − 1/2(4 bonding) = 6 − 4 − 2 = 0, matching oxygen's usual neutral bonding pattern.
6 valence electrons − 2 nonbonding − 1/2(6 bonding) = 6 − 2 − 3 = +1, which is why an oxygen with 3 bonds (like a protonated ether oxygen) carries a positive formal charge.
5 valence electrons − 2 nonbonding − 1/2(6 bonding) = 5 − 2 − 3 = 0, confirming that a nitrogen with 3 bonds and 1 lone pair is neutral, as expected.
5 valence electrons − 4 nonbonding − 1/2(4 bonding) = 5 − 4 − 2 = -1, which is why a nitrogen with only 2 bonds typically carries a negative formal charge.
Formal charge assumes perfectly even sharing of bonding electrons, which isn't physically exact, but it's extremely useful for judging which of several Lewis structures is more reasonable.
5 valence electrons − 0 nonbonding − 1/2(8 bonding) = 5 − 0 − 4 = +1, matching the overall +1 charge carried by the ammonium ion.
Structures with smaller (closer to zero) formal charges, and with any unavoidable negative formal charge on the more electronegative atom, are considered more stable and realistic.
More electronegative atoms are better able to stabilize extra electron density, so placing a negative formal charge there produces a more reasonable, lower-energy structure.
Oxygen's high electronegativity makes it far better suited to hold extra negative charge than carbon, so structures matching charge to electronegativity are favored.
Giving carbon 1 lone pair and 3 bonds yields a formal charge of -1, while oxygen with 1 lone pair and 3 bonds yields +1 — an unusual but correct result for CO.
1 valence electron − 0 nonbonding − 1/2(2 bonding) = 1 − 0 − 1 = 0, the normal, neutral state for bonded hydrogen.
7 valence electrons − 6 nonbonding − 1/2(2 bonding) = 7 − 6 − 1 = 0, matching fluorine's usual neutral, single-bonded state.
7 valence electrons − 8 nonbonding − 1/2(0 bonding) = 7 − 8 − 0 = -1, matching the known -1 charge of the fluoride ion.

Formal charges don't need to be zero individually — they only need to sum to the species' true overall charge, and +1 + 0 + 0 + (-1) = 0... more precisely +1 and three oxygens summing to -2 gives an overall -1, matching the nitrate ion.
Unlike neutral molecules (which must sum to zero), ions are expected to have formal charges summing to their actual net charge, whether +1, -1, or otherwise.
3 valence electrons − 0 nonbonding − 1/2(8 bonding) = 3 − 0 − 4 = -1, consistent with boron's contribution to the ion's overall -1 charge.

Converting 2 nonbonding electrons into 2 bonding electrons removes 2 from the nonbonding count (+2 to formal charge) but only adds 1 to the half-bonding count (-1 to formal charge), for a net change of +1.
Since a neutral molecule has no net charge, all of its individual atomic formal charges must add up to zero overall.
Oxygen's high electronegativity and its role as a terminal atom with extra lone pairs make it the atom that typically carries the ion's formal negative charge.
Carbocations (+1) and carbanions (-1) are valid, commonly drawn species in organic chemistry, showing that carbon's formal charge is not always zero.
These are each atom's 'normal' bonding patterns in a neutral molecule, for which the formal charge works out to zero by design.
5 valence electrons − 0 nonbonding − 1/2(10 bonding) = 5 − 0 − 5 = 0, showing that an expanded octet on a period-3+ element doesn't automatically create a formal charge.
lewis-structures: You need the total valence electron count before you can distribute bonds and lone pairs correctly.
Less electronegative atoms tend to form more bonds and sit centrally; hydrogen can never be central (only 1 bond).
Converting a lone pair on a neighboring atom into a pi bond (multiple bond) often completes the octet without changing the molecular formula.
A bonding pair is represented either as two dots between the bonded atoms or, more commonly, as a single line connecting them.
Lone pairs belong to just one atom, so they're shown as a pair of dots on that atom rather than as a line connecting to another atom.
Hydrogen can form only one bond (it has just one valence electron and no available orbitals to expand), so it must always be a terminal (outer) atom, never central.
Carbon contributes 4 valence electrons and each of the 4 hydrogens contributes 1, giving 4 + 4(1) = 8 total valence electrons.
Carbon contributes 4 and each oxygen contributes 6, giving 4 + 6 + 6 = 16 total valence electrons.
Carbon (4) plus three oxygens (6 each = 18) gives 22, plus 2 extra electrons for the 2− charge, totaling 24.
A negative charge means the species has gained that many extra electrons beyond the neutral sum of its atoms' valence electrons, so they must be added to the total before distributing them.
Once the basic skeleton is bonded, remaining electrons are placed as lone pairs, typically satisfying the outer (terminal) atoms' octets before addressing the central atom.
Moving a lone pair from an outer atom into a new pi bond gives the electron-deficient central atom the electrons it needs without changing the total electron count.

The true electron distribution in such ions is an average (delocalized) across several equivalent arrangements, which a single fixed structure can't represent alone — resonance structures together approximate the real picture.
Every valence electron counted up front must appear somewhere in the final structure — none can be added or left out along the way.
Hydrogen and the halogens generally form only one bond each, making them well suited as terminal atoms rather than as a central, multiply-bonded atom.
Elements in period 3 or lower have accessible d orbitals (or simply larger atomic size) that allow them to accommodate more than 8 electrons around them, unlike strict period-2 elements.
Carbon, a period-2 element, has no available orbitals beyond 2s and 2p, so it is strictly limited to 8 electrons, unlike period-3+ elements that can expand their octets.
Knowing the total electron budget up front is essential — every later step (bonds, lone pairs, multiple bonds) depends on correctly distributing that fixed total.
Less electronegative atoms are usually less 'greedy' for electrons and can form more bonds, making them well suited to sit at the center, surrounded by more electronegative terminal atoms.

Just as with nitrate, azide's electron density is spread across multiple equivalent bonding arrangements, and drawing several resonance structures better represents the real, delocalized bonding than any single structure alone.
With 4 valence electrons, neutral carbon needs 4 more (shared) to complete its octet, so it reliably forms 4 total bonds (single, double, and triple bonds all counted toward that total).
With 6 valence electrons, oxygen needs 2 more to complete an octet, so it typically forms 2 total bonds (plus 2 lone pairs) when neutral.
With 5 valence electrons, nitrogen needs 3 more to complete an octet, so it typically forms 3 total bonds (plus 1 lone pair) when neutral.
Period-2 elements like carbon and nitrogen lack accessible orbitals beyond the octet, so any structure giving them more than 8 electrons signals a mistake that needs correcting.
Sulfur in SF6 forms 6 bonds (12 electrons around it), which is only possible because sulfur, a period-3 element, can exceed the standard octet — something carbon in CH4 (period 2) cannot do.
Electrons can only be placed once you know which atoms are actually connected — getting the skeleton right first is essential to arriving at a sensible final structure.
The entire process is essentially careful electron bookkeeping: the total electrons placed in bonds and lone pairs must exactly match the total counted up front.
Carbon forms a C=O double bond plus two C–H single bonds (4 bonds total, 0 lone pairs), giving it a complete octet with no formal charge.
Since fluorine needs only 1 bond to complete its octet, it naturally sits at the edge of a structure rather than at the center, where more bonds are usually needed.

When electron density can be equally well placed in more than one equivalent arrangement, drawing several resonance structures together gives a more accurate picture of the real, averaged bonding than any single structure alone.
molecular-geometry: 4 electron domains with no lone pairs arrange tetrahedrally (VSEPR) — 109.5° angles.
VSEPR counts lone pairs as occupying space — with 4 total domains around O, the electron geometry is tetrahedral, but the molecular shape (just the atoms) comes out bent.
4 total electron domains give a tetrahedral electron geometry, but with one domain as a lone pair, the atoms alone form a trigonal pyramidal shape (like NH₃).
With only 2 electron groups and no lone pairs to push them around, they spread as far apart as possible: 180° apart, giving a linear shape.
Three electron groups with no lone pairs spread out evenly in a single plane, 120° apart, giving a trigonal planar shape.
VSEPR (Valence Shell Electron Pair Repulsion) theory's core idea is that electron groups (bonds and lone pairs) arrange themselves to be as far apart as possible, minimizing repulsion.

Electron-pair geometry considers every region of electron density (including invisible lone pairs), while molecular geometry describes the shape traced out by the actual atoms, which can look different when lone pairs are present.
Although the electron-pair geometry is tetrahedral (4 total electron groups), one position is a lone pair, so only 3 atoms are visible, giving a trigonal pyramidal shape.
Each extra lone pair adds more repulsion pushing the bonding pairs closer together; with 2 lone pairs instead of ammonia's 1, water's H–O–H angle gets squeezed down the most.
Because lone pairs aren't held between two nuclei, they spread out more and exert stronger repulsive forces, compressing bond angles involving bonding pairs nearby.
Four identical electron groups with no lone pairs spread out symmetrically to 109.5° apart, the ideal tetrahedral angle.
Three electron groups with no lone pairs spread evenly in a plane at 120° apart to minimize repulsion.
With only 2 electron groups and no lone pairs, the maximum possible separation is a straight 180° angle.
The underlying electron-pair geometry is tetrahedral (4 total groups), but with 2 lone pairs removed from view, only the 2 bonded atoms remain visible, producing a bent shape.

With 3 total electron groups (2 bonds + 1 lone pair), the electron-pair geometry is trigonal planar; removing the invisible lone pair from the picture leaves the 2 oxygens in a bent arrangement, not a straight line.
Five electron groups with no lone pairs arrange themselves into a trigonal bipyramidal shape, with three equatorial and two axial positions.
Six electron groups with no lone pairs spread into an octahedral arrangement, the most symmetric way to separate 6 groups evenly.
Lone pairs aren't drawn into the final molecular shape, but their repulsive effect on the bonding pairs still shapes the angles and arrangement that we actually observe.
In an ideal tetrahedral arrangement, every pair of substituents around the central atom is separated by approximately the same 109.5° angle.

The electron-pair geometry (4 total groups) is tetrahedral, but since one of those groups is an unseen lone pair, only 3 hydrogen atoms plus the nitrogen are visible, producing the trigonal pyramidal molecular shape.
A double bond still counts as just one electron group for VSEPR purposes, so with 3 total groups and no lone pairs, the carbon is trigonal planar.

VSEPR treats an entire multiple bond (single, double, or triple) as one region of electron density occupying one position around the central atom, since the pi bonds don't point in separate directions.
A double bond occupies only one spatial position around the central atom (toward the same neighboring atom), so it always counts as a single electron group, not two.
With only 3 electron groups (the 3 bonds) and no lone pair present, the 3 substituents spread out in a plane at 120°, giving trigonal planar geometry.

An empty orbital holds no electrons and therefore exerts no repulsion, so with only 3 true electron groups present, the molecule minimizes repulsion by going flat (120° apart) rather than puckering into a tetrahedron.
With just 2 total electron groups and no other groups to consider, the only way to minimize repulsion is to place them 180° apart, giving a linear arrangement.
Water's oxygen has 2 bonding pairs (to the 2 hydrogens) plus 2 lone pairs, for a total steric number of 4, even though the visible molecular shape only shows 2 atoms.

A tetrahedral electron-pair geometry only produces a tetrahedral molecular shape when there are no lone pairs; if lone pairs are present, the molecular shape becomes trigonal pyramidal or bent instead.
Each double bond counts as just one electron group, so carbon has 2 total groups with no lone pairs, giving a linear molecule with 180° bond angles.
Two electron groups with nothing else around the central atom always spread as far apart as possible, producing a straight, linear shape.
bond-polarity: Small/zero difference = nonpolar covalent; moderate difference (~0.4–1.7) = polar covalent; large difference = ionic.
Oxygen is more electronegative than carbon, so it pulls the shared electron density toward itself, becoming δ⁻.
Molecular polarity depends on the vector sum of all bond dipoles — symmetric arrangements (like CO₂ or CCl₄) can cancel polar bonds into a net nonpolar molecule.
Carbon (electronegativity ≈ 2.5) is slightly more electronegative than hydrogen (≈ 2.1), so carbon pulls the shared electrons marginally toward itself, giving it a small partial negative charge.
Oxygen is far more electronegative than hydrogen, pulling the shared electrons toward itself and leaving hydrogen with a partial positive charge.
Identical atoms have exactly equal electronegativity, so there is zero tendency for the shared electrons to shift toward one side, making the bond perfectly nonpolar.
Chlorine is more electronegative than bromine, so the C–Cl bond has a larger electronegativity difference and is therefore more polar than C–Br.
Fluorine is the most electronegative of the three atoms, giving C–F the largest electronegativity gap and the greatest degree of ionic character among typical organic bonds.
The dipole arrow represents the net pull on the shared electrons, which always points toward the more electronegative (more electron-hungry) atom in the bond.
The delta (δ) symbol denotes a partial charge resulting from unequal electron sharing in a polar covalent bond, not a full formal ionic charge.
Like δ+, the δ− symbol represents a partial charge from unequal electron sharing, showing which end of a polar bond carries extra (but not whole) negative character.
Because CO2 is linear and symmetric, the two equal-but-opposite C=O dipoles point directly away from each other and sum to zero, leaving no net molecular dipole.
The size of the electronegativity difference between two bonded atoms is the standard criterion used to classify a bond along the spectrum from nonpolar covalent to polar covalent to ionic.
Because CCl4's tetrahedral geometry places the 4 equal C–Cl dipoles in perfectly symmetric directions, their vector sum is zero, making the overall molecule nonpolar even though each bond is polar.
Since both atoms in the bond are carbon, there is zero electronegativity difference, making the C–C bond essentially nonpolar.
When two atoms have essentially equal electronegativity, the shared electrons are distributed evenly, producing little to no bond polarity.
Once the electronegativity gap is large enough, the bonding electrons are held so strongly by one atom that the bond is better described as mostly ionic rather than simply polar covalent.
Bond polarity and molecular polarity don't always match — if a molecule's shape is symmetric enough, individual bond dipoles can cancel out, leaving a nonpolar molecule despite polar bonds.
Nitrogen is more electronegative than carbon, so the N–H bond has a larger electronegativity difference from hydrogen than C–H does, making N–H more polar.
Oxygen's much higher electronegativity pulls the shared pi and sigma electrons toward itself, giving it the partial negative (δ−) end of the carbonyl dipole.

Even though carbon is usually the less electronegative partner compared to oxygen or nitrogen, it is considerably more electronegative than a metal like magnesium, reversing the usual polarity seen in most organic bonds.
Oxygen is more electronegative than sulfur (despite being in the same group), giving O–H a larger electronegativity difference and therefore greater polarity than S–H.
Electronegativity difference is essentially a direct proxy for bond polarity — bigger gaps mean more unequal electron sharing and a more polar bond.
With only one strongly polar C–Cl bond and three much weaker C–H dipoles that don't offset it, the molecule ends up with an unbalanced, net dipole moment overall.
The electronegativity difference between carbon and hydrogen (about 0.4) is much smaller than between oxygen and hydrogen (about 1.4), making C–H nearly nonpolar by comparison.

Because a double bond includes both a sigma and a pi bond, there's more total electron density being pulled toward the electronegative oxygen, amplifying the charge separation compared to a single C–O bond.

Because the trans arrangement places the two equal C–Cl dipoles pointing opposite each other, they largely cancel, giving the trans isomer a much smaller net dipole than the cis isomer, where the dipoles add together.
H–H connects two identical atoms with zero electronegativity difference, making it the only purely nonpolar bond among these three options.
Bonding actually exists along a continuous spectrum, with nonpolar covalent and ionic bonds as the two extremes and polar covalent bonds occupying the wide middle ground.
Because water is bent (not linear), the two O–H dipoles reinforce rather than cancel each other, summing into a single net molecular dipole pointing toward the electronegative oxygen.
skeletal-structures: Every vertex and both ends are carbons: four internal vertices plus two ends makes six. Counting the segments instead of the carbons is off by one every time.
A line is a bond. The atoms sit at its ends, and if nothing is written there, they are carbons.
Carbon makes four bonds. Two are drawn, so the other two are hydrogens: CH2.
One bond drawn, three left over: CH3. Chain ends are the methyl groups of the molecule.
The notation keeps what reacts. An O-H hydrogen is acidic, hydrogen bonds and is removed by base; a C-H along a chain almost never is.
Six corners, six carbons, two hydrogens on each. Benzene needs three alternating double bonds drawn in, or a circle.
A bare hexagon is the saturated ring. The alternating double bonds, or a circle for the delocalized system, mark benzene.
An oxygen drawn with two bonds has two lone pairs whether anyone drew them or not, and arrow-pushing needs them.
Carbon is the only atom left implied. O, N, S, Cl and the rest are always drawn, and so are their hydrogens.
Two bonds plus two hydrogens is already four. A fifth means something was counted twice, usually the vertex itself.
Four segments means five carbons: pentane. Two CH3 ends and three CH2 vertices gives C5H12.
It hides the uninformative half and keeps the skeleton and the functional groups, which is the whole trade.
Four bonds total, three drawn, one hydrogen left. This is a branch point, a CH.
All four bonds go to other atoms, so there is no room for hydrogen. This is a quaternary carbon.
A zigzag of five segments is six carbons, not four. Both ends are carbons and are easy to miss.
Only the O-H hydrogen. The nine hydrogens on carbon are implied.
It is the reverse: every atom not drawn is a carbon, so anything written out is something else.
A hexagon says 'six carbons joined in a ring' in one stroke, and how it is drawn can carry geometry too.
One carbon per corner of the pentagon: five.
Work it in a fixed order and the hydrogens are subtracted rather than guessed.
Nitrogen has five valence electrons and three bonds here, leaving one lone pair.
The notation hides what does not matter. C-H bonds along a chain are close to inert through most of this course.
The hydrogen count is inferred by subtracting the drawn bonds from four — that is the trade the notation makes.
A hexagon has six corners; a five-segment zigzag has four vertices plus two ends. Both are six.
They say which bonds come toward you and which go away, which is what stereochemistry needs.
The O and its hydrogen are written; the five hydrogens on carbon are implied.
The chlorine takes one of the four bonds. Whatever bonds remain after the drawn ones are hydrogens.
You have to see the implied carbons and the undrawn lone pairs as clearly as the drawn ones.
Six ring carbons; the OH replaces one hydrogen, giving five CH2 groups and one CH-OH.
It is a deliberate asymmetry: the hydrogens left visible are the ones that take part in the chemistry.
resonance: Resonance structures show the same atoms in the same positions — only electron placement (lone pairs/pi bonds) differs.
The actual molecule is a single resonance hybrid — a weighted average of the contributing structures, not an equilibrium between them.
Lower-energy (more stable) resonance structures — full octets, minimized/well-placed formal charges — contribute more to the actual hybrid.
Only electrons move between resonance structures — the atoms themselves never move, so connectivity (which atom is bonded to which) is identical in every resonance structure.
This is a common misconception. The molecule has only one real structure, a hybrid of all the contributing structures; it never actually becomes any single drawn structure.

The negative charge and the C=O double bond can each be placed on any of the three equivalent oxygens, giving three equivalent resonance structures that average to give each C–O bond equal, partial double-bond character.
Delocalizing electrons over more atoms lowers the overall energy of the real hybrid below that of any one localized contributing structure — this is the resonance (delocalization) energy.
Structures with incomplete octets on carbon, or other atoms that normally want 8 electrons, are high in energy and contribute very little to the real hybrid.
Electronegative atoms like oxygen stabilize negative charge better than carbon does, so resonance structures with negative charge on O are usually major contributors.
The adjacent pi bond's electrons shift toward the empty orbital on the cationic carbon, moving the double bond over by one position and relocating the positive charge to the far end.
A resonance structure places the nitrogen lone pair in a pi bond to carbon (with the negative charge moving to oxygen), giving real double-bond character to the C–N bond and restricting its rotation.
Negative charge is better stabilized on the more electronegative oxygen, so the O-centered structure is the major contributor even though both are valid resonance forms.

Two equivalent resonance structures (swapping which oxygen carries the double bond and which carries the negative charge) mean the real structure is a hybrid with both N–O bonds equivalent and of intermediate bond order.
Resonance structures share identical atomic connectivity and total electron count; only the positions of pi electrons and lone pairs differ, which can indeed change individual atoms' formal charges.
The two Kekule structures are equal contributors, so the actual molecule has six equivalent bonds with bond order 1.5, not alternating single and double bonds.
Both directions are valid ways of redistributing electrons between resonance structures, as long as connectivity and total charge are conserved.

In pyrrole the N–H leaves the lone pair in a p orbital that overlaps the ring pi system (delocalized), whereas in pyridine the lone pair occupies an in-plane sp2 orbital perpendicular to the pi system and cannot delocalize.

The two oxygens in a carboxylate are equivalent by symmetry, so the two resonance structures (negative charge/double bond swapped between the two oxygens) contribute equally, giving two identical C–O bond lengths.

Minimizing formal charge and charge separation generally increases a structure's stability and contribution; a neutral, fully-satisfied-octet structure is usually favored over one with separated charges.

Like allylic cations and anions, an allylic radical has resonance structures that place the odd electron on either terminal carbon, so the true structure has partial radical character spread over both ends.
Isomers are distinct, isolable compounds, whereas resonance structures are just different ways of drawing electrons in the one real molecule; you cannot isolate a single resonance structure.

Pushing electrons from the oxygen lone pair into the ring, and then around the ring pi system, generates resonance structures with negative charge at the ortho and para positions, explaining phenoxide's extra stability and its reactivity there.
A complete octet is usually weighted more heavily than minimizing which atom bears a positive charge; an atom with an incomplete octet is a high-energy, minor contributor.

Nitrate has one N=O pi bond (2 electrons) that resonance delocalizes across the three equivalent N–O linkages, plus the overall negative charge; conventionally two pi electrons are shown shifting position among the three equivalent structures.

Greater delocalization spreads charge or electron density over more atoms, lowering the energy of the real structure relative to a localized one — more good resonance structures usually means more stabilization.

A resonance hybrid is one real, single structure; the multiple drawings are just an artificial way of depicting delocalized electron density using the tools of simple bonding diagrams, not a literal equilibrium or blend of separate species.
Resonance structures never move atoms (including hydrogens) — only electrons move. Moving an atom creates a different molecule (often a tautomer), not a resonance structure.
Each ring carbon bears a p orbital that is part of a continuous conjugated system, allowing the lone pair (and thus negative charge) to be distributed by resonance across all five equivalent carbons.
Because the two equivalent resonance structures contribute equally, the real acetate ion has two identical C–O bonds with bond order about 1.5, not one single and one double bond.

Charge-separated resonance structures are generally higher in energy and minor contributors; the neutral structure (with the lone pair still largely on nitrogen in the parent drawing, or no charge separation) is favored, even though the zwitterion correctly predicts the nucleophilic character of the terminal carbon.
curved-arrows: Curved arrows track electron movement — they start where electrons already are (a lone pair or an existing bond).
The arrowhead marks the destination of the moving electron pair — a new bond or a new lone pair.
The arrow starts at the electron source doing the attacking — the base’s lone pair — and points to the proton it is grabbing.
A curved arrow always represents electrons moving, so its tail must start at a source of electron density (a lone pair, a bond, or a negative charge), never at an empty orbital or cation.
Because both electrons of the pi bond move together as a unit, the tail is drawn from the middle of the double bond line, not from either individual atom.
One arrow shows the nucleophile's lone pair attacking the carbon, and a second arrow shows the C–leaving group bond breaking as electrons move onto the leaving group.
When a C–H bond's electrons become a new pi bond (as in E1/E2 elimination), the arrowhead points to the middle of the forming C=C double bond, not at an individual atom.

Radical mechanisms use single-barbed 'fishhook' arrows to show one electron moving, which is a variant of curved-arrow notation — curved arrows (full double-barbed) are used for two-electron (ionic) steps, but electron-movement notation exists for radicals too.

Carbon can never exceed four bonds (an octet at most); forming a new bond to carbon requires that carbon simultaneously break an existing bond (a leaving group departing) unless it already has room, such as being cationic.
A formal negative charge implies an available lone pair at that position, so the arrow tail may start there even without redrawing the dots explicitly.

A bare proton (H+) has no electrons to donate, so an arrow can never start from H+; instead, the arrow starts from the base's lone pair and points to the H, while a separate arrow shows the H–X bond breaking.
Multiple arrows within one mechanism arrow-pushing 'step' (one structure to the next) represent bond-breaking and bond-forming events happening at the same time, i.e., concertedly.

As in any nucleophilic substitution, one arrow shows the nucleophile (even if intramolecular) attacking, and a second shows the leaving group departing, regardless of whether the nucleophile is in the same molecule.
Placing the tail on the bond line itself (rather than on an atom's lone pair) shows that the whole bonding pair associated with that bond is the electron source.
The pi electrons act as the nucleophile and are shown attacking the electrophilic proton; the arrowhead lands on the H atom that is being bonded.

Each arrow must independently originate from a genuine source of electrons (the nucleophile's lone pair, or the breaking bond) and terminate at a genuine electron sink; you cannot draw one continuous arrow that skips the reacting carbon.
The electrons of the adjacent C–H bond shift to fill the empty orbital on the cationic carbon, so the tail starts on that C–H sigma bond and the head points to the cationic carbon.

Since formal charge tracks an atom's electron count relative to its neutral state, moving electrons away from an atom (tail) raises its formal charge while electrons arriving (head) lower the formal charge at the destination.

E2 is a single concerted step: base removes the beta-hydrogen, those electrons form the new pi bond, and simultaneously the leaving group departs with the sigma bond electrons — three synchronized arrows.

Curved arrows are a precise bookkeeping tool: tails mark the electrons' starting location and heads mark their ending location, corresponding exactly to the bonding changes between the starting and product structures.
The amine's lone pair is the base's electron source (tail), and it forms a new bond to the acidic proton (head); a second arrow would then show the O–H bond breaking, with electrons going to oxygen.

An arrowhead marks the destination of electron density — either a new bond (so it points between two specific atoms) or a new lone pair (so it points at a specific atom) — never an arbitrary empty location.

Protonating an alkene needs only one arrow (the pi bond attacking H+) because the resulting carbocation, while electron-deficient, doesn't violate any rule since carbocations legitimately have fewer than 8 electrons around carbon.

If two new bonds or lone pairs are being added to one atom in the same step without anything leaving, that atom would exceed its normal valence (e.g., carbon exceeding four bonds), which is why such steps require a compensating departure.

The polarized C–Mg bond's electrons attack the electrophilic carbonyl carbon (first arrow), and the pi electrons of C=O simultaneously shift onto oxygen to avoid carbon exceeding four bonds (second arrow), generating an alkoxide.

While less common in introductory reactions than lone pairs or pi bonds, C–C sigma bonds can act as electron sources in rearrangements (such as carbocation rearrangements where an alkyl group shifts), so this is valid.
Curved arrows track the flow of electron density, and electrons always flow from a source with available density toward a site that can accept it (an electrophile), never the reverse.

Under acid catalysis, the mechanism usually begins with protonation of the carbonyl oxygen (its lone pair attacks H+), which increases the electrophilicity of the carbonyl carbon before the alcohol attacks.
Every arrow tail needs a genuine electron source at that exact location — a lone pair, a bond, or charge implying available electrons; an atom with none of these cannot be a valid tail location.

The base supplies the electrons that form the new bond to the proton, so the arrow tail sits on the base's lone pair and the head points at the hydrogen; a separate arrow then shows the O–H bond breaking toward oxygen.
nucleophiles: Nucleophiles ("nucleus-loving") are electron-rich species that donate an electron pair to form a new bond.
Larger, more polarizable atoms (like I⁻ vs F⁻) donate electron density more easily, making them better nucleophiles especially in aprotic solvents.
The extra negative charge makes the lone pairs more available/reactive, generally making anions better nucleophiles than their neutral conjugate acids.
A bare proton has no electrons to donate and is instead a classic electrophile; true nucleophiles must have a lone pair, negative charge, or pi bond available to donate.

Basicity is thermodynamic (affinity for a proton at equilibrium), while nucleophilicity is kinetic (rate of attack on an electrophilic carbon); steric bulk and solvent can make the two rankings diverge, as with bulky bases that are poor nucleophiles.

Larger, more polarizable atoms have a more diffuse, easily distorted electron cloud that can reach out and begin bond formation with an electrophile more effectively, increasing nucleophilicity down a group.

Protic solvents hydrogen-bond strongly to small, localized-charge anions like F-, caging it and lowering its reactivity; in aprotic solvents with no hydrogen bonding, F- is not solvated as heavily and its small size/high charge density can make it more nucleophilic than I-.

In protic solvents, strong solvation (hydrogen bonding) cripples small, charge-dense nucleophiles like F-; the large, weakly solvated, highly polarizable I- is freest to attack and is the best nucleophile.

Steric bulk around the nucleophilic atom hinders its ability to approach and bond with an electrophilic carbon in an SN2-type attack, reducing nucleophilicity even when basicity (proton affinity) remains high.

Sulfur is larger and more polarizable than oxygen, so its lone pairs can more easily reach out and form a new bond, even though its lone pairs are held less tightly (making it a weaker base) than oxygen's.
Neutral species with an available lone pair (like NH3, H2O, or amines) are common, effective nucleophiles; a negative charge increases nucleophilicity but is not required.

A localized, non-resonance-stabilized alkoxide is a stronger nucleophile than a neutral amine, and the resonance-stabilized, delocalized carboxylate is the weakest of the three because its negative charge is spread out and less available.
The electron density of a pi bond is available to attack an electrophile (as in addition of HBr to an alkene), making alkenes legitimate, if relatively weak, nucleophiles.
Higher electronegativity means an atom holds its electrons more tightly, making it less willing to donate them to an electrophile, which generally decreases (not increases) nucleophilicity.

When charge is shared across several atoms via resonance, less electron density sits at any one reactive site, so the species is both more stable (weaker base/nucleophile) and slower to attack an electrophile.

Removing a proton from water to give hydroxide increases the electron density around oxygen without adding extra nuclear charge to hold it, making the anion considerably more reactive as a nucleophile (and stronger base).

Good nucleophiles and good leaving groups tend to have opposite characteristics (strong nucleophiles are typically poor leaving groups, like amines or alkoxides, and vice versa, like halides or sulfonates), so this statement is false in general.

Although formal charge considerations might suggest nitrogen, the carbon atom of cyanide is the kinetically preferred nucleophilic site in most SN2-type reactions due to its orbital characteristics and accessibility.
More polar protic solvents solvate small, charge-dense anions even more strongly via hydrogen bonding, further shielding their electron density and reducing their ability to attack an electrophile.

An sp3 lone pair has less s-character than an sp2 lone pair, so it sits farther from the nucleus and is held less tightly, making it somewhat more available to donate; this fits pyridine's sp2 nitrogen being a weaker nucleophile and base than a typical sp3 trialkylamine.

Because carbon is not very electronegative, a negative charge on carbon is poorly stabilized and very reactive, making carbanions some of the strongest nucleophiles (and bases) encountered in introductory organic chemistry.

Ambident nucleophiles (like enolates, which can react through carbon or oxygen, or cyanide through carbon or nitrogen) have more than one potential reactive atom, and which one reacts can depend on conditions.

Moving right across a period, atoms hold electron density more tightly due to increasing electronegativity, so their lone pairs are less available to donate, generally reducing both basicity and nucleophilicity.

Because an SN2 nucleophile must approach a tetrahedral, often crowded carbon from a specific backside angle, bulky substituents on the nucleophile or substrate create steric clashes that aren't nearly as significant when a small, exposed proton is simply being removed by a base.
Azide is a small, negatively charged, relatively unhindered nucleophile commonly used in SN2 substitutions to introduce a nitrogen functional group, later reducible to an amine.
Polar aprotic solvents cannot hydrogen-bond to and cage anionic nucleophiles the way protic solvents do, leaving the nucleophile's electron density more exposed and reactive.

A negative charge raises the electron density on the donor atom, so the anion of a conjugate pair is always the better nucleophile. Going the other way is worse than it looks: protonating an amine consumes the lone pair entirely, so the ammonium ion is not a weak nucleophile but no nucleophile at all.

In typical introductory treatments, additional alkyl groups are electron-donating and increase electron density on nitrogen, generally increasing nucleophilicity/basicity unless steric bulk becomes severe (as with very hindered tertiary amines), which intro courses usually simplify away.

Hydride attacks the electron-poor carbonyl carbon, with its electron pair forming a new C–H bond while the C=O pi electrons shift onto oxygen, ultimately giving an alkoxide (and after protonation, an alcohol).

Neutral nucleophiles like water are weaker than their anionic counterparts but are still perfectly capable nucleophiles, especially toward highly reactive electrophiles such as carbocations formed in SN1 pathways.
electrophiles: Electrophiles ("electron-loving") are electron-poor and accept an electron pair to form a new bond.
Oxygen’s electronegativity polarizes the C=O bond, giving carbon a δ+ that nucleophiles attack.
Hydroxide is electron-rich (a nucleophile/base), not electron-poor — it seeks to donate electrons, not accept them.
Hydroxide is electron-rich and negatively charged, making it a nucleophile/base rather than an electrophile; electrophiles are electron-poor and seek electron density.

Many electrophiles are neutral but electron-poor (such as the carbon of a carbonyl group, or boron in BF3), so a full positive charge is not required, only a deficiency of electron density at the reactive atom.

The electronegative oxygen pulls electron density from the ring carbons (inducing partial positive charge), and the strained three-membered ring geometry adds extra driving force for nucleophiles to open the ring at carbon.

BF3's boron has an empty p orbital and no octet, making it a very strong electrophile (Lewis acid); CH3Cl's carbon is moderately electrophilic due to the polar C–Cl bond; CH4 has no polarized bonds and is essentially non-electrophilic.

Oxygen's high electronegativity polarizes the C=O bond, leaving carbon electron-deficient (δ+) and well-suited to accept an incoming nucleophile's electron pair, with the pi electrons shifting onto oxygen.

Electron-withdrawing groups intensify the positive character at the carbonyl carbon by further depleting its electron density, which is why acid chlorides and anhydrides are more electrophilic (more reactive to nucleophiles) than simple ketones or esters.
Carbocations are highly electron-deficient, with an empty p orbital and a full positive charge on carbon, making them extremely reactive toward any available nucleophile or pi bond.
The polar C–Br bond leaves carbon partially positive (δ+), and because Br- can leave as a stable anion, a nucleophile can attack that carbon while the C–Br bond breaks, as in SN1/SN2 reactions.

As the alkene's pi electrons approach Br2, they induce a dipole in the Br–Br bond, making one bromine electrophilic; the alkene attacks it, displacing bromide and forming a bromonium ion intermediate.

Aluminum in AlCl3 has only six electrons around it (no octet), giving it a strongly electron-accepting empty orbital, which is the hallmark of a Lewis acid/electrophile used to activate other electrophiles in reactions like Friedel-Crafts.

Protonating the oxygen gives it a formal positive charge, which pulls even more electron density away from the attached carbon through the sigma bond, increasing that carbon's electrophilicity and making it far more reactive to nucleophilic attack or departure as a leaving group.

Chlorine is a strong electron-withdrawing group and a poor electron donor by resonance, leaving the acid chloride's carbonyl carbon the most electron-poor and electrophilic; amides are the least electrophilic because nitrogen donates its lone pair into the carbonyl most effectively, reducing electrophilicity.

The negative charge and resonance delocalization in a carboxylate actually increase electron density at the carbonyl carbon (compared to a neutral ester or acid), making it a very poor electrophile and resistant to nucleophilic attack.

Without a polarized bond, an empty orbital, or a good leaving group, there is no electron-poor site available, so simple alkanes are essentially unreactive toward nucleophiles under standard conditions.

Once the leaving group departs in the first (rate-determining) step, a planar carbocation intermediate forms with an empty p orbital, and this highly electrophilic cation is what the nucleophile subsequently attacks.

Alkyl groups are weakly electron-donating and bulky; a ketone has two of them stabilizing and shielding the carbonyl carbon, while an aldehyde's single alkyl group (plus a small hydrogen) leaves it more electrophilic and more accessible to nucleophiles.
In electrophilic aromatic substitution, a Lewis acid (like FeBr3) helps generate a highly electrophilic species (such as Br+) that the electron-rich aromatic ring then attacks as the nucleophile.

Just as nucleophile strength affects rate, a more electron-deficient and accessible electrophile is attacked more readily and rapidly by a given nucleophile, since there is a greater driving force for electron transfer.
A bare proton has zero electrons and a full positive charge, making it an extremely strong and simple electrophile that reacts instantly with essentially any available lone pair or pi bond.

A resonance structure of an enone shows the C=C pi electrons shifting all the way to the very electronegative oxygen, leaving a positive charge on the beta carbon; this explains why nucleophiles can add either directly to the carbonyl carbon or to this more remote beta carbon (conjugate addition).

The two electronegative oxygens withdraw significant electron density from the central carbon, making it quite electrophilic; Grignard reagents readily attack this carbon to eventually form a carboxylic acid after workup.

Fluorines are highly electronegative and can withdraw electron density (inductively) even while donating some back by resonance in certain cases, but generally a boron center surrounded by electron-withdrawing groups maintains strong electrophilic (Lewis acidic) character, accepting electron pairs readily.
The acidic C–H proton is the electrophilic site being attacked by the base's lone pair; the carbon framework itself is not what is directly attacked in this proton-transfer step.

Like halides, the oxygen in a sulfonate ester polarizes the attached carbon (making it electrophilic), and the resulting sulfonate anion is exceptionally stable (weak base) due to extensive resonance and charge delocalization, making it depart easily as a leaving group.

Alkyl groups are weak electron donors (by induction/hyperconjugation) and also physically block approach, so more substitution at a potentially electrophilic carbon generally reduces how strongly and how accessibly electrophilic it is (this is part of why more substituted carbonyls are less reactive toward nucleophiles).

Alkyl groups stabilize an adjacent positive charge through hyperconjugation and induction, so tertiary carbocations are more stable and form more readily than primary ones, even though all carbocations remain strong electrophiles once formed.

Even though the C–I bond is only modestly polarized, the weak, long C–I bond breaks easily and iodide is a very stable, weakly basic leaving group, so the overall reaction is fast even if carbon itself is not the most electron-poor among the halomethanes.
leaving-groups: Good leaving groups are stable as the departed anion/molecule — i.e., weak bases, since weak bases are comfortable holding the extra electron density.
Iodide is a large, very weak base — very stable once it leaves — making it an excellent leaving group, unlike OH⁻, NH₂⁻, or CH₃⁻ which are strong bases.
Among the halide ions, F⁻ is the strongest base (least electronegative-stabilized charge relative to its small size/high charge density), so it’s the worst leaving group of the group.
Good leaving groups are stable, weak bases, which are exactly the conjugate bases of strong acids (like HI, HBr, or TsOH); weak bases hold their extra electron pair loosely and leave readily.

Hydroxide is a strong base (conjugate base of water, a weak acid), so it is a poor leaving group; alcohols typically need to be protonated (forming water as the leaving group) or converted to a sulfonate/halide before substitution proceeds well.

Leaving group ability tracks with anion stability (weak basicity); I- is the weakest base of the three halides and the most stable once it leaves, making it the best leaving group, followed by Br- then Cl-.

F- is a much stronger base than the other halide ions because its small size concentrates negative charge, making the C–F bond strong and fluoride reluctant to depart with the electron pair, unlike the larger, more stable, weaker-base halide ions.

The negative charge on a sulfonate leaving group is delocalized over multiple oxygens by resonance (and stabilized further by the electron-withdrawing sulfonyl group), making it a very weak base and thus an excellent, stable leaving group.
NH2- is the conjugate base of ammonia, an extremely weak acid, making amide ion an extremely strong base that holds on tightly to its electrons and essentially never leaves under normal conditions.

Once protonated, the group that leaves is neutral water rather than negatively charged hydroxide; water is a much weaker base (conjugate base of the strong acid H3O+) and leaves far more easily, which is why acid catalysis activates alcohols for substitution/elimination.

A carbanion like CH3- is an extraordinarily strong base (conjugate base of methane, an exceedingly weak acid) and essentially never acts as a leaving group under normal conditions, unlike halides or neutral water.

Delocalizing the negative charge over several atoms lowers the energy of the anion, making it more stable (a weaker base) and thus more willing to depart, which is exactly why sulfonate esters are popular synthetic leaving groups.

As a nucleophile attacks a ring carbon, the strained C–O bond breaks and the oxygen (now bearing the electron pair) becomes an alkoxide leaving group still attached elsewhere in the molecule, relieving ring strain.

Base strength measures how strongly a species wants to grab and hold a proton (or, analogously, electron density); weak bases are inherently stable on their own and 'happy' to leave with the bonding electron pair, which is the core reason leaving group ability and base strength are inversely related.
Acetic acid (pKa ≈ 4.8) is a much stronger acid than ethanol (pKa ≈ 16), meaning acetate is a much weaker base than ethoxide and therefore a considerably better leaving group.

Because the leaving group departs with the bonding electrons, its ability to stabilize that extra electron density (i.e., be a weak, stable base) directly controls how readily ionization occurs and therefore the rate of SN1/E1 reactions.

Sulfonate esters are prepared under mild, non-acidic conditions and then provide a highly stabilized, weak-base leaving group, giving chemists a practical alternative to strongly acidic activation of alcohols.

E1 is a two-step (stepwise) mechanism: the leaving group departs first to form a carbocation intermediate, and only afterward does a base remove a proton to form the alkene; this differs from E2, where both events are concerted.

Tosylate's negative charge is spread over three oxygens and stabilized further by the adjacent aromatic sulfonyl group, making it one of the best common leaving groups, generally outperforming simple halides.

A simple amide anion (R-NH-) would be much too strong a base to leave; however, once protonated so the leaving species is neutral (or the nitrogen already bears a positive charge, as in some quaternary ammonium salts), the departing amine becomes weak-base-like and feasible as a leaving group.

Since leaving groups are conjugate bases, the pKa of their conjugate acid directly reflects base strength: a low pKa (strong acid) means a weak, stable conjugate base, and therefore a good leaving group.

A conjugate acid pKa of -7 corresponds to an extremely strong acid (such as HI), meaning its conjugate base is extremely weak and stable — exactly the profile of an excellent leaving group, far better than one with a conjugate acid pKa of 9.

HCN is only a moderately weak acid (pKa around 9), making cyanide a fairly strong base relative to halides or sulfonates, so it does not readily depart as a leaving group under typical substitution conditions.

Because strong bases/nucleophiles and good leaving groups are generally opposite ends of the same stability spectrum, a reactive carbanion (strong base) is a very poor leaving group — it simply does not want to depart and take the electron pair in an already-stable low-energy form elsewhere.

Protonation shifts the leaving species from hydroxide (conjugate base of water, pKa ≈ 15.7, a fairly strong base) to water itself (conjugate base of H3O+, pKa ≈ -1.7, a very weak base), dramatically improving its willingness to leave.

Leaving group ability is governed overwhelmingly by stability of the resulting anion (base strength/pKa of the conjugate acid), not primarily by steric bulk; steric effects matter more for the nucleophile's approach than for how readily a group departs.

Like sulfonates and carboxylates, phosphate leaving groups spread their negative charge over several oxygen atoms via resonance, lowering their basicity and making them effective leaving groups despite the formal negative charge, which is central to many biochemical substitution reactions.

Tosylate and iodide are both excellent, weak-base leaving groups (conjugate bases of strong acids), while hydroxide is a comparatively strong base and a poor leaving group, so the order is OTs- > I- >> OH-.

The three highly electronegative fluorine atoms further withdraw electron density and help delocalize/stabilize the negative charge on the departing sulfonate oxygen, making triflate an exceptionally weak base and outstanding leaving group, even better than a simple tosylate.

Since SN1 rate depends on how readily the substrate ionizes, a poor leaving group (strong base, high-energy anion) makes that ionization step slow or unfavorable, often requiring the substrate to be activated first (e.g., protonation or conversion to a sulfonate) before substitution can proceed.
electron-rich-poor: Electron-rich atoms have extra electron density to donate, making them nucleophilic.
The electronegativity difference polarizes the pi bond, making O δ− (electron-rich) and C δ+ (electron-poor).
Carbon is more electronegative than magnesium, so the bonding electrons sit closer to carbon, making it electron-rich (and strongly nucleophilic/basic).
Electron-poor atoms lack sufficient electron density and therefore seek it out from an electron-rich partner, which is exactly the defining behavior of an electrophile.

Electronegative substituents pull electron density away from the attached carbon through the polar sigma bond (an inductive effect), leaving that carbon partially positive (δ+) relative to one surrounded only by similarly electronegative C and H.

Magnesium is a much less electronegative (more electropositive) element than carbon, so the bonding electrons sit closer to carbon, making the carbon electron-rich (carbanion-like) and strongly nucleophilic/basic.

The resonance structure placing the negative charge on oxygen is the larger contributor to the hybrid, since oxygen is far better suited to stabilize a negative charge than carbon is — making the oxygen the more electron-rich site overall.

Electron-donating substituents push additional electron density into the aromatic ring (by resonance and/or induction), increasing the ring's overall nucleophilicity and accelerating electrophilic aromatic substitution.

The halogen is more electronegative than hydrogen, pulling bonding electron density toward itself and leaving hydrogen partially positive (δ+), which is why H–X compounds act as proton (acid) sources.

The nitro group is strongly electron-withdrawing (both by induction and resonance, since nitrogen is positively charged with electronegative oxygens), making an attached ring more electron-poor, not electron-rich.

Alkyl groups are weak electron donors (through hyperconjugation with adjacent C–H/C–C bonds and simple induction), so each additional alkyl substituent on a double bond increases the electron density of the pi bond, making the alkene a better nucleophile.

Fluorine's very high electronegativity creates a strongly polarized C–F bond, pulling substantial electron density away from carbon, more so than the much less electronegative iodine does in a C–I bond, even though the C–I bond is actually weaker and breaks more easily.

A carbanion carries a full negative charge and a lone pair (electron-rich, nucleophilic), while a carbocation has an empty orbital and a full positive charge (electron-poor, electrophilic) — they sit at opposite ends of the electron-density spectrum.

A resonance structure of the enol places a lone pair from oxygen into the pi system, shifting electron density to the terminal (alpha) carbon and giving it significant nucleophilic, electron-rich character, which is why enols react with electrophiles at that carbon.

Conjugation of the nitrogen lone pair with the carbonyl pi system pulls electron density away from nitrogen toward the electronegative oxygen, leaving the amide nitrogen considerably less electron-rich than an isolated amine nitrogen.

The nitrogen of a nitrile carries a lone pair in an sp orbital and, despite nitrogen's electronegativity pulling some density toward it within the triple bond, this lone pair is the most electron-rich, available site for interacting with electrophiles or protons.

The three highly electronegative fluorines in a CF3 group inductively withdraw electron density through the sigma bond network, making the attached carbon significantly more electron-poor (more δ+) than if it were bonded to hydrogens instead.

Boron's electronegativity is lower than carbon's, so the shared electrons in a C–B bond sit closer to carbon, making that carbon somewhat electron-rich, similar to the polarization seen in Grignard C–Mg bonds though less pronounced.

Inductive effects act through sigma bonds and fall off quickly with distance, so a halogen's electron-withdrawing influence is strongest on the carbon it's directly attached to and becomes much weaker two or three carbons away.

Adding a full positive charge directly onto the already electronegative oxygen dramatically increases its pull on the shared electrons, making the attached carbon even more electron-deficient and far more reactive to nucleophilic attack.

The negatively charged oxygen of an enolate strongly donates its extra electron density through resonance into the adjacent carbon, making the enolate's nucleophilic carbon considerably more electron-rich (and thus more reactive) than a simple, unactivated alkene carbon.

Although oxygen holds its own electrons more tightly (higher electronegativity, stronger base), sulfur's larger, more polarizable, more loosely held electron cloud makes it more willing to donate electron density in bond-forming reactions, so it behaves as more nucleophilic/electron-rich in a reactivity sense.

The carbon directly bonded to the electronegative chlorine experiences the strongest inductive pull of electron density, making it the most electron-poor carbon in the molecule; the effect diminishes sharply at the next carbon over.

One of the hydroxyl oxygen's lone pairs conjugates with the carbonyl pi system, pulling electron density toward the carbonyl oxygen; this depletion of electron density on the OH oxygen is part of why the O–H bond is more acidic (and the oxygen less basic) than in a simple alcohol.

Nitrogen's higher electronegativity polarizes the triple bond, leaving the nitrile carbon partially positive and electrophilic, which is why Grignard and organolithium reagents can add to nitriles to eventually form ketones after hydrolysis.
