Inductive (sigma-bond) electron withdrawal falls off rapidly with each bond, so while the alpha carbon feels the halogen's pull strongly, the beta carbon experiences only a faint residual effect.

Just as an enolate's oxygen lone pair activates the alpha carbon through resonance, an enamine's nitrogen lone pair conjugates through the C=C pi system to make the beta carbon unusually electron-rich and nucleophilic, a key feature exploited in many carbon-carbon bond-forming reactions.

A classic example is a halogen substituent on an aromatic ring: it withdraws electron density inductively (making the ring somewhat electron-poor overall) while donating electron density by resonance at the ortho/para positions (making those specific positions more electron-rich), so the two effects can genuinely pull in opposite directions.

An s orbital keeps electron density closer to the nucleus than a p orbital does, and an sp carbon is one third s against one quarter for sp3. That is why an sp carbon behaves as the most electronegative of the three, and why a terminal alkyne C-H at pKa 25 is far more acidic than an alkane C-H at 50.

Although bromine formally bears the positive charge in the strained three-membered bromonium ring, the nucleophile actually attacks one of the electrophilic ring carbons from the backside, displacing bromine and opening the ring; formal charge location does not always mark the exact site of nucleophilic attack.
naming-parent-chain: Prefix (what is hanging off it), root (how long the parent chain is), suffix (the main functional group). In 2-methylbutan-1-ol that is 2-methyl, but, and -1-ol.
meth 1, eth 2, prop 3, but 4, pent 5, hex 6, hept 7, oct 8, non 9, dec 10. The first four are historical; the rest are Greek and Latin numbers.
Seven is hept. 'Sept' is Latin but is not the root organic chemistry uses.
The longest unbroken path of carbons, turning as many corners as it needs to. It is very often not the row lying across the page.
It reads backwards, but a name should describe as much of the molecule as possible with locants rather than burying it inside a complex branch name.
Always one fewer than the number of carbons. Counting the lines and calling it pentane is the standard off-by-one error.
You compare the two possible numberings and take the one giving the lowest locants, decided at the first point of difference.
Compare term by term and stop where they differ: both open at 2, then 3 beats 5. Totals are not what the rule uses, even when they agree with it.
A decane substituted at {2,7,8} versus {3,4,9} is decided one way by first point of difference and the other way by totals. The first is correct.
Six carbons gives hex, no functional group gives -ane, and 3 beats 4 so number from the left.
Hyphens between numbers and letters, commas between numbers: 2,3-dimethylpentane.
Commas between numbers, hyphens between a number and a letter. The punctuation carries meaning rather than decorating it.
No space anywhere inside the name of a single compound, except in names like 'acetic acid' where the second word names a class.
Modern IUPAC puts the locant immediately before the part of the name it refers to. Older texts write 2-butene, so read both and write the first.
It is the default suffix, and the rest of nomenclature is about replacing it with something that names a functional group.
Tracing from one end of the row through the middle carbon and out along the ethyl gives six continuous carbons, which beats the five drawn horizontally.
The parent is the six-carbon path, and what is left over is a single carbon: a methyl at C3.
A chain is a path. You may turn corners freely, but you may not revisit a carbon or jump a gap.
The root is purely the count of carbons in the parent chain: meth through dec.
Pick the wrong parent and the numbering, the locants and the substituent names that follow are all wrong too.
Ten is dec, as in decane. 'Deca' is the multiplying prefix, not the chain root.
When chains tie on length, the one carrying more substituents is the parent.
hept means seven. The -ane says it is saturated with no functional group.
Structures are drawn for the convenience of whoever drew them, and the longest path very often turns a corner.
Find the longest continuous carbon chain. Everything else in the name is positioned relative to it.
That is the point of a systematic name: a name you have never seen still tells you exactly what to draw.
prop is the three-carbon root, so propane is CH3CH2CH3.
Comma between the two numbers, hyphen between the numbers and the word, and no space anywhere.
A tie on length is broken by taking the chain with more substituents attached, so the name is never ambiguous.
hex means six. The methyl at C3 is a substituent and is not part of the parent.
naming-substituents: One carbon is methyl, two ethyl, three propyl. The -yl says the fragment is attached to something rather than standing alone.
Isopropyl, systematically propan-2-yl, attaches at C2 of a three-carbon fragment. Propyl attaches at an end.
It attaches through a carbon bearing three methyls. Almost nobody says it aloud, but you should be able to decode it.
Isobutyl is a three-carbon chain with a methyl on C2, attached at the end of that chain.
fluoro, chloro, bromo, iodo. They never become a suffix and never outrank anything.
An ether has no suffix of its own in substitutive nomenclature; it is always an alkoxy substituent on something else.
di- two, tri- three, tetra- four, penta- five. Each substituent still keeps its own locant.
di- promises two locants and only one is supplied, so the reader cannot tell where the second methyl went. It should be 2,2-dimethylpentane.
The number is written twice. That repetition is not redundant — it is the only thing stating where the second methyl is.
Multiplying prefixes di-, tri-, tetra- are ignored, as are the italic sec- and tert-. iso, neo and cyclo are counted.
Ignore the multiplying prefix and alphabetize on methyl, so it files under m.
iso is joined to the word and counts as part of the name, so isopropyl files under i — unlike di- or tert-.
The italic hyphenated tert- is ignored, so it files under b. The typography is the tell: hyphenated italic prefixes are skipped.
Compare ethyl with methyl, since di- is ignored. e comes before m.
iso counts, so isopropyl files under i. e comes before i, so ethyl is cited first.
Only when both directions give an identical locant set. Otherwise the structure decides the numbering and the alphabet only orders the words.
First number for lowest locants, then break an exact tie alphabetically if one exists, then write the substituents in alphabetical order.
Alphabetical order sets the order of words: chloro, ethyl, methyl. The locants ending up out of numerical order is normal.
Parentheses tell the reader that the branch's own number counts along the branch, not along the parent chain.
The attaching carbon is C1 of the substituent, always.
Numbered from the attachment point, the methyl sits on C2. This group is also called isobutyl.
A complex substituent files under the first letter of its complete name, which here is m.
nitro (-NO2), chloro and methoxy are all standard prefixes. 'Hydro' is not used this way for a substituent.
Methane is a molecule; methyl is a piece of one. The -yl marks the fragment as attached.
sec-Butyl is butan-2-yl. C1 of a four-chain is butyl; a carbon with three methyls is tert-butyl.
Counting the locants against the multiplying prefix is the fastest self-check in nomenclature.
Alphabetical, whatever their locants. So 4-ethyl-2-methylhexane, with ethyl first despite its higher number.
On a genuine tie the alphabetically first substituent takes the lowest available locant, and ethyl beats methyl.
Ignore di-, tri-, tetra- and the italic sec-, tert-. Do not ignore iso, neo or cyclo.
A halogen is a prefix wherever it sits, never a suffix, and never outranks anything. Its only job is to collect a locant.
naming-functional-groups: Exactly one is the principal characteristic group and takes the suffix. Every other functional group is demoted to a prefix.
acid > ester > amide > nitrile > aldehyde > ketone > alcohol > amine > alkene/alkyne.
Ethers, halides and nitro groups are always prefixes. An ether is cited as alkoxy- wherever it appears.
A demoted alcohol becomes hydroxy-. Nothing about the oxygen changed; its rank did.
The IUPAC prefix is oxo-, not keto-. A compound chemists call a keto acid has no mention of a ketone in its systematic name.
And its carbon is necessarily C1, so no locant is written: ethanoic acid needs no number.
An aldehyde carbon sits at the end of a chain, so it is always C1 and the locant is not written: butanal.
Propan-2-one is the systematic name for acetone. A ketone carbon is interior, so it does need a locant.
-amine. An amide, which outranks it, takes -amide.
Aldehyde is above ketone. That pair is a genuine oxidation difference: an aldehyde carbon is at +1 and a ketone carbon at 0.
All four carbons sit at +3. The order within that block is a convention, though it usefully runs in the same direction as their reactivity.
The principal group claims the low number before multiple bonds or substituents are considered at all.
The alcohol outranks the methyl and takes the 2; the methyl is left with the 5. Giving the low number to the substituent out of habit is the commonest error here.
Priority beats length. 'Longest chain' was only ever the rule for a molecule with nothing to outrank it.
The functional carbon is necessarily at the end of a chain. Writing butan-1-al is redundant for the same reason.
When the suffix begins with a vowel the parent's final e is dropped. With a consonant it stays: propanenitrile.
The suffix begins with a consonant, so the e is kept.
The acid takes the suffix and fixes C1; the ketone is demoted to oxo-; prefixes are cited alphabetically, bromo before oxo.
Acetone is a retained common name. Its systematic name can be read back into a structure; 'acetone' cannot.
Two carbons, so eth. Methanoic acid is formic acid.
One carbon plus the aldehyde suffix. Acetaldehyde is ethanal.
Hydroxybenzene is essentially never used. Aniline and toluene are similar cases.
carboxy- is a demoted acid, cyano- a demoted nitrile, and oxo- a demoted ketone or aldehyde.
A demoted amide takes carbamoyl-, and a demoted amine takes amino-.
It is chosen by the fixed priority order, not by size, position or interest.
Alkenes and alkynes rank below every group in the list, so a functional group always claims the lower locant.
An amine is near the bottom of the list and still wins, because an ether is not on the list at all.
It joins the alkyls and halogens in the prefix, often under a different name: -ol becomes hydroxy-.
Methyl ethanoate, for instance. The alkyl group from the alcohol half is cited as a separate word.
The top of the list is close to the reactivity ladder in the Carboxylic Acids chapter: an acid converts to an ester, an ester to an amide, never back up.
naming-rings-unsaturation: cyclo- in front of the root for the number of ring carbons.
Substituent forms take -yl, as with chains: cyclopentyl, cyclopropyl.
You choose both the starting carbon and the direction, subject to the same priority rules as a chain.
With only one substituent no locant is written, because there is nowhere else it could be.
With no higher-priority group present, the parent is whichever has more carbons. Eight beats six, so the ring becomes a cyclohexyl substituent.
Six beats one, so the ring is the parent: methylcyclohexane.
Benzyl is a different group — phenyl plus a CH2, so PhCH2-. Confusing them changes the molecule by a carbon.
PhCH2-. Phenyl is the bare ring, C6H5-.
-ene for a double bond, -yne for a triple bond.
-yne. Both need a locant, cited as the lower-numbered of the two carbons.
Only the first of the pair is cited; the reader infers the bond runs to the next carbon. But-1-ene is a different compound.
By convention the locant is the lower-numbered of the two carbons the bond joins.
-diene takes two locants, one for each double bond.
The alcohol outranks the double bond and claims the lower locant, even though it means the double bond gets a 5 rather than a 1.
With a genuine choice of direction, the double bond is given the lower locant.
Both appear, the multiple bond first: hex-5-en-1-ol.
ortho is 1,2. meta is 1,3 and para is 1,4.
Straight across a six-membered ring is three bonds away, the 1,4 relationship.
meta is 1,3 — one carbon between them.
The whole question of directing effects is phrased in it: a substituent is an ortho, para director or a meta director.
The two carbons cannot rotate, so the methyls are fixed either on the same side or on opposite sides.
cis/trans works informally when each alkene carbon has one hydrogen. E/Z uses the same priority rules that assign R and S.
The bond takes the lowest possible locants before substituents are considered.
The double bond takes C1 and C2, then you choose the direction giving the methyl the lower number: 3 rather than 6.
Three carbons, so prop: cyclopropane.
The parent must contain the principal characteristic group, overriding the more-carbons rule.
You start at a substituted carbon and go round the way that gives the lowest locants.
Both methyl-bearing carbons give the locant set {1,3}, so both are equally correct.
Five ring carbons and no multiple bond.
The double bond is understood to start at C1 in a cyclohexene, so the locant is commonly omitted in practice.
bronsted: Brønsted-Lowry acids are proton donors; bases are proton acceptors.
After losing H⁺, the acid becomes its conjugate base (one less proton, one more negative/less positive charge).
A species that can donate or accept a proton depending on the reaction partner is called amphoteric (or amphiprotic).
NH3 accepts a proton from water to form NH4+, making it the Bronsted base while water acts as the acid.
This is the core definition of Bronsted-Lowry theory: the acid donates H+ and the base accepts it.
Accepting H+ turns a base into its conjugate acid, which now carries one more proton.
HCl donates a proton to water, forming H3O+ and Cl-, the defining Bronsted-Lowry acid behavior.
Any species with a removable proton, such as HCl or an alkyne C-H, can act as a Bronsted acid; oxygen is not required.
Acetic acid donates a proton to ammonia, so it is the proton donor (acid) in this transfer.
Amphoteric species like water or bicarbonate can donate a proton to a stronger base or accept one from a stronger acid.
HSO4- can donate its remaining proton to become SO4^2- (acid) or accept a proton to become H2SO4 (base), making it amphoteric.
The conjugate base of HCl is Cl-, formed by loss of H+; OH- is not related to HCl by a single proton loss.
Bicarbonate accepts the proton from the carboxylic acid, forming carbonic acid (which decomposes to CO2 and water), acting as a Bronsted base.
F- is the conjugate base of the weakest acid (HF) among the hydrohalic acids, making it the strongest base of the group, though still weak in water.
Proton transfer reactions occur in many settings, such as HCl gas reacting directly with NH3 gas to form solid NH4Cl smoke.
Even a weak acid like acetic acid has a small tendency to accept a proton from another acetic acid molecule, forming its protonated conjugate acid form.
The sp-hybridized C-H of a terminal alkyne is weakly acidic (pKa about 25) and can be deprotonated by a sufficiently strong base like amide ion.
A Bronsted acid donates a proton, and it is really the proton itself that behaves as the electron-pair acceptor; the parent species (like HCl) is not typically classified as a Lewis acid.
Any X-H bond can formally act as a Bronsted acid, but methane's conjugate base (CH3-) is extremely unstable, giving methane an extremely high pKa (about 50) and negligible real-world acidity.
Lower electronegativity means the lone pair on N is held less tightly, making it more available to bond with an incoming proton, so NH3 is the stronger base.
By definition, Bronsted-Lowry theory defines bases strictly as proton acceptors.
HCl transfers a proton to hydroxide ion in a classic neutralization, a proton-transfer reaction; the other options are not proton transfers.
One water molecule donates a proton (acid) to the other, which accepts it (base), producing hydronium and hydroxide.
The presence of an aromatic ring does not block the O-H proton from being donated; phenol is a well-known weak Bronsted acid.
In the zwitterion, -COOH has already given up its proton to -NH2 (forming -COO- and -NH3+), an internal proton transfer consistent with Bronsted theory.
There is an inverse relationship: a strong acid readily gives up its proton, leaving behind a conjugate base with little attraction for protons, i.e. a weak base.
Trimethylamine has no N-H bond at all (every substituent is a methyl group), so unlike ammonia or primary and secondary amines, it cannot donate an N-H proton and behaves purely as a Bronsted base.
H3O+ is formed when water accepts a proton, making it water's conjugate acid.

A naked proton has an extremely high charge density and is instantly bound by an available electron-pair donor in solution, which is part of why Bronsted-Lowry reactions are really proton transfers rather than release of a free proton.
H2CO3 loses one proton to become HCO3-; they differ by exactly one H+ and are therefore a conjugate acid-base pair.
lewis-acids: Lewis acids are electron pair acceptors — a broader definition than Brønsted acids, which must involve a proton.
BF₃ has an empty p orbital on boron and readily accepts an electron pair, making it a Lewis acid despite having no acidic protons.
Metal cations have empty orbitals and coordinate to electron-rich atoms like carbonyl oxygen, pulling electron density away and making the carbon more electrophilic.
Lewis base theory defines a base strictly by its ability to donate an electron pair to form a new bond.
Accepting a proton requires donating an electron pair to form the new bond, so every Bronsted base (proton acceptor) is necessarily also a Lewis base.
AlCl3 has an incomplete octet on aluminum and readily accepts an electron pair, making it a powerful Lewis acid catalyst in Friedel-Crafts alkylation and acylation.
Boron in BF3 has only six valence electrons around it, leaving an empty orbital that readily accepts an electron pair from a Lewis base.
Lewis acids are defined by their ability to accept an electron pair, not by containing hydrogen; BF3 and AlCl3 have no acidic protons at all.
Ethylene has no lone pairs; it donates electron density from its pi bond to electrophiles such as Br2 or H+, a hallmark of alkene reactivity in organic chemistry.
The carbonyl oxygen's lone pair coordinates to the electron-deficient boron of BF3, activating the carbonyl toward nucleophilic attack, a common strategy in Lewis acid catalysis.
Many Lewis acid-base adducts, such as BF3 binding NH3, form purely through electron-pair donation with no proton ever changing hands; proton transfer is a narrower, Bronsted-specific phenomenon.
A carbocation's central carbon has only six valence electrons, leaving an empty p orbital that strongly attracts electron pairs from Lewis bases (nucleophiles).

Lewis acid-base theory extends beyond proton transfer to any electron-pair donation or acceptance, so it encompasses Bronsted acid-base reactions plus additional reactions, like BF3 plus NH3, that involve no protons at all.
Like other metal halides such as TiCl4 and AlCl3, SnCl4 can accommodate additional ligands by expanding its coordination number, accepting electron pairs from Lewis bases.
Forming the new B-N bond gives boron four bonding pairs instead of three, changing its hybridization from sp2 (trigonal planar) to sp3 (tetrahedral).
BF3 cannot donate a proton since it has none, so it cannot be a Bronsted acid, yet it is a textbook strong Lewis acid, showing the two acid categories are not equivalent.
The electrophilic carbonyl carbon accepts the electron pair donated by the carbanion-like carbon of the Grignard reagent, consistent with it acting as the Lewis acid in that bond-forming step.

Lewis acid or base character depends on the reaction partner, so the same species can play different roles with different partners depending on which one is electron-rich or electron-poor in that specific interaction.
Nitrogen's lone pair on NH3 is donated into the empty p orbital on boron, making ammonia the Lewis base and BF3 the Lewis acid.
The oxygen of a carbonyl group has lone pairs that readily coordinate to Lewis acids such as BF3 or AlCl3, a common activation strategy in synthesis.
Many neutral Lewis acids exist, such as BF3 and AlCl3, which are electron-deficient due to incomplete octets rather than formal positive charge.
Chloride ion has a full octet and a lone pair to donate, making it a Lewis base, not a Lewis acid; the other three are classic electron-pair acceptors.
TiCl4's electron-deficient titanium center coordinates to the carbonyl oxygen's lone pair, increasing the electrophilicity of the carbonyl carbon for the incoming nucleophile.
A bare proton has no electrons at all, so when it bonds to a base, that bond forms entirely from the base's donated electron pair, the defining behavior of a Lewis acid.
By accepting a lone pair from the epoxide oxygen, the Lewis acid withdraws electron density from the ring, weakening the C-O bonds and activating the epoxide carbons for nucleophilic ring-opening.
Singlet carbenes have an empty p orbital on carbon in addition to a lone pair, giving them both electrophilic (Lewis acidic) and nucleophilic character.
In a Lewis acid-base adduct, the base supplies both electrons of the new bond while the acid simply provides the empty orbital to receive them.
Bulky substituents can physically block a Lewis base from approaching the empty orbital, so steric hindrance, not just electronics, influences a Lewis acid's real-world reactivity.
The electron-poor sulfur center in SO3 accepts a lone pair from a Lewis base like water, generating sulfuric acid via an addition reaction.

Chiral Lewis acids coordinate to an electrophile's lone-pair-bearing atom, such as a carbonyl oxygen, lowering the energy of the reactive orbital while imposing a chiral environment that biases which face reacts, enabling asymmetric induction.
pka: pKa and acid strength are inversely related — lower pKa means the acid dissociates more, so it’s stronger.
Proton transfer equilibria favor forming the weaker acid (higher pKa) — the reaction runs toward the more stable, less acidic species.
A much lower (more negative) pKa means HCl dissociates far more completely — it is the much stronger acid.
pKa is defined as the negative base-10 logarithm of the acid dissociation constant, Ka.
pKa and acid strength are inversely related; a lower pKa means a larger Ka and a stronger acid, while a higher pKa means a weaker acid.
Lower pKa corresponds to a larger Ka, meaning greater dissociation, so the acid with pKa = 2 is significantly stronger.
When pH equals pKa, the concentrations of the acid and its conjugate base are equal, meaning the acid is 50 percent dissociated.

Both O-H bonds sit in a similar electronic environment, so their pKa values are close, though water is very slightly more acidic since ethanol's alkyl group is weakly electron-donating and slightly destabilizes the alkoxide.

Since pKa is a log scale, a difference of about 12 pKa units corresponds to roughly 10^12 difference in Ka, reflecting the large stabilizing effect of resonance in the carboxylate compared to the alkoxide.
For a favorable, forward-driven acid-base reaction, the base's conjugate acid should be a weaker acid (higher pKa) than the starting acid, ensuring the equilibrium lies toward products.
Since pKa = -log(Ka), an extremely large Ka for a very strong acid produces a negative pKa value.
Higher s-character (sp versus sp3) stabilizes the lone pair left behind in the conjugate base, making sp C-H bonds considerably more acidic than sp3 C-H bonds.

pKa values are measured in a specific solvent, commonly water, because the degree to which that solvent stabilizes the separated charges through solvation strongly affects the measured equilibrium constant.
A pKa difference of 27 units corresponds to an enormous difference in Ka, showing the oxygen-protonated form is vastly more acidic than the alpha C-H, which needs a much stronger base to deprotonate.
When pH lies between pKa1 and pKa2, the species has lost the first, more acidic proton but retained the second, so the intermediate form dominates.
pKa values depend on the solvent because solvation stabilizes ions differently in different media; the same acid can show noticeably different pKa values in water versus a solvent like DMSO.
Simple alcohols like ethanol have O-H pKa values around 16 to 18, close to but slightly less acidic than water.
Carboxylic acids like acetic acid typically have pKa values around 4 to 5, due to strong resonance stabilization of the carboxylate conjugate base.
The conjugate acids of typical alkyl amines have pKa values in the range of about 9 to 11, reflecting amines' moderate basicity.
pKa = -log(Ka), so a Ka of 10^-5 gives pKa = 5 and a Ka of 10^-3 gives pKa = 3; acid A, with the smaller Ka, has the higher pKa, a difference of 2 units.

In solution, polar solvents like water stabilize charged conjugate bases through solvation, which can significantly change or even reverse relative acidity trends compared to the gas phase, where no such stabilization exists.
Comparing the pKa values of two acids against a common base's conjugate acid lets you predict which acid-base pair favors products versus reactants at equilibrium.
Because H3O+ is the strongest acid species that persists in water, stronger acids added to dilute water are converted essentially completely to H3O+, a phenomenon known as the leveling effect.
HCl is a strong mineral acid with pKa around -7, far lower than the weak O-H acids methanol and acetic acid, or the essentially non-acidic C-H of ethane.

The negative charge on phenoxide can delocalize into the pi system of the benzene ring through resonance, stabilizing the conjugate base and making phenol more acidic than a non-resonance-stabilized alcohol like cyclohexanol.

The highly electronegative fluorine atoms withdraw electron density through the sigma bonds (induction), stabilizing the adjacent carboxylate's negative charge and making the compound considerably more acidic than acetic acid.
By definition, pKa equals the negative base-10 (common) logarithm of Ka.
A pKa of 4.2 means ascorbic acid only partially dissociates in water, placing it firmly in the weak acid category, similar in strength to acetic acid.

Powerful inductive electron withdrawal from nearby electronegative groups can dramatically stabilize the conjugate base (alkoxide), lowering the pKa well below that of an ordinary alcohol, as seen in highly fluorinated alcohols.

Ka, and its logarithmic form pKa, directly reflects the equilibrium constant for proton dissociation, making it the correct quantity for predicting whether an acid-base reaction favors products, unlike unrelated physical properties.
conjugate: Losing H⁺ from an acid gives its conjugate base — exactly one fewer proton.
Strong acids give up protons easily because their conjugate base is very stable (weak) once formed.
Adding a proton (H⁺) to NH₃ gives NH₄⁺, its conjugate acid.
Removing a single proton from H2SO4 gives the bisulfate ion, HSO4-, its conjugate base.
Adding one proton to hydroxide ion gives water, its conjugate acid.
By definition, a conjugate acid and its conjugate base are related by the gain or loss of a single proton, with no other atoms changing.
Removing the single proton from HF gives fluoride ion, F-, its conjugate base.
Because HCN is a much weaker acid than HF (higher pKa), its conjugate base, cyanide, holds onto protons more strongly and is therefore the stronger base of the two.
Water is a much weaker acid than HCl or acetic acid, so its conjugate base, hydroxide, is a correspondingly much stronger base than chloride or acetate.
NH4+ loses a proton to become NH3, making them a properly matched conjugate acid and conjugate base pair, differing by exactly one H+.
Because a strong acid dissociates almost completely, its conjugate base has very little affinity for protons and is correspondingly a weak base, such as Cl- from HCl.
Removing one proton from ammonia (NH3) gives amide ion, NH2-, a very strong base often used to deprotonate weak acids like terminal alkynes.
Adding one proton to carbonate gives bicarbonate, HCO3-, its conjugate acid.
In water at 25 degrees C, the pKa of an acid plus the pKb of its conjugate base always equals pKw (14), reflecting the relationship Ka times Kb equals Kw.

Resonance stabilization in acetate spreads the negative charge over two equivalent oxygens, making it a comparatively weak, stable base, whereas ethoxide's charge is localized on a single oxygen, making it a much stronger, more reactive base.

Bicarbonate forms when carbonic acid (H2CO3) loses a proton, making HCO3- its conjugate base, and also when carbonate (CO3^2-) gains a proton, making HCO3- its conjugate acid; this dual role is why it is amphoteric.
Adding one proton to a carboxylate ion regenerates the neutral carboxylic acid, its conjugate acid.
By definition, a conjugate base reacting with a proton reforms the acid it came from, since conjugate acid-base pairs differ by exactly one H+.
The weaker the conjugate acid, the stronger the conjugate base; since methane is the weakest acid of the four (highest pKa), methyl anion is the strongest base.
Because a weak acid holds onto its proton fairly well, its conjugate base, once formed, has a correspondingly stronger pull on protons, meaning it is a relatively strong base.
In a buffer, the conjugate base component, acetate, absorbs any added strong acid's protons, converting back to the weak acid and resisting a large pH change.

Because N-H, with pKa around 35 to 38, is far less acidic than O-H, with pKa around 16 to 18, the nitrogen-based conjugate base holds its electron pair much more tightly and is therefore a much stronger base than an alkoxide.

Base strength depends on which acid is considered its conjugate partner; OH- is a strong base relative to water's acidity, while water is a weak base relative to the much stronger acid H3O+, showing that strength is tied to a specific conjugate pair.
Adding one proton to chloride ion gives HCl, its conjugate acid.

Because a strong acid dissociates almost completely, its conjugate base is essentially non-basic and does not meaningfully re-associate with protons, so the pair cannot buffer against pH changes the way a weak acid and its conjugate base can.

Each functional group has its own independent conjugate acid-base relationship: protonated amine (-NH3+) is the conjugate acid of the amine (-NH2), and sulfonate (-SO3-) is the conjugate base of sulfonic acid (-SO3H); they are not conjugates of each other.
Removing the proton from A-H leaves behind A-, carrying one fewer proton and one additional unit of negative charge, its conjugate base.

The weaker the conjugate acid, the stronger the base; since HI is the strongest acid (most negative pKa) and NH3 is the weakest (highest pKa) of the three, their conjugate bases rank I- as weakest, then OH-, then NH2- as strongest.

Since acid strength and conjugate base strength are inversely linked through Ka and Kb, with Ka times Kb equal to Kw in water, two acids must share the same pKa for their conjugate bases to have identical base strength.

HCN loses a proton to become CN-, forming one conjugate pair, while OH- gains that proton to become H2O, forming the other conjugate pair, illustrating the two pairs present in every proton-transfer reaction.
acidity-factors: A more stable (resonance-delocalized) conjugate base means the acid gives up its proton more readily — higher acidity.
More electronegative atoms stabilize the extra negative charge of the conjugate base better, increasing acidity (e.g., HF > CH₄ in acidity trend logic, comparing across a period).

A nearby electron-withdrawing group (like a halogen) inductively pulls electron density away, stabilizing the negative charge on the conjugate base and increasing acidity — this is why chloroacetic acid is more acidic than acetic acid.

Comparing acidity across a row or column of the periodic table by looking at the atom bearing the acidic proton is the atom effect, one of the four classic factors (often remembered as ARIO: atom, resonance, induction, orbital or hybridization).

Larger halogens form longer, weaker H-X bonds, and their larger conjugate base anions are more polarizable and better able to spread out the negative charge, both of which increase acidity going down the column, making HI more acidic than HF.

Delocalization by itself is not automatically stabilizing; the atoms receiving the spread-out charge must be able to tolerate negative charge well, such as oxygen, otherwise resonance contributes little additional acid-strengthening effect.
An electron-withdrawing group pulls electron density away through sigma bonds, which helps spread out and stabilize the negative charge on the conjugate base, increasing acidity.
Moving left to right across period 2, electronegativity increases, which better stabilizes the conjugate base's negative charge, so acidity increases in the order NH3 less than H2O less than HF.

Removing that specific proton produces a fully conjugated, aromatic cyclopentadienyl anion, whose resonance and aromatic stabilization dramatically lowers the pKa compared to a typical alkane C-H, around 50.

Orbitals with more s-character are lower in energy and hold electron density closer to the nucleus; since sp has the most s-character of the three, its conjugate base is the most stabilized, making the alkynyl C-H the most acidic.

Inductive effects are transmitted through sigma bonds and weaken rapidly with distance, so a substituent closer to the site of deprotonation exerts a stronger acid-strengthening effect than the same group several bonds away.

Chlorine's high electronegativity withdraws electron density through the sigma bond framework, helping stabilize the adjacent carboxylate anion and thus increasing acidity relative to unsubstituted acetic acid.

Each additional chlorine contributes further inductive electron withdrawal, and since these effects are roughly additive, going from zero to three chlorines produces a cumulative, substantial increase in acidity.

The aromatic ring in phenoxide can accept electron density from the negatively charged oxygen through resonance, delocalizing it to the ortho and para ring positions, a stabilization pathway unavailable to a simple alkoxide like tert-butoxide.

A para-nitro group can both inductively withdraw electron density and, through resonance reinforced by its para position, help delocalize and stabilize the phenoxide's negative charge, combining two acid-strengthening effects at once.
Hybridization of the atom holding the negative charge in the conjugate base is one of the four classic factors (atom, resonance, induction, orbital/hybridization) used to predict relative acidity.

Alkyl groups are weakly electron-donating by induction compared to a hydrogen atom, which slightly destabilizes the negative charge on acetate's conjugate base relative to formate, making formic acid marginally more acidic.
A larger atom forms a longer, weaker bond to hydrogen, making the proton easier to remove, which is part of why acidity increases going down a group, for example HI being more acidic than HF.

Moving left to right across period 2 (C, N, O, F), electronegativity increases, better stabilizing the conjugate base's negative charge, so acidity increases in the order CH4 less than NH3 less than H2O less than HF.

While electronegativity dominates acidity trends across a period, down a group the increasing atom size and weaker, more polarizable H-X bond dominate instead, making HI far more acidic than HF even though fluorine is more electronegative.

The O-H formed by protonating a carbonyl oxygen has a pKa around -7, vastly lower than a typical alpha C-H, which has a pKa around 20, because oxygen stabilizes the resulting species far better than an unstabilized carbanion at carbon.

The second carbonyl-containing group, while not a halogen, is still electron-withdrawing by induction since carbonyl carbons are electron-poor, and its proximity to the first carboxylic acid group stabilizes the conjugate base, lowering pKa1 relative to acetic acid.

A carboxylate's negative charge is delocalized equally over two oxygen atoms via resonance, a major stabilization unavailable to an alkoxide where the charge sits on a single oxygen, and this resonance effect is the dominant reason carboxylic acids are far more acidic than alcohols.

Orbitals with more s-character hold electron density closer to the nucleus, stabilizing a negative charge placed in that orbital, which is why sp-hybridized C-H bonds are more acidic than sp3-hybridized ones.

Each nitro group withdraws electron density both by induction and, when positioned ortho or para to the oxygen, by resonance; with three such groups stacking their effects, the phenoxide anion becomes extraordinarily stabilized, producing an acid nearly as strong as some mineral acids.

Acidity is ultimately about conjugate base stability, and multiple factors often operate simultaneously, so a careful comparison must weigh all of them together rather than applying a single rule in isolation.

Inductive, sigma-bond electron withdrawal diminishes quickly with each intervening bond, so a substituent close to the acidic proton has a much larger acid-strengthening effect than the same substituent several carbons farther away.

Resonance and induction are independent stabilizing mechanisms that can act together on the same conjugate base, as seen with a para-nitro group on phenoxide, and their combined stabilization typically exceeds what either effect would provide on its own.

Resonance delocalizes the actual negative charge onto additional atoms, a more fundamental stabilization, which is generally a stronger effect than induction's more modest shift in electron density through sigma bonds, though exact magnitudes vary case by case.

Halogens like chlorine are weak inductive electron-withdrawers but are actually resonance electron donors through lone pair donation into the ring, so the two effects partly cancel, producing only a small acidity increase compared to a nitro group, which strongly withdraws electrons by both mechanisms.
newman: The front atom is represented as a point with three lines radiating out; the back atom is the circle behind it.
Anti-staggered puts substituents as far apart as possible, minimizing steric and torsional strain.
A full rotation passes through 3 staggered (60°, 180°, 300°) and 3 eclipsed (0°, 120°, 240°) conformations.
The front atom sits at the center (its three bonds radiate from the center dot), while the back atom is represented by the circle itself, so its bonds are drawn from the circle's edge.
The dihedral angle describes the angular relationship, looking straight down the C-C bond, between a substituent on the front carbon and one on the back carbon.
Staggered conformations space the front and back substituents as far apart as possible, giving dihedral angles of 60 degrees, 180 degrees, and 300 degrees around the full rotation.
Anti means the two largest groups point in exactly opposite directions when viewed down the bond, which is a 180 degree dihedral angle.
Gauche conformers are staggered but have the two reference groups only 60 degrees apart, rather than fully opposite as in the anti conformer.
Eclipsing bonds forces electron pairs in the C-H sigma bonds closer together, raising energy through torsional strain, so every eclipsed form of ethane is less stable than every staggered form.
Ethane's hydrogens are small, so the energy penalty in the eclipsed form comes mainly from torsional strain, the electronic repulsion of aligned sigma bonds, not from bulky steric clashes.
Rotation barriers around single C-C bonds are typically only a few kcal/mol, so at room temperature molecules rotate through all conformations far too quickly to separate them.
Each of the three hydrogens on the front carbon lines up directly with one hydrogen on the back carbon, giving three separate eclipsing interactions.
The anti conformation keeps the two bulky methyl groups as far apart as possible, minimizing steric strain and making it the most stable conformer.
Gauche conformers are staggered forms with the reference substituents 60 degrees apart, rather than the 180 degrees seen in the anti form.
Even though gauche butane is staggered and free of torsional strain, the two methyl groups are close enough at 60 degrees apart to experience unfavorable steric crowding.
Butane's methyl groups are much bulkier than ethane's hydrogens, so in addition to any torsional effects, gauche butane suffers extra steric strain that small hydrogens in ethane never experience.
C2 of propane is bonded to C1 (the front atom in this view), C3 (a methyl group), and two hydrogens, so in the Newman projection the back atom shows a methyl group and two hydrogens.

Anti butane is the global energy minimum because the methyls are farthest apart, while the two gauche conformers are mirror-image-like and therefore equal in energy to each other, both higher than anti.
The two gauche conformers are related by reflection (one has the methyl rotated +60 degrees, the other -60 degrees from anti) and are otherwise structurally equivalent, so they have identical energy.

When both bulky methyl groups line up directly with each other (0 degree dihedral angle), the combination of torsional strain and severe steric clash makes this the highest point on the rotational energy profile.

Lining up two bulky methyl groups directly on top of each other produces more steric clash than lining up a methyl with a small hydrogen, so the methyl-methyl eclipsed form sits at the top of the energy profile.

Rotating 360 degrees passes through three eclipsed arrangements; the one eclipsing both methyl groups is distinctly higher than the other two, which eclipse a methyl with a hydrogen and are equal to each other.
There are three minima (anti plus two gauche) and three maxima (one methyl-methyl eclipsed plus two methyl-hydrogen eclipsed), but anti is lower than the two equal-energy gauche minima.
With only small hydrogens attached, there isn't much steric bulk to clash; the energy penalty in the eclipsed form comes from the quantum mechanical repulsion of electrons in aligned C-H sigma bonds.

Each central carbon bears two methyl groups; fixing one pair anti to each other still leaves the remaining methyl groups positioned gauche to groups on the neighboring carbon, contributing extra strain beyond simple butane.

Conformers interconvert by rotation around a single bond with a very low barrier, so at room temperature they equilibrate on a timescale far too fast to separate; only configurational isomers like cis/trans can be isolated.
Bulkier substituents add steric strain on top of the intrinsic torsional strain present even in ethane, so rotational barriers tend to rise as the groups attached to the rotating bond get larger.
C3 is bonded to C2 (the bond being viewed), to C4 (a methyl group), and to two hydrogens, so the back atom in this Newman projection shows a methyl group and two hydrogens.

Anti and gauche butane are both staggered conformations, so there is no eclipsing (torsional) strain difference between them; the energy gap is due to steric strain from the methyl groups being closer together in the gauche form.

With three methyl groups on each central carbon, there is no way to rotate the molecule into a conformation free of substantial steric clash, so all conformers, even the most staggered one, carry extra strain compared to butane.
cyclohexanes: The chair avoids angle strain (near-tetrahedral angles) and torsional strain (fully staggered), unlike boat or planar forms.
The boat has eclipsing interactions along its sides and a steric clash between the two "flagpole" hydrogens.
The twist-boat is a slightly lower-energy variant of the boat that partially relieves the flagpole steric clash, but it’s still well above the chair in energy.
The chair conformation allows every ring carbon to keep its bonds at the ideal tetrahedral angle of about 109.5 degrees, which is a major reason it is so stable.
Cyclohexane, as the name indicates, is a six-membered ring of carbons, each bearing two hydrogens.
The boat has several eclipsed C-H bonds along its sides (torsional strain) plus two hydrogens at the flagpole positions that point toward each other and clash sterically.
The half-chair is actually a high-energy transition state along the ring-flip pathway, not a resting conformation; molecules pass through it only briefly while interconverting between other forms.

Chair is the global minimum; twist-boat is next lowest because twisting relieves some strain present in the regular boat; boat is higher still; and the half-chair, a transition state, is highest in energy.
The twist partially un-eclipses the ring C-C bonds that were aligned in the regular boat and pulls the flagpole hydrogens slightly apart, so twist-boat sits lower in energy than boat.
The chair is a non-planar, puckered arrangement with alternating carbons above and below an average plane; this puckering is exactly what allows ideal tetrahedral angles and staggered bonds.
The chair achieves perfect 109.5 degree bond angles and has every neighboring C-H and C-C bond staggered, so it is essentially free of both angle strain and torsional strain.
A ring flip converts one chair into the other possible chair form, so there are exactly two chairs that any cyclohexane ring can flip between.
Experimentally, the boat conformation sits roughly 6 to 7 kcal/mol above the chair, reflecting the substantial torsional and flagpole steric strain present in the boat.
In the chair every ring bond is staggered with its neighbors, whereas in the boat several ring C-C bonds end up eclipsed, contributing torsional strain.
Every ring carbon in the chair conformation has one bond pointing axially (roughly perpendicular to the ring's average plane) and one pointing equatorially (roughly outward in the plane).
The half-chair is a saddle point on the conformational energy surface, the highest-energy structure molecules pass through while ring-flipping from one chair-related form to another.
The boat conformation has two carbons that point upward out of the main ring plane; the hydrogens on these two 'tip' carbons point toward each other and are called flagpole hydrogens.
The ring-flip barrier for cyclohexane is experimentally around 10 to 11 kcal/mol, still low enough that flipping occurs rapidly (thousands of times per second) at room temperature.
The chair staggers every neighboring bond around the ring, but the boat has several ring bonds that end up eclipsed, introducing torsional strain that the chair avoids.
The chair remains the global energy minimum; twist-boat is only the lowest-energy member of the boat family, still several kcal/mol above the chair.

The twist partially un-eclipses ring bonds and separates the flagpole hydrogens, producing a net stabilization relative to the symmetric boat, even though a slight new strain is introduced by the twist itself.
Chair is lowest, twist-boat is next (lower than the plain boat due to relieved strain), boat is higher still, and half-chair, being a transition state, sits at the top of this energy ordering.
The ring flip proceeds chair to half-chair to twist-boat to half-chair to chair, so two distinct half-chair transition states are crossed in a single flip.
The boat and half-chair are distinct geometries with different numbers and arrangements of eclipsed bonds and ring puckering; they are not interchangeable descriptions of the same structure.

The chair's puckering is a geometric solution unique to a six-membered ring that allows perfect bond angles with no eclipsing, whereas smaller rings like cyclopropane are forced into angle strain and cyclopentane into some torsional strain regardless of puckering.
Because twist-boat is lower in energy than the plain boat, real molecules passing between chairs overwhelmingly populate the twist-boat rather than lingering in the higher-energy symmetric boat.

The actual lowest-energy pathway passes predominantly through twist-boat intermediates, since twist-boat is more stable than the symmetric boat; the plain boat is a higher-energy, less-traveled point on the overall surface.

Because the chair is several kcal/mol more stable than any boat-family conformation, the equilibrium population strongly favors the chair, leaving only a tiny fraction in higher-energy forms at any given moment.
Both chair and boat keep bond angles reasonably close to tetrahedral; the boat's extra energy comes mainly from torsional strain (eclipsed bonds) and flagpole steric strain, not from angle strain.

The chair's near-total absence of both angle and torsional strain is a special geometric outcome of the six-membered ring; larger and smaller rings typically cannot fully escape some strain in any conformation they adopt.
axial-equatorial: Equatorial positions point outward around the ring’s perimeter, avoiding the 1,3-diaxial interactions that axial groups face.
Equatorial placement avoids steric clashes (1,3-diaxial interactions) with other axial substituents, so bulky groups prefer equatorial.
Each ring carbon has exactly one axial and one equatorial position available for its substituent/hydrogen.
Axial positions alternate, pointing up on one carbon and down on the next as you go around the ring, all roughly parallel to the ring's main symmetry axis.
Each of the six ring carbons has exactly one axial position, giving six axial positions total around the ring.
Just as with axial positions, each of the six ring carbons contributes exactly one equatorial position, for six total.
Because the ring carbons alternate slightly above and below the average plane, their axial bonds alternate direction, up on one carbon, down on the next, all the way around.
Since cyclohexane is CH2 repeated six times, each carbon's two hydrogens occupy the one axial and one equatorial position available on that carbon.
An axial group points toward axial hydrogens (or groups) on the carbons three atoms away around the ring (1 and 3 relationship), creating steric clashes called 1,3-diaxial interactions.
Counting around the ring, an axial group at C1 points toward the axial substituents at C3 and C5, which are close enough in space to clash with it.
With only hydrogens attached, flipping the ring just swaps which hydrogens are labeled axial versus equatorial on an otherwise identical molecule, so there is no energy difference.
Equatorial bonds radiate outward around the 'equator' of the ring, lying much closer to the average ring plane than the axial bonds do.
The methyl group's modest A-value (about 1.7 kcal/mol) corresponds to roughly a 95:5 equatorial-to-axial ratio at room temperature, strongly favoring equatorial but not completely excluding axial.
When axial, the methyl group clashes sterically with the axial hydrogens at the 3 and 5 positions; moving it equatorial removes most of that strain, making the equatorial conformer more stable.
The tert-butyl group has an enormous A-value because three methyl groups would all clash in 1,3-diaxial fashion if axial, essentially locking the ring with tert-butyl equatorial.
The A-value is defined as the free energy preference for equatorial over axial, so by definition a larger A-value means a stronger equatorial preference.
Isopropyl is bulkier than methyl, so its 1,3-diaxial clashes when axial are more severe, giving it a larger A-value and a stronger preference for the equatorial position.

Geometrically, an axial substituent and an axial hydrogen three carbons away around the ring are positioned much like the two methyl groups in gauche butane, so the strain is often compared to a gauche interaction.
Both C3 and C5 are positioned symmetrically relative to C1 around the ring, so an axial group at C1 clashes with whatever is axial at both of those positions.
An axial group at one carbon clashes with the axial hydrogens at exactly two other ring positions, the ones three bonds away on each side (the 3 and 5 positions relative to it).
Methylcyclohexane's A-value, the equatorial preference energy, is experimentally about 1.7 kcal/mol, consistent with roughly a 95:5 equilibrium ratio at room temperature.
Fluorine is a small atom with a short C-F bond, so its 1,3-diaxial clash is mild; its A-value (roughly 0.2 to 0.3 kcal/mol) is considerably smaller than methyl's (about 1.7 kcal/mol).

A-value scales roughly with steric bulk: small fluorine has the weakest equatorial preference, methyl is intermediate, and the very bulky tert-butyl group has by far the strongest equatorial preference.

Because tert-butyl is essentially three methyl groups bundled on one carbon, placing it axial would force multiple severe steric clashes simultaneously, vastly exceeding the strain from a single axial methyl.

Equatorial substituents still have some gauche-type interactions with neighboring ring bonds; they simply avoid the much larger 1,3-diaxial clashes that axial substituents face, so their strain is reduced, not zero.

Geometrically, the equatorial orientation directs a substituent away from other ring atoms, while the axial orientation aims it straight at the axial groups on the 1,3-related carbons, which is the structural root of the steric difference.
An A-value of zero means there is no free energy preference between the two positions, which corresponds to an equal, 50:50 population at equilibrium.

Because an axial substituent experiences 1,3-diaxial clashes with both the C3 and C5 positions simultaneously, its total strain is often approximated as about twice that of a single gauche interaction.

A-values are empirically derived mainly from steric 1,3-diaxial effects; in special cases additional stabilizing interactions (like intramolecular hydrogen bonds) can favor an axial position despite a typically unfavorable A-value.

Even though chlorine is a larger atom, its longer carbon-halogen bond moves it farther from the ring, and its roughly spherical shape clashes less than the three hydrogens of a methyl group, giving it a smaller A-value than expected from atomic size alone.
ring-flips: A ring flip interconverts the two chair forms — every axial position becomes equatorial and vice versa.
Ring flips are conformational changes, not bond-breaking — cis/trans relationships (configuration) are preserved; only which substituents are axial vs. equatorial changes.

For a single non-hydrogen substituent, axial and equatorial chairs differ in energy (the equatorial is lower); only when the "substituent" is H (unsubstituted cyclohexane) are both chair forms identical in energy.
A ring flip interconverts the two chair forms, and every substituent that was equatorial in one chair ends up axial in the other, and vice versa.
Ring flipping only involves rotation about existing sigma bonds to reshape the ring; it never breaks or forms any covalent bonds, unlike a configurational change such as a reaction.
Ring flipping is purely a reshaping of the ring through bond rotations; all carbon-carbon bonds remain intact throughout the entire process.

A substituent's up/down face assignment is a fixed structural (configurational) feature of the molecule; the ring flip changes only whether that same substituent happens to be axial or equatorial in the new chair.

With an activation barrier of only about 10 to 11 kcal/mol, cyclohexane rings flip extremely quickly at room temperature, far faster than can typically be observed as separate species by most everyday techniques.
As the ring flips, it must pass over an energy barrier corresponding to the half-chair geometry before relaxing into the twist-boat and eventually the other chair.
Because all six ring carbons bear only hydrogens, flipping just relabels which hydrogens are axial and which are equatorial on an otherwise indistinguishable structure, so there is no energy change.
A ring flip always converts one chair into the other possible chair arrangement of the same ring, so there are exactly two interconverting chair forms.
In the trans-1,4 pattern both methyl groups flip together from equatorial to axial (or vice versa), so the ring flip swaps a diequatorial conformer for a diaxial one.
In the cis-1,4 pattern, one methyl is always axial while the other is equatorial; flipping swaps which carbon has which, but the overall strain, and therefore the energy, stays the same.
When both substituents move together from equatorial to axial (as happens for trans-1,4 or trans-1,2 patterns), the flip directly swaps a diequatorial conformer for a diaxial one.
Placing both methyl groups equatorial avoids all the 1,3-diaxial strain that the diaxial alternative would create, making the diequatorial conformer strongly favored.
Cis/trans relationships are configurational, fixed by which face of the ring each substituent is attached to; a ring flip only changes axial/equatorial positions, never the underlying configuration.

Cis-1,4-disubstitution always places one substituent axial and one equatorial; flipping just swaps which carbon carries which role, leaving the overall energy unchanged when the two groups are identical.
The full lowest-energy pathway goes from chair up over a half-chair transition state, down into the twist-boat, back up over a second half-chair, and finally down into the other chair.
With any substituent bulkier than hydrogen, the axial conformer suffers 1,3-diaxial strain that the equatorial conformer avoids, so the two ring-flip conformers are no longer equal in energy.

Since every ring carbon in unsubstituted cyclohexane just has two hydrogens, flipping the ring swaps which hydrogen is axial versus equatorial on an otherwise identical, symmetric molecule, producing no net energy change; any other substituent breaks that symmetry.

Since both substituents are identical methyl groups on the same carbon, one is always axial and the other equatorial; flipping swaps which one is which but keeps the total strain, and thus the energy, the same.

Because both tert-butyl groups must move together on a ring flip, the only alternative to the diequatorial conformer is a diaxial one with two extremely bulky groups clashing severely, making that conformer vanishingly rare.
Cis-1,2-disubstitution always gives one axial and one equatorial methyl; flipping swaps which ring carbon carries which role, producing a conformer of identical energy to the first.
Like trans-1,4, the trans-1,2 relationship allows both substituents to be equatorial together in one chair, and the ring flip moves both of them to axial together in the other chair.

Plain cyclohexane's axial and equatorial hydrogens are interchangeable by symmetry, but once distinct substituents are placed on specific carbons, the two chairs generally differ in how much 1,3-diaxial strain they contain.
The flip passes chair to half-chair to twist-boat to a second half-chair to the other chair, crossing two distinct half-chair energy barriers along the way.

Twist-boat relieves some of the torsional and flagpole strain present in the symmetric boat, so the ring flip pathway favors passing through twist-boat rather than lingering in the higher-energy plain boat.

Cis-1,3-disubstitution allows both substituents to be equatorial together in one chair; ring flipping moves them both to axial together in the other chair, just as with trans-1,4 and trans-1,2 patterns.
Because axial substituents suffer 1,3-diaxial strain that scales with their size, the equilibrium strongly favors whichever chair places a bulky group equatorial, minimizing that strain.

Large substituents can increase steric strain in the half-chair and twist-boat transition states as well as in the ground states, raising the activation barrier and slowing the rate of ring flipping compared to unsubstituted cyclohexane.
conformational-analysis: Placing bulky groups equatorial minimizes 1,3-diaxial strain, giving the lowest-energy conformation.
tert-Butyl is so bulky that the axial conformer is dramatically higher in energy — essentially locking it equatorial.
For 1,2-disubstitution, cis substituents are one axial/one equatorial (and trans are both axial or both equatorial) — the reverse of the 1,3 relationship.
Conformational analysis of substituted cyclohexanes comes down to comparing how much 1,3-diaxial strain each possible chair form would create and choosing the one with the least.
Trans-1,4 substitution geometrically allows both substituents to be equatorial simultaneously, which is almost always the lower-energy, preferred arrangement.
The 1,4-cis relationship geometrically forces one substituent to be axial whenever the other is equatorial, so a diequatorial arrangement is never possible for this pattern.
For the 1,3 relationship, it is the cis isomer (not trans) that allows both substituents to occupy equatorial positions simultaneously in one of the two chairs.
For 1,3-disubstitution, it is the cis isomer that allows diequatorial placement; the trans-1,3 isomer is always forced into an axial/equatorial mixture.
As with trans-1,4, the trans-1,2 relationship allows both substituents to be equatorial together, which is normally the more stable choice.
The cis-1,2 relationship geometrically requires one substituent to be axial whenever the other is equatorial, so neither chair conformer is ever diequatorial.

Because a bulkier group (higher A-value) suffers a larger energy penalty when forced axial, the lowest-energy conformer is the one that places the substituent with the greater A-value in the equatorial position.

The cis-1,4 pattern forces one group axial; since tert-butyl's A-value vastly exceeds methyl's, the lower-energy conformer puts the much bulkier tert-butyl group equatorial and accepts methyl axial instead.
Because the trans-1,4 relationship allows both groups to be equatorial simultaneously, and both substituents prefer equatorial, this diequatorial conformer is overwhelmingly the most stable.
Since each axial substituent contributes a strain penalty approximated by its A-value, comparing the summed penalties for each possible chair lets you predict which conformer is lower in energy.
Since A-values approximate the strain penalty of having a given group axial, the conformation with less total axial strain corresponds to the more stable structure.
The cis-1,3 relationship is the pattern that geometrically permits both substituents to sit equatorial simultaneously, and that diequatorial form is indeed the most stable.

Because trans-1,3 substitution cannot achieve a diequatorial arrangement, both chair conformers have one methyl axial and one equatorial, and the molecule is forced to accept some axial strain either way.
This systematic approach, summing A-value-based penalties for axial groups in each chair, is the standard method for predicting which conformer of a multiply-substituted cyclohexane will dominate.
When neither conformer has a net strain advantage over the other, there is no free energy difference driving the equilibrium toward one side, giving an approximately equal population.

Since ethyl has a somewhat larger A-value than methyl, putting the bulkier ethyl group equatorial (and accepting methyl axial instead) minimizes the total axial strain, making that conformer more stable.

The trans isomer enjoys a genuinely diequatorial lowest-energy conformer, avoiding all 1,3-diaxial strain, whereas the cis isomer is stuck with at least one substituent axial no matter which chair it adopts.

Since both methyls contribute their own A-value penalty when axial, the diaxial conformer's strain roughly doubles a single A-value contribution, giving an estimated few kcal/mol preference for the diequatorial form.

For cis-1,2, both interconverting chairs are ax,eq combinations of roughly comparable strain, so the energy gap between them is small; for trans-1,2, one chair is diequatorial (very favorable) and the other diaxial (very unfavorable), producing a much larger gap.

Whether diequatorial placement is possible depends on the specific combination of cis/trans relationship and substitution pattern: trans works for 1,2- and 1,4-, while cis works for 1,3-; the other combination in each case cannot be diequatorial.

The geometric rule is that trans works for the 1,2 and 1,4 relationships while cis works for the 1,3 relationship; the opposite stereochemistry in each case is always forced into a mixed axial/equatorial arrangement.

Because trans-1,4 substitution permits both substituents to be equatorial at once, and both OH and tert-butyl individually prefer equatorial, the diequatorial conformer is strongly favored with no conflict between them.

Since cis-1,4 substitution forces one group axial, the molecule 'sacrifices' the position of the substituent with the smaller A-value (OH) to keep the much bulkier, higher-A-value tert-butyl group equatorial.

While the bulkiest substituent's A-value often dominates the decision, every substituent contributes some strain energy when axial, so a rigorous analysis sums the contributions of all substituents rather than ignoring the smaller ones.

Because tert-butyl presents three methyl groups on one carbon, forcing it axial creates multiple simultaneous 1,3-diaxial clashes rather than just one, which is why its A-value is so much larger than a simple alkyl group's.

A-values are empirically averaged steric parameters; real molecules can have additional effects (electronic, hydrogen bonding, or unusual geometries) not captured by a simple sum of standard A-values, so predictions are approximate.
radical-halogenation: Br2 and an alkane in a dark flask do nothing at all. The light or heat is what initiates the chain, which is why bromine water distinguishes an alkene from an alkane.
Homolysis sends one electron to each atom, giving two neutral radicals rather than a cation and an anion.
Two fishhooks are needed to break one bond, one for each electron. Mixing arrow types is the commonest drawing error here.
Up from zero is initiation, unchanged is propagation, down to zero is termination. The product is not what distinguishes them.
The count is unchanged, so the chain can go round again. This is propagation even when the product appears in this very step.
Two radicals in, none out. That is what ends the chain.
Two radicals have to collide, and there are very few in the flask at any moment. A single initiation can turn over thousands of molecules first.
Radicals follow the same order as carbocations, and for the same reason: hyperconjugation from neighboring C-H bonds into the half-filled orbital.
Bromine is highly selective. Chlorine's corresponding figure is only about 5, which is why chlorination gives mixtures.
Chlorine barely distinguishes them, so chlorinating a branched alkane gives a mixture you would have to separate.
Abstraction by bromine is endothermic, so by Hammond's postulate the transition state resembles the radical, and the radical's stability shows up in the rate.
Abstraction by chlorine is exothermic, so the transition state resembles the reactants, at which point the radical has barely formed and its stability hardly matters.
The carbon radical is essentially planar with its electron in a p orbital, so the halogen arrives on either face equally. No conditions make this enantioselective.
Six primary hydrogens at rate 1 against two secondary at about 4 gives 6 to 8 — close to even, because the counts nearly offset the modest selectivity.
So predicting a ratio means multiplying each rate by how many equivalent hydrogens there are.
N-bromosuccinimide releases bromine slowly and keeps its concentration permanently low.
Adding Br2 to an alkene is faster than the radical chain, but addition needs a reasonable Br2 concentration and the chain does not. Starve it and substitution wins.
The unpaired electron is delocalized across the pi system, which makes the abstraction much easier than the substitution pattern alone would suggest.
Bromine can end up at either end of the delocalized system. Drawing both resonance forms of the radical is how you predict the second product.
The peroxide starts a radical chain, so a bromine radical adds first rather than a proton.
The first species to add is no longer a proton seeking the better carbocation, but a bromine radical seeking the more stable carbon radical — which puts Br on the other carbon.
The last one consumes one radical and makes one, leaving the count unchanged. That is a propagation step.
The alkene adds Br2 readily in the dark; the alkane does nothing without light or heat.
Radical steps move single electrons and give neutral species. A charge means a pair of electrons moved, which is a different mechanism.
A halogen radical abstracts a hydrogen, giving H-X and a carbon radical that then attacks X2.
On 2-methylpropane, bromine gives about 99% of the tertiary bromide while chlorine gives more of the primary product than the tertiary one.
Initiation is the slow, expensive step and only has to happen once per chain. That is the whole trick.
The molecular ion fragments to leave the most stable radical it can, which is the same stability order you learned here.
That planarity is exactly why a new stereocenter formed this way comes out racemic.
Every bond is C-C or C-H, close to nonpolar, with nothing for a nucleophile or electrophile to aim at.
chirality: Chirality means the molecule and its mirror image are distinct, non-superimposable objects — like left and right hands.
An internal mirror plane (plane of symmetry) means the molecule is superimposable on its mirror image — achiral.
A shoe is a classic macroscopic chiral object — its mirror image (the other foot’s shoe) is not superimposable on the original.
The defining test for chirality is whether a molecule's mirror image can be rotated and translated to exactly overlap the original. If not, the molecule is chiral.

Chirality is a property of the whole molecule's symmetry, not just of individual carbons. Substituted allenes and certain biphenyls are chiral through axial or restricted-rotation chirality without a classic stereocenter.
Dichloromethane's central carbon carries two identical chlorine atoms and two identical hydrogens, giving it an internal mirror plane, so it is achiral.
If a molecule has two or more such stereocenters arranged symmetrically, their effects can cancel, producing an achiral meso compound even though individual centers have four different substituents.
Chiral compounds (in non-racemic form) rotate the plane of polarized light passing through them; this optical activity is measured with a polarimeter.
Glycine's alpha carbon bears two identical hydrogen atoms in addition to the amino and carboxyl groups, so it fails the four-different-groups test and is achiral.

A stereocenter is a single atom whose substituents can be arranged two ways; chirality is a property of the entire molecule's overall symmetry, which can differ from what any one center suggests (as in meso compounds).

Biological receptors are themselves chiral, so they often bind the two enantiomers of a chiral molecule differently, which is why mirror-image compounds can have different biological or sensory effects despite having identical formulas.
Thalidomide's two enantiomers have very different biological activities, showing why distinguishing and controlling chirality matters in drug development, not just in academic classification.
Any internal improper symmetry element, such as a mirror plane or center of inversion, makes a molecule superimposable on its own mirror image, which is the formal definition of achiral.

Stereocenter counting is a useful shortcut, but meso compounds show that a molecule with multiple stereocenters can still be achiral overall, so the mirror-image superimposability test is the truly reliable method.

Count outward from C3 in both directions: one way is C2-C1, an ethyl group; the other is C4-C5-C6, a propyl group. With a methyl and a hydrogen as well, that is four different groups, so C3 is a stereocenter and the molecule is chiral. The chains only look symmetric until you count them.
Enantiomers differ only in how they interact with other chiral influences, such as polarized light or chiral reagents; their standard bulk physical properties in an achiral environment are identical.

When bulky ortho substituents prevent free rotation about the biaryl bond, the molecule is locked into a twisted, non-planar shape whose mirror image cannot be superimposed, producing chirality without a traditional stereocenter.

Chirality is a geometric property of overall molecular shape; it can also arise at nitrogen, phosphorus, sulfur centers, or from axial chirality in carbon-free frameworks, so carbon is not strictly required.
CHFClBr has a single carbon bonded to four completely different atoms (H, F, Cl, Br) and no internal symmetry to cancel the effect, making it chiral.
Simple rotation of a molecule (or its drawing) in space never changes its configuration or identity; only reflecting it (or swapping substituents) converts it into its mirror image.
In a racemic (50:50) mixture, the rotation caused by one enantiomer is exactly canceled by the equal and opposite rotation from the other, so the net optical rotation observed is zero.

Meso-tartaric acid's two stereocenters have opposite configurations that create an internal mirror plane, so the molecule as a whole coincides with its mirror image even though each center individually has four different substituents.

A center of symmetry is an improper symmetry element; any molecule possessing one is automatically superimposable on its mirror image and therefore achiral, so a truly chiral molecule cannot have one.
C3 carries four distinct groups (H, Br, CH3, and -CH=CH2), satisfying the stereocenter criterion, and there is no internal symmetry to cancel it, so the molecule is chiral.
Stereocenters are a strong clue toward chirality, but because of possible internal symmetry (as in meso compounds), the only fully reliable check is comparing the whole molecule to its mirror image.

Left and right hands look alike but cannot be perfectly overlaid on one another no matter how they are rotated, which is exactly the geometric relationship that defines chiral molecules and their enantiomers.

The alpha carbon of a standard amino acid is attached to a hydrogen, an amino group, a carboxyl group, and a unique side chain, four different substituents that make it a stereocenter and the molecule chiral.
This is exactly the situation in meso compounds: individual carbons qualify as stereocenters, yet the molecule's overall internal symmetry makes it achiral.

While sp3 stereocenters are the most common source of chirality in intro organic chemistry, axial chirality (as in certain allenes and biphenyls) shows that chirality does not require any sp3 carbon stereocenter.
The single carbon in CHFClBr carries four different atoms with no internal symmetry, so the molecule and its mirror image are non-superimposable enantiomers, confirming the molecule is chiral.
stereocenters: A stereocenter (typically a carbon) must have four different groups attached for swapping two to create a distinct stereoisomer.
Each stereocenter independently can be R or S, giving up to 2ⁿ possible stereoisomers.
Nitrogen can be a stereocenter in specific cases (e.g., locked in a ring, or quaternary ammonium with 4 different substituents) where pyramidal inversion is prevented or irrelevant.

C2 is bonded to Br, H, a methyl group, and an ethyl group, four different substituents, making it the stereocenter; the other carbons each have at least two identical substituents (such as extra hydrogens).

The defining requirement for a tetrahedral stereocenter is four different groups attached; if two substituents are identical, swapping them gives the same structure back, so it cannot be a stereocenter.
Both C2 and C3 are each bonded to Br, H, a methyl group, and a chain leading to the other substituted carbon, all different, so each qualifies independently as a stereocenter.
A classic tetrahedral stereocenter has four single bonds arranged tetrahedrally around an sp3 carbon; sp2 and sp carbons do not have the tetrahedral geometry needed for this type of stereocenter.
The carbon in CH2Cl2 bears two identical chlorine atoms and two identical hydrogens, so it fails the four-different-groups test, unlike the other examples listed.

Tracing outward from C3 in both directions gives an ethyl group on each side, so two of C3's four substituents are identical; this classic trick shows that branching alone does not guarantee a stereocenter.

What matters is whether the four substituents are different from each other, not whether they are carbon groups or include hydrogen; a quaternary carbon bonded to four different carbon chains is a valid stereocenter.

Amines undergo fast umbrella-like pyramidal inversion at room temperature, rapidly racemizing any configuration at nitrogen, so the two mirror-image forms interconvert too quickly to be isolated or to show net optical activity.

Because nitrogen in a quaternary ammonium ion has no lone pair and cannot undergo pyramidal inversion, its four-different-group configuration is locked in place, unlike in a neutral trisubstituted amine.
Each independent stereocenter can be one of two configurations, so the maximum number of stereoisomers is 2 raised to the number of stereocenters: 2 cubed equals 8.

Although 2 independent stereocenters could give up to 4 stereoisomers, the molecule's internal symmetry makes the R,S and S,R combinations identical (a meso compound), leaving only 3 distinct stereoisomers: R,R; S,S; and meso.
The alpha carbon carries four distinct groups: a hydrogen, an amino group, a carboxylic acid group, and a methyl group, satisfying the requirement for a stereocenter.
Ring carbons can absolutely be stereocenters; for example, in 1,2-dimethylcyclohexane, C1 and C2 are each bonded to four different groups once the two distinct ring paths are taken into account.
C1 and C2 each bear a methyl group, a hydrogen, and two different paths around the ring (one shorter, one longer, to reach the other substituted carbon), making each of them a stereocenter.

In a sulfoxide, sulfur's lone pair behaves like a fourth substituent, and unlike nitrogen in amines, the pyramidal inversion at sulfur in a sulfoxide is slow enough at room temperature that the two configurations can be isolated as separate stereoisomers.
Axial chirality, found in certain allenes and restricted biphenyls, shows that a molecule can be chiral without containing any classic tetrahedral stereocenter.

Terminal or symmetric carbons are rarely stereocenters; the reliable method is to identify a tetrahedral (four single-bonded) carbon and compare its four attached groups by tracing outward until a difference (or confirmed sameness) is found.
C4 is flanked by a propyl group on each side of the main chain, making two of its four substituents identical, so despite the methyl branch it is not a stereocenter.
That central carbon carries four completely different groups (Br, Cl, F, and CH3), satisfying the stereocenter definition, while the methyl carbon has three identical hydrogens and cannot qualify.
