With only a single stereocenter there is no possibility of internal symmetry canceling its effect (that requires at least two stereocenters arranged symmetrically), so one isolated stereocenter always makes the molecule chiral.

The formula 2^n for n stereocenters gives the maximum possible number of stereoisomers; internal molecular symmetry, as seen in meso compounds, can reduce the actual distinct count below that maximum.
Both C2 (bonded to OH, H, CH3, and the rest of the chain) and C3 (bonded to Br, H, CH3, and the rest of the chain) have four different substituents, giving two independent stereocenters.
All four substituents, hydrogen, chlorine, bromine, and the vinyl group, are distinct from one another, so this carbon meets the requirement of four different groups and is a stereocenter.

In an unsymmetrical secondary alcohol, the carbon bearing OH is also bonded to a hydrogen and two alkyl chains of different length or branching, giving four distinct substituents and thus a stereocenter; this is not automatic for every alcohol, such as symmetric ones like 3-pentanol's C3.

The same four-different-groups rule applies inside rings; a ring carbon with two distinguishable ring paths, a substituent, and a hydrogen can absolutely be a stereocenter, as shown in disubstituted cyclohexanes.

A single, unopposed stereocenter is enough to generate a pair of enantiomers; this answer reflects the typical stereocenter-based route to chirality taught in intro courses, even though chirality can rarely arise without any stereocenter.

Constitutional isomers are not identical groups; as long as no two of the four substituents are exactly the same, the carbon satisfies the four-different-groups requirement and is a valid stereocenter.
enantiomers: Enantiomers are mirror images of one another that cannot be superimposed — differing at every stereocenter.
Enantiomers rotate plane-polarized light in opposite directions and behave differently only in chiral environments (e.g., with enzymes).
A racemic mixture is an equal (50:50) mixture of both enantiomers, which shows no net optical rotation.

Enantiomers are constructed from the same atoms connected in the same order (same connectivity), but they differ in how those atoms are arranged in three-dimensional space, as mirror images of each other.

Enantiomers have identical physical properties, such as boiling point, melting point, and density, in an achiral environment; they differ only in chiral interactions, such as with polarized light or other chiral molecules.

Biological receptors and enzymes are chiral structures, so they can bind the two mirror-image forms of a drug with very different affinities or effects, even though the enantiomers are chemically identical outside a chiral environment.
Enantiomers rotate plane-polarized light by equal magnitudes but in opposite directions, so the mirror-image enantiomer under the same conditions rotates light by -25 degrees.
Zero net rotation occurs either when opposite rotations from equal amounts of both enantiomers cancel out (a racemic mixture) or when the compound itself is achiral and has no rotation to begin with.

Optical rotation drops to zero upon racemization, and in some compounds the racemic mixture also crystallizes differently than the pure enantiomer (sometimes called a racemic compound), giving it a different melting point from the pure enantiomer.

Without any chiral catalyst, reagent, or influence to distinguish the two faces or configurations, a reaction that does not touch the stereocenter preserves its original configuration, yielding a single enantiomer product rather than a racemic mixture.

Since enantiomers share identical achiral physical properties like boiling point, melting point, and density, only a chiral-sensitive measurement such as optical rotation can tell the two pure enantiomer samples apart.
A racemic mixture, containing equal parts of both enantiomers, is conventionally labeled with the prefix rac- or the symbol (±), reflecting that it shows no net optical rotation.

In a standard achiral NMR or IR solvent, enantiomers give identical spectra because these techniques do not distinguish mirror-image forms; a chiral shift reagent or chiral environment is needed to tell enantiomers apart by NMR.

The enantiomer of a molecule with a single stereocenter is obtained by inverting the configuration at that stereocenter, converting R to S while keeping the same constitution, giving (S)-2-chlorobutane.

A single stereocenter has exactly two possible spatial arrangements, R and S; these two forms are mirror images of one another, so there is exactly one enantiomer for any given single-stereocenter compound.

Because enzyme active sites are chiral three-dimensional pockets built largely from chiral L-amino acids, they typically bind one enantiomer of a substrate much more effectively than its mirror image.

A chiral catalyst can favor formation of one transition state over its mirror image, leading to an enantioselective synthesis that produces one enantiomer in excess, something an achiral catalyst cannot do from achiral starting materials.

The (+) and (-) signs describe the experimentally measured direction of rotation of polarized light, which must be determined by measurement and is not something that can be predicted directly from the R or S configurational label alone.

While this is often approximately true, some racemic mixtures form a distinct crystal packing (a racemic compound) with a melting point that differs, sometimes substantially, from that of the pure enantiomer.

An achiral reagent reacting with two enantiomers experiences mirror-image transition states that are equal in energy, so the reaction rates with each enantiomer are identical unless a chiral influence is introduced.

Because enantiomers share identical boiling points, melting points, and solubilities in ordinary achiral solvents, standard separation techniques fail; a chiral resolving agent or chromatography using a chiral stationary phase is needed to separate them.
By definition, an achiral molecule is superimposable on its own mirror image, so its 'mirror image' is identical to the starting molecule rather than being a separate enantiomer.

Inverting the configuration at every stereocenter converts a molecule into its full mirror image; since both stereocenters are flipped here (R to S at both), these two structures are enantiomers of each other.

Enantiomeric excess quantifies how far a sample is from racemic by reporting the percentage by which the major enantiomer exceeds the minor one; 100 percent ee means a single pure enantiomer, while 0 percent ee means fully racemic.

Combining each of the two original enantiomers with the same chiral resolving agent produces two diastereomeric adducts, which (unlike the original enantiomers) have different melting points and solubilities and so can be separated by standard techniques; this is the classic method of resolving a racemic mixture.

An ordinary achiral stationary phase cannot distinguish the two mirror-image shapes, so both enantiomers travel through at the same rate; a chiral stationary phase forms diastereomeric-like interactions of different strengths with each enantiomer, giving them different retention times.

Refractive index and solubility in an achiral solvent are both achiral physical properties, so like melting point and boiling point they are identical for a pair of pure enantiomers, differing only in chiral interactions.

Standard NMR in an achiral solvent cannot distinguish between enantiomers, so a racemic mixture and a pure single enantiomer of the same compound give indistinguishable spectra unless a chiral shift reagent or chiral solvent is added.

Biology strongly favors a single enantiomeric series; nearly all amino acids incorporated into natural proteins are of the L configuration, reflecting the chiral machinery (itself built from L-amino acids) that synthesizes and uses them.

Enantiomeric excess is calculated as the percent major enantiomer minus the percent minor enantiomer; since the two percentages must sum to 100, an ee of 60 percent corresponds to 80 percent major and 20 percent minor (80 minus 20 equals 60).
diastereomers: Diastereomers differ in configuration at some, but not all, stereocenters, so they are not mirror images.
Diastereomers are genuinely different compounds with different shapes, so their physical properties differ, unlike enantiomers.
Cis/trans ring isomers are stereoisomers that are not mirror images of each other — classic diastereomers.
Diastereomers share the same connectivity but differ in configuration at one or more (but not all) stereocenters, meaning they are stereoisomers that are not related as mirror images.

Unlike enantiomers, diastereomers are genuinely different compounds in terms of shape and polarity in an achiral sense, so they typically have distinct physical properties such as melting point, boiling point, and solubility.
Only one of the two stereocenters (C3) has its configuration flipped while the other (C2) stays the same, so these are stereoisomers but not full mirror images, making them diastereomers.
Cis and trans forms of a disubstituted ring differ in the spatial arrangement at the ring stereocenters but are not mirror images of each other, so they fit the definition of diastereomers.

With three stereocenters there are up to eight stereoisomers total; one of them is the full mirror image (the enantiomer), and the remaining six are diastereomers that differ in configuration at only one or two of the three centers.

Because diastereomers differ in shape and interactions in ways that change melting point, boiling point, and solubility, standard separations can exploit those differences, unlike with enantiomers, which share those properties.

That equal-and-opposite relationship is specific to enantiomers; diastereomers are different compounds, so their specific rotations are generally unrelated in magnitude or sign and must be measured independently.
Epimers are a subset of diastereomers that differ in configuration at exactly one of several stereocenters while all other stereocenters remain the same, making them easy to compare directly.
Since glucose and galactose differ at only one stereocenter (C4) out of several, while sharing the same configuration everywhere else, they are epimers, a specific case of diastereomers.

By definition, diastereomers are stereoisomers, meaning they share the same molecular formula and connectivity and therefore the same set of potential stereocenters; they differ only in the spatial configuration at some of those centers.
(2R,3R)- and (2S,3S)-tartaric acid have every stereocenter inverted relative to each other, making them full mirror images, or enantiomers, rather than diastereomers.

When two stereocenters are symmetric with respect to each other (as in 2,3-dibromobutane), the R,S and S,R combinations become the same meso compound, reducing four possible stereoisomers down to three distinct ones: two enantiomers plus one meso diastereomer.

Because diastereomers have genuinely different three-dimensional shapes and steric environments (unlike enantiomers in an achiral setting), they can and often do react at different rates with the same achiral reagent.

Diastereomers are stereoisomers, meaning atoms are connected in the same order but arranged differently in space, while constitutional isomers have atoms bonded together in a genuinely different sequence or pattern.

With two independent stereocenters there are four stereoisomers; each one is the mirror image (enantiomer) of exactly one other and a diastereomer of the remaining two, since those two differ in configuration at only one of the two centers.

Cis and trans alkene isomers have the same connectivity but different spatial arrangement around the double bond, and they are not mirror images of one another, so they fall under the broader category of diastereomers.

Because diastereomers are chemically distinct compounds with different local environments around their atoms, they generally give different NMR chemical shifts and coupling patterns even in a standard achiral solvent, unlike enantiomers which appear identical.
Flipping no stereocenters at all leaves the configuration completely unchanged, so you simply reproduce the original compound rather than generating any new stereoisomer.

Since diastereomers are genuinely different compounds with potentially very different properties and activities, chemists often need diastereoselective reactions to favor the desired diastereomer rather than forming an unwanted (though separable) mixture.

With 2 pairs of enantiomers (2 relationships) among the 4 stereoisomers, the remaining pairings across the two pairs are diastereomeric — there are 4 such cross-pairs out of the 6 total pairs possible among 4 stereoisomers.
Same connectivity plus not mirror images plus not identical is exactly the definition of diastereomers — stereoisomers that are not enantiomers.
They share the same connectivity but differ in configuration at one of two stereocenters (not all of them), making them diastereomers rather than enantiomers.
Because diastereomers have genuinely different 3D shapes, their bond vectors add up differently, so their dipole moments (and other physical properties) can differ.
When a reaction favors formation of one diastereomer over another, that preference is called diastereoselectivity.
Since enantiomers are identical in every scalar physical property, their relationship (same or different) to any achiral third compound is identical as well.
Differing at only one of the two stereocenters (not both) means they are not mirror images of each other — that relationship is diastereomeric.

Since diastereomers are different compounds with different shapes, even simple achiral reagents can react with them at different rates, unlike enantiomers which need a chiral environment to be distinguished.
meso: A meso compound has stereocenters, but an internal mirror plane makes the whole molecule superimposable on its mirror image — achiral, optically inactive.
A classic meso case is a molecule with two stereocenters bearing the same substituents arranged symmetrically (e.g., meso-tartaric acid).
Because a meso compound is achiral (despite having stereocenters), it does not rotate plane-polarized light.

A meso compound has two or more stereocenters whose configurations are arranged so that an internal mirror plane relates one half of the molecule to the other, making the whole molecule superimposable on its mirror image despite containing stereocenters.

A meso compound is a single, defined achiral substance that shows zero rotation on its own because of internal symmetry, whereas a racemic mixture is a 50:50 blend of two different chiral enantiomers that together also show zero net rotation; they are conceptually different even though both give zero rotation.

Meso-tartaric acid, one of the three possible stereoisomers of tartaric acid, has two stereocenters of opposite configuration related by an internal mirror plane, making it the textbook example of a meso compound.
Tartaric acid's two stereocenters give (R,R) and (S,S) as a pair of enantiomers, while the (R,S) (equivalent to S,R by the molecule's internal symmetry) combination is the single meso diastereomer.

Meso compounds typically require at least two stereocenters positioned so that the molecule's two halves mirror each other, which is why they commonly show up in symmetrically disubstituted chains or rings.

Because a meso compound is achiral as a whole molecule due to its internal mirror symmetry, it shows zero optical rotation, the same as any other achiral substance, regardless of how many individual stereocenters it contains.

The two symmetric stereocenters in 2,3-dibromobutane give a chiral (R,R)/(S,S) enantiomeric pair and a separate achiral meso (R,S) form, totaling three stereoisomers instead of the four that unrelated stereocenters would give.

The meso form and the chiral enantiomeric pair of the same constitution are stereoisomers that are not mirror images of one another, so by definition the meso compound is a diastereomer relative to each of the chiral forms.

Due to the molecule's internal symmetry, simply rotating the (2R,3S) structure in space reproduces the (2S,3R) labeling of the same physical molecule, confirming that they are not two different compounds but one single meso compound.

A meso compound requires an internal mirror relationship between parts of the molecule, which is only possible when the relevant stereocenters sit in a symmetric arrangement; if the two stereocenters have completely different substituent sets, no such internal symmetry can form.

The cis isomer of 1,2-dibromocyclohexane has a plane of symmetry passing through the molecule that relates its two stereocenters, making it achiral overall even though each ring carbon individually qualifies as a stereocenter, so it is meso.

Unlike the cis isomer, the trans arrangement of substituents breaks the internal mirror symmetry, so trans-1,2-dibromocyclohexane exists as a genuinely chiral pair of enantiomers rather than a single meso compound.

Because the meso form is a diastereomer, not an enantiomer, of the chiral (R,R)/(S,S) pair, it is a genuinely different compound and commonly shows a distinct melting point and other physical properties from that chiral pair.

Regardless of whether the achirality comes from having no stereocenters at all or from an internal mirror symmetry relating multiple stereocenters (as in a meso compound), the underlying reason for zero optical rotation is the same: the molecule is superimposable on its own mirror image.

The definitive test is to look for an internal symmetry element, most commonly a mirror plane, that maps one half of the molecule (including its stereocenters) onto the other; simply having two stereocenters is not enough, since asymmetric stereocenters give no meso form.

Tartaric acid's two stereocenters would normally allow up to four stereoisomers, but the symmetric substitution pattern collapses the R,S and S,R combinations into one meso form, leaving three total stereoisomers: two enantiomers and one meso diastereomer.

Since the meso form and the chiral (R,R)/(S,S) pair are diastereomers of each other with different physical properties, they can be separated by standard, non-chiral separation techniques, unlike a true pair of enantiomers.

Because of the molecule's internal symmetry, the (R,S) and (S,R) labels describe the exact same physical meso molecule once you account for the fact that you can rotate the structure to match either labeling, leaving three genuinely distinct compounds overall.

While the simplest and most common meso examples have two stereocenters, molecules with larger numbers of stereocenters arranged with internal symmetry (including some odd totals when one center lies on the symmetry element itself) can also produce meso forms, so an even count is not a strict requirement.
Being achiral, a meso compound does not rotate plane-polarized light at all — its specific rotation is 0.
Meso forms can occur in molecules with more than two stereocenters as long as the overall structure has an internal mirror plane or similar symmetry relating the configurations.

A meso compound is one molecule that is internally achiral; a racemic mixture is a blend of two different, still-chiral molecules (the two enantiomers) that happens to show zero net rotation because they cancel each other out.

A meso form requires an internal symmetry element (commonly a mirror plane) relating parts of the molecule to each other; this is possible with three stereocenters arranged symmetrically, not just with two.

While R/S labels can sometimes hint at symmetric relationships (like R,S for a symmetric molecule), confirming the meso form reliably requires checking the actual structure for an internal mirror plane, since naming conventions alone can be ambiguous for more complex cases.

Although the two halves of a meso compound are related by an internal mirror plane, a chiral reagent experiences them as distinguishable environments (similar to how enantiomers are distinguished by chiral reagents), so reactivity at each half can differ.
Meso-tartaric acid is a diastereomer of the chiral tartaric acid enantiomers (which share one melting point as a pair), so as a genuinely different compound it has its own distinct melting point.

A meso form requires the kind of internal symmetry that only arises when the two (or more) stereocenters are related by equivalent substituent patterns; an unsymmetric arrangement has no such mirror relationship available.
rs-configuration: CIP priority ranks by atomic number at the first point of difference, moving outward if there’s a tie.
Clockwise with the lowest priority group pointing away = R (rectus); counterclockwise = S (sinister).
Priority is based on atomic number at the point of attachment — bromine (35) outranks chlorine (17).
The Cahn-Ingold-Prelog (CIP) rules rank substituents mainly by the atomic number of the atom directly bonded to the stereocenter, moving outward to break ties as needed.
By CIP convention, a clockwise path from the highest to the second to the third priority group, viewed with the lowest priority pointing away, defines the R (rectus, right-handed) configuration.
CIP priority is based on atomic number, not electronegativity; bromine (atomic number 35) outranks chlorine (atomic number 17) regardless of which one is more electronegative.
When the directly attached atoms tie, CIP rules direct you to compare the sets of atoms attached one bond farther out, continuing outward until a difference in atomic number is found.

CIP rules treat a double bond as if each atom were singly bonded to a duplicate 'phantom' copy of the atom on the other end, so a carbon double-bonded to oxygen is treated as bonded to oxygen twice for priority purposes.

The R/S rule strictly requires viewing with the lowest-priority group pointing away; if it points toward the viewer instead, the observed clockwise or counterclockwise sense must be reversed to get the true configuration, so an apparent clockwise trace actually corresponds to S.
Priority follows the atomic number of the directly attached atom: oxygen (8) outranks nitrogen (7), which outranks carbon (6), which outranks hydrogen (1), giving the order OH ≻ NH2 ≻ CH3 ≻ H.
Ranking is by atomic number of the attached atom: bromine (35) outranks chlorine (17), which outranks oxygen (8), which outranks hydrogen (1), giving Br ≻ Cl ≻ OH ≻ H.

R and S describe the three-dimensional spatial configuration based on CIP priority rules, while (+) and (-) describe the experimentally measured direction of optical rotation; there is no simple, universal rule linking R/S directly to the sign of rotation, it must be measured.
Numbering each stereocenter and assigning its own R or S label lets a single name fully specify the configuration at every stereocenter in a molecule with more than one, as in (2R,3S)-.

R/S labels depend entirely on the relative CIP priority ranking of substituents; if a substituent is replaced with a group that reorders the priorities (for example replacing an H with a D, which outranks H), the same physical spatial arrangement can receive a different descriptor.

All three carbon groups tie at carbon, so compare their substituent sets. The double bond to oxygen counts twice, making -CHO (O, O, H), which beats -CH2OH at (O, H, H) at the first point of difference. Duplicating the atoms of a multiple bond is the step people skip.

Because both substituents tie at the first carbon, CIP rules require comparing the sets of atoms (real and duplicated, for multiple bonds) attached to that carbon to determine which substituent truly outranks the other.

When a lone pair functions as the fourth 'substituent' at a stereocenter (for example, in some nitrogen or sulfur stereocenters), it is assigned the lowest possible priority, effectively ranked as if it had an atomic number of zero, below even hydrogen.

CIP priority for atoms directly attached increases with atomic number, and among the halogens iodine (53) has the highest atomic number, followed by bromine (35), chlorine (17), and fluorine (9) last.

R/S configuration is an intrinsic property of the actual three-dimensional arrangement of atoms; simply rotating or redrawing the same molecule without breaking any bonds cannot change its true configuration, even if it looks different on paper.

Both groups tie at the first carbon (C,H,H becomes irrelevant until you look one bond further); isopropyl's first carbon is attached to two carbons and a hydrogen (C,C,H), outranking n-propyl's first carbon, which is attached to only one carbon and two hydrogens (C,H,H).
A counterclockwise path from highest to second to third priority, viewed properly with the lowest-priority group pointing away, defines the S (sinister, left-handed) configuration by CIP convention.

The R descriptor is a configurational label assigned purely from applying CIP priority rules to the four groups at a specific stereocenter; it says nothing directly about observed optical rotation or alkene geometry.
Comparing the directly attached atoms Cl (17), O (8), C (6), and H (1), hydrogen has by far the lowest atomic number, so -H is the lowest-priority substituent among these four.

CIP rules rank substituents by atomic number at the point of attachment, not atomic mass — this is why isotopes (same atomic number, different mass) are ranked by mass only as a tiebreaker after atomic number ties.
When atomic number is tied (both are hydrogen, Z=1), CIP rules break the tie using atomic mass — deuterium, being heavier, ranks slightly higher than protium.

The four attached groups must be different from each other, but they don't need to differ at the very first atom — e.g., -CH2CH3 and -CH2CH2CH3 are both carbon-attached but are still different groups that can be ranked by CIP rules going further out.

All three carbon groups tie at the first atom (C), so you compare what's attached to each of those carbons: Br (Z=35) outranks Cl (Z=17), which outranks the three H's on plain -CH3, giving -CH2Br > -CH2Cl > -CH3, with -H lowest overall.

If the lowest-priority group already points away from the viewer in the drawing, you can read the R/S assignment directly from the remaining three groups' clockwise/counterclockwise order without any further manipulation.

Both -NH2 and -NHCH3 attach through nitrogen, so they tie at the first atom; you must then compare what's attached to that nitrogen (H,H vs. H,C) to break the tie, with -NHCH3 ranking higher since carbon outranks hydrogen.

The priority ranking alone only tells you which group is 1st, 2nd, 3rd, and 4th — you still need the actual 3D geometry (which way the groups point) to determine whether 1→2→3 traces clockwise or counterclockwise.
fischer: By convention, horizontal bonds in a Fischer projection come toward the viewer; vertical bonds go back into the page.
One swap inverts configuration at that center, generating the enantiomer (for a single stereocenter) or flipping that one center’s configuration in a larger molecule.
Fischer projections of sugars are drawn with the carbon backbone vertical and the most oxidized carbon (e.g., the aldehyde in an aldose) at the top.
By the standard Fischer projection convention, horizontal bonds are understood to project out of the page toward the viewer, while vertical bonds project into the page, away from the viewer.

Vertical bonds in a Fischer projection are conventionally drawn going into the page, away from the viewer, which together with the horizontal (toward-viewer) bonds encodes the full tetrahedral geometry in a flat 2D drawing.
A single swap of any two groups at a stereocenter in a Fischer projection corresponds to inverting that center's configuration, which converts the molecule into its mirror image, the enantiomer.

Each single swap inverts the configuration once; performing two swaps inverts it twice, returning the drawing to represent the same original configuration, even though the groups' positions on paper have changed.

Fischer projections of sugars are conventionally drawn with the carbon backbone running vertically and the carbon with the highest oxidation state (such as the aldehyde carbon, C1) placed at or near the top of the structure.

A full 180-degree in-plane rotation of a Fischer projection preserves the relationship of toward-viewer and away-from-viewer bonds, so it represents the same molecule with the same configuration, unlike a 90-degree rotation, which is not allowed.

A 90-degree rotation swaps which bonds point toward versus away from the viewer (turning former horizontal, toward-viewer bonds into vertical, away-from-viewer bonds), which actually inverts the apparent configuration, so it is not a valid operation for preserving identity.

Cyclically rotating any three of the four groups around the stereocenter while keeping the fourth fixed is a valid manipulation that preserves the actual configuration, producing an equivalent representation of the same molecule.
By the historical convention that defines the D and L sugar series, D-glyceraldehyde is drawn with its -OH group on the right side of the Fischer projection at the stereocenter.

By convention, a sugar is classified as D or L based on whether the hydroxyl group at the stereocenter nearest the bottom of the Fischer projection (the reference carbon) points to the right (D) or left (L).

While horizontal bonds do point toward the viewer and vertical bonds away, the specific spatial arrangement implied (with the molecule's backbone curving away from the viewer at the top and bottom) means a careless direct translation can give an incorrect 3D picture unless you apply the conversion method consistently and carefully.

Inverting the configuration at only one of two stereocenters while leaving the other unchanged produces a stereoisomer that is not the full mirror image, making the two structures diastereomers rather than enantiomers.
Inverting the configuration at every stereocenter in the molecule produces its full mirror image, so swapping groups at both stereocenters converts the Fischer projection into that of the enantiomer.
L-glyceraldehyde is the enantiomer of D-glyceraldehyde, differing only by a single swap at the one stereocenter, placing its -OH group on the left side of the Fischer projection instead of the right.

Fischer projections are actually especially useful for molecules with several stereocenters in a chain, such as sugars, because stacking the centers vertically makes it easy to compare configurations at each position at a glance.

Because horizontal bonds point toward the viewer and vertical bonds point away, you must check which type of bond holds the lowest-priority group; if it's on a horizontal bond (toward the viewer), the observed clockwise/counterclockwise sense of the other three groups must be reversed to get the true configuration.

Because a meso compound has an internal mirror plane relating parts of the molecule, its Fischer projection often visibly shows the top half mirroring the bottom half (or similar symmetric patterns), which is part of why Fischer projections are convenient for spotting meso compounds.

A 90-degree (or any odd multiple of 90-degree) in-plane rotation swaps which bonds point toward versus away from the viewer, which inverts the configuration and therefore is not a valid identity-preserving manipulation, unlike a full 180-degree rotation or a three-group rotation.
A standard aldohexose has its aldehyde at C1 and a terminal CH2OH at C6, leaving C2, C3, C4, and C5 as the four carbons that typically bear a hydroxyl group and qualify as stereocenters.
A full 180° in-plane rotation is equivalent to two 90° rotations (or viewing from the opposite side twice), which is a valid symmetry operation that leaves the represented molecule unchanged.
By convention, D/L sugar nomenclature is based on the configuration at the stereocenter farthest from the carbonyl group (for glucose, C5), with -OH on the right defining D.
Swapping the two horizontal groups at a lone stereocenter is a single swap, which inverts configuration and produces the enantiomer.

Flipping only one of two stereocenters (leaving the other unchanged) changes the relative configuration between the centers, producing a diastereomer rather than the enantiomer (which requires flipping both).
By long-standing convention (especially for sugars), the carbon chain is numbered from the top, with the most oxidized carbon placed at the top of the projection.
A three-group rotation (holding one group fixed and cycling the other three) is a valid symmetry operation for Fischer projections that preserves the molecule's identity, just like a full 180° flip.

There is a well-defined, consistent mapping from Fischer horizontal-group positions to 'up' or 'down' substituent positions in the Haworth projection, which is exactly why Fischer projections remain useful for sugar chemistry.
A meso compound's defining feature is an internal mirror plane; in the Fischer projection of meso-tartaric acid, this shows up as the top half being a direct mirror reflection of the bottom half.
sn2: SN2 ("substitution, nucleophilic, bimolecular") happens in one step: the nucleophile attacks from the backside as the leaving group departs.
Backside attack requires open space behind the leaving group — methyl/primary carbons have the least steric hindrance.
Backside attack forces the other three groups to flip to the opposite side as the new bond forms — this inversion is called a Walden inversion.
SN2 is second order overall and first order in each reactant, so rate is directly proportional to nucleophile concentration.
SN2 needs a nucleophile that is both reactive (strong) and able to physically reach the backside of the carbon, so small size matters as much as strength.
The single concerted step involves both the substrate and the incoming nucleophile, so both concentrations appear in the rate law.
Polar aprotic solvents dissolve ions without hydrogen-bonding to the nucleophile, so the nucleophile stays highly reactive and free to attack.
Backside attack lets the nucleophile's electron pair align with the antibonding orbital of the C-leaving group bond, which is what drives inversion.
Tertiary carbons are surrounded by three alkyl groups that sterically block the nucleophile from approaching from the backside, so SN2 is essentially shut down.
In the transition state the carbon is partially bonded to both the incoming nucleophile and the departing leaving group, giving five groups arranged around it.
With no substituents around the reacting carbon at all, the nucleophile has a completely open path for backside attack.
Bond-breaking and bond-forming happen simultaneously in one transition state, unlike the two-step SN1 mechanism.
SN2 rate decreases as alkyl substitution increases because more groups crowd the backside approach path; methyl is fastest and tertiary essentially does not react.
Iodide is the weakest base of the four and the most stable once it leaves, making it the best leaving group and giving the fastest reaction.
Steric hindrance isn't limited to the reacting carbon itself; a bulky neighboring group can crowd the backside approach just as effectively.
Removing a proton from the nucleophile to generate its anion greatly increases its electron-donating ability, so the charged species attacks much faster.
SN2 rate depends directly on nucleophile concentration and strength, while SN1 rate depends only on substrate ionization, which doesn't involve the nucleophile at all.
Backside attack forces the three remaining groups to flip through the carbon like an umbrella turning inside out, inverting the spatial arrangement.
The trigonal planar geometry and the pi electron density around an sp2 carbon prevent the clean backside trajectory that SN2 requires.
This classic term describes the clean flip in spatial arrangement caused by backside nucleophilic attack.
Backside attack means the nucleophile approaches directly opposite the leaving group, so the two are roughly in a straight line through the central carbon at the transition state.
A polarizable nucleophile, like iodide, can more easily distort its electron cloud toward the electrophilic carbon during the approach, even if it is a comparatively weak base.

When the leaving group is axial, the nucleophile can approach from the opposite axial direction without the ring itself blocking the path; an equatorial leaving group has its backside trajectory obstructed by the ring.
Even though no cation forms in SN2, the nearby double bond can partially delocalize electron density in the transition state, lowering its energy.
Steric bulk mainly interferes with the tight backside approach needed for substitution, while the base can still reach outward hydrogens for elimination.
Solvating (caging) the nucleophile with hydrogen bonds lowers its ground-state energy and effectively shields it, so more energy is needed to free it for attack.
SN2's single transition state has an absolute geometric requirement (backside approach); no amount of favorable electronics can compensate if that pathway is physically blocked.
Every one of these factors independently speeds up SN2: an open backside path, a reactive unshielded nucleophile, and a stable departing group.
Protic solvents solvate small anionic nucleophiles tightly through hydrogen bonding, tying up the electron density that would otherwise attack the substrate.
Azide attacks from the backside in a single concerted step, flipping the spatial arrangement at the carbon that held the leaving group.
sn1: SN1 ("unimolecular") has two steps: ionization to form a carbocation, then nucleophilic attack on that cation.
Tertiary carbocations are the most stable (hyperconjugation/inductive effects from 3 alkyl groups), so SN1 favors tertiary substrates.
Once the carbocation forms, it is planar (sp²) and symmetric, so the nucleophile can attack from either face with roughly equal probability, giving racemization.
SN1 is unimolecular in its rate-determining step, so only the substrate's concentration appears in the rate law.
The leaving group departs first to form a planar carbocation, and only then does the nucleophile attack in a separate second step.
Breaking the C-leaving group bond without any assistance is the slow, high-energy step; capturing the cation afterward is fast.
Since ionization is rate-determining, anything that stabilizes the departing group once it leaves speeds up the whole reaction.
The flat carbocation intermediate can be attacked from either face, so the product is typically a racemic (or nearly racemic) mixture rather than cleanly inverted.
Polar protic solvents can hydrogen-bond to and stabilize both the developing carbocation and the departing anion, speeding up the ionization step.
Methyl and primary carbocations are far too unstable to form at any appreciable rate, so ionization never gets going.
Because the nucleophile only participates in the fast second step, changing its concentration does not change the overall observed rate.
Since the rate-determining step involves only the substrate breaking apart, the overall rate law is first order in substrate.
More alkyl substituents donate electron density and provide hyperconjugation to the empty p-orbital, stabilizing the positive charge; tertiary cations are stabilized the most.
Because SN1 generates a real, freestanding carbocation intermediate, that intermediate has time to rearrange to a more stable cation before being trapped.
A neighboring hydrogen can migrate with its bonding electrons to the cationic carbon, shifting the positive charge to a position where it is better stabilized.
The adjacent pi system spreads the positive charge over multiple atoms through resonance, which lowers the cation's energy similarly to extra alkyl substitution.
A weaker carbon-halogen bond combined with a more stable leaving anion makes ionization easier and faster for the iodide.
Since the slow step only involves the substrate ionizing, even a weak nucleophile can still efficiently capture the carbocation once it forms.
The planar carbocation can in principle be attacked equally from both faces, giving near-racemization, though ion pairing can sometimes partially shield one face and skew the ratio slightly.
A more polar, ionizing solvent stabilizes the separating charges (the carbocation and the departing anion) as the bond breaks, lowering the activation energy.
Vinylic and aryl cations place the positive charge in an sp2 orbital that is not well stabilized by the adjacent pi system, making ionization prohibitively unfavorable.
SN1's rate-determining step is ionization, which benefits specifically from a solvent that can stabilize charged species through hydrogen bonding.
Since the rate-determining step is ionization, anything that lowers the solvent's overall polarity and ability to stabilize charge slows the reaction, even if both solvents are polar protic.
A carbocation intermediate has a finite lifetime in which nearby groups can migrate with their bonding electrons if doing so reaches a more stable, lower-energy structure.
Ionization is an equilibrium; adding more of the product anion pushes that equilibrium back toward the un-ionized substrate, slowing the forward (productive) rate.
Before it fully diffuses away, the leaving group can linger near one face of the cation as a tight ion pair, partially blocking nucleophilic attack from that side.
A benzylic cation can spread its positive charge into the ring through resonance in addition to any alkyl hyperconjugation, adding extra stabilization beyond a purely alkyl-substituted cation.
SN1 rate tracks carbocation stability, and stability increases from primary to secondary to tertiary, so the tertiary chloride ionizes fastest and the primary essentially does not react.
Once the carbocation forms, nothing commits it to one specific fate; it is simply captured by whichever available species reacts with it first.
Because the nucleophile isn't involved in the rate-determining step, a solvent's ionizing power (not its nucleophilicity) is what controls SN1 rate.
e1: E1 and SN1 both begin by ionizing the leaving group to form a carbocation; E1 then loses a proton instead of being attacked by a nucleophile.
E1 goes through a carbocation and loses a proton to give the most stable (most substituted) alkene — the Zaitsev product.
E1 and SN1 share the same first step (ionization to a carbocation); from there the cation either loses a proton (E1, elimination) or is attacked by a nucleophile (SN1, substitution).
Just like SN1, the slow step is ionization to form the carbocation; deprotonation afterward is fast.
Both mechanisms share the same first step, the unassisted departure of the leaving group to generate a carbocation, which depends only on substrate concentration.
A base plucks off a hydrogen from a neighboring (beta) carbon, and the electrons from that C-H bond form the new pi bond.
Because deprotonation in E1 happens fast and isn't rate-limiting, even a weak base can remove the proton once the cation has formed; strict base strength or geometry is not required.
Since the first step is identical to SN1, E1 needs a substrate capable of forming a reasonably stable carbocation.
Heat favors elimination pathways generally, and since the rate-determining step doesn't need a strong base, a weak one is often sufficient to pull off the final proton.
E1 is first order overall because its rate-determining step, ionization, only involves the substrate.
Because E1 shares the same carbocation intermediate as SN1, that cation can rearrange to a more stable structure before a proton is ever removed.
Losing the leaving group leaves behind an empty p-orbital on a planar, trigonal carbon, exactly as in SN1's carbocation intermediate.
More alkyl groups attached to the double bond carbons donate electron density into the pi system, lowering its overall energy and making that alkene more stable and, usually, more abundant.
Elimination pathways generally have a more favorable entropy of activation, so heating a reaction mixture tends to push the product distribution toward more alkene.
If the initially formed cation rearranges to a more stable one, the final elimination step occurs from that rearranged structure, changing the product's carbon skeleton.

The chloride leaves from C3, which carries a methyl and two ethyls. Losing a hydrogen from either ethyl gives the trisubstituted 3-methylpent-2-ene; losing one from the methyl gives the disubstituted 2-ethyl-1-butene. Zaitsev takes the more substituted alkene.

Heat favors the entropically-preferred elimination pathway, and having an actual base present (rather than just a weak nucleophilic solvent) makes proton removal more competitive with nucleophilic capture.
Since the leaving group and the beta-hydrogen depart in two separate steps through a freely rotating carbocation, there's no need for them to have been aligned in any particular way beforehand.
E1's rate-determining step is identical to SN1's, so any solvent effect that helps stabilize a developing carbocation speeds up E1 specifically.
Because the second (deprotonation) step is fast and not rate-limiting, the concentration of the base influences product selectivity far more than it influences overall reaction rate.
With no strict geometric constraint like E2's anti-periplanar requirement, E1 product selection is governed mainly by the relative stability of the possible alkenes.
Elimination proceeds from whichever cation is actually present at that moment, so if rearrangement occurs first, the final alkene reflects the new, rearranged carbon skeleton.

Each distinct carbocation present in solution, whether original or rearranged, has its own competing fates (substitution or elimination), so the overall outcome can be a mixture of several structurally different products.

Since the cation can rotate freely before deprotonation, there is no anti-periplanar-style constraint linking starting material stereochemistry to product alkene geometry; stability considerations dominate instead.
Since E1's rate-determining step is the same ionization step as SN1's, a better leaving group accelerates E1 in exactly the same way it accelerates SN1.
E1's rate-determining ionization step is highly sensitive to how well the solvent can stabilize developing charge, so diluting the more polar water with less polar ethanol slows that step.

Because the cation exists as a discrete intermediate, there is more opportunity for the more stable transition state (leading to the more stable alkene) to be favored, compared to E2's single, more geometry-constrained step.
Ionization is an equilibrium step; adding more of the anion product (common ion effect) shifts that equilibrium backward and slows the overall forward reaction.
Unlike E2, where the base must be strong and well-positioned to drive a single slow concerted step, E1's second step is inherently fast and forgiving of a less capable base.
Following Zaitsev's rule, E1 favors loss of the beta-hydrogen that generates the more stable, more highly substituted double bond.
e2: E2 ("bimolecular elimination") is concerted: base removes a proton as the leaving group departs, all in one step.
Anti-periplanar alignment lets the breaking C–H bond’s electrons align with the empty orbital forming as the leaving group departs — the best orbital overlap.
A bulky base struggles to approach the crowded carbon for SN2 backside attack, but has no trouble reaching an exposed, less hindered proton for E2.
Since the base participates directly in the single concerted step, both the substrate and the base concentrations appear in the rate law.
Proton removal, pi bond formation, and loss of the leaving group all happen at the same time in a single transition state.
All of this bond reorganization occurs in one coordinated transition state, which is what makes E2 concerted rather than stepwise.
A strong base is needed to remove the relatively unreactive beta-hydrogen in a single concerted step, and bases that are poor nucleophiles help elimination compete successfully against substitution.
Removing a beta-hydrogen, rather than the leaving group's carbon itself, is what allows the new double bond to form between those two adjacent carbons.
Since base concentration appears directly in the E2 rate law, doubling it doubles the reaction rate (all else equal).

Unlike SN2 (blocked at tertiary carbons) or SN1/E1 (essentially unavailable at primary carbons), E2 doesn't require carbocation formation or backside attack at the leaving-group carbon, so it tolerates all substitution levels.
E2 doesn't need to approach the crowded leaving-group carbon directly; the base simply needs access to a hydrogen on an adjacent carbon, which is much less hindered.
If there's only a single position from which a beta-hydrogen can be removed, there is only one possible carbon-skeleton outcome for the alkene, though E and Z isomers may still both form.
Small bases can reach any available beta-hydrogen, so the more stable transition state leading to the more substituted alkene is generally favored.
A bulky base has trouble reaching the more crowded, more substituted hydrogens, so it preferentially grabs a more exposed, less hindered hydrogen, giving the less substituted alkene.
This geometry lets the orbitals that are breaking and forming align properly in a single transition state, minimizing torsional strain as the pi bond develops.
The chair conformation's geometry means only two adjacent axial groups are oriented 180 degrees apart from each other, which is the alignment E2 needs.

A small strong base reaches the internal beta-hydrogens easily, so the more stable, more substituted double bond is favored, and the less sterically strained E geometry is typically the major stereoisomer.
The transition state leading to the E alkene generally has larger groups positioned farther apart, lowering steric strain and making it the lower-energy, more commonly favored pathway.
Because E2 is concerted and doesn't generate a free ionic intermediate, it doesn't depend as strongly on a solvent's ability to stabilize charge the way the ionization step of SN1/E1 does.
Hydroxide is simultaneously a good nucleophile and a good base, so on a substrate that is accessible enough for backside attack, both substitution and elimination pathways remain viable and compete.
Since the leaving group departs in the same single step as proton removal, a more stable, easier-to-lose leaving group lowers the activation energy for E2 just as it does for SN2.
Without a hydrogen positioned anti-periplanar to the leaving group on that side, the required transition-state geometry simply cannot be reached, so that elimination pathway is blocked.
E2's strict geometric requirement can override simple product-stability preferences; if the only anti-periplanar hydrogen happens to give the less stable alkene, that's still the product that forms.

Because only certain conformations place a given hydrogen anti-periplanar to the leaving group, the starting material's three-dimensional arrangement directly dictates which hydrogen is removed and therefore the resulting double bond geometry.

A kinetic isotope effect appears specifically when the bond to the isotope is broken in the rate-determining step; since E2's only step breaks the beta C-H bond, while SN2's step does not touch that bond at all, only E2 shows this effect.
Steric bulk in the base both hinders its approach somewhat and redirects it toward whichever hydrogen is least crowded, which usually leads to the less substituted alkene and less competing SN2.
Since no cationic intermediate ever forms in E2, the usual instability of a primary carbocation is simply irrelevant to whether E2 can proceed.
When geometry restricts the reaction to only one accessible hydrogen, that constraint, not which alkene would otherwise be most stable, controls which product actually forms.

Because the leaving group departs in the same concerted step as proton removal, a more stable, weaker-base leaving group like tosylate lowers the activation energy for elimination just as it does for substitution.

As basicity increases sharply, a reagent's tendency to grab a proton (driving elimination) increasingly outcompetes its tendency to attack the carbon directly (driving substitution), even without added steric bulk.
substrate-effects: Bulky strong bases have trouble doing backside attack (poor SN2) but easily deprotonate, favoring E2.
Polar protic solvents solvate (stabilize) carbocations and leaving groups well, favoring the ionization step in SN1/E1.
Primary carbons have minimal steric hindrance for backside attack and cannot stabilize a carbocation well, so SN2 dominates with a decent nucleophile.
With essentially no steric hindrance at the carbon and no ability to form a stable carbocation, backside attack (SN2) dominates.

Tertiary carbons can form stable carbocations, polar protic solvent stabilizes that ionization, and a weak base/nucleophile can't force a bimolecular pathway, so unimolecular substitution and elimination dominate.
No matter how strong or small the nucleophile, the geometric backside approach is physically obstructed at a tertiary carbon.
With minimal alkyl substitution to stabilize the positive charge, a primary cation's energy is too high to form at a useful rate under normal conditions.
SN2's requirement for a clear backside approach is a geometric barrier that no change in reagent or solvent can overcome at a tertiary carbon.
Secondary carbons are sterically open enough for some backside attack yet can also form a moderately stable carbocation, so the outcome hinges heavily on the specific reagents and solvent chosen.
Polar aprotic solvents dissolve ionic reagents without caging the nucleophile/base through hydrogen bonding, keeping it highly reactive for a bimolecular attack.

Bulk mainly matters where it blocks backside attack; on a primary carbon, which is already quite open, a bulky base can still give substantial SN2 unless it is extremely hindered or other factors intervene.

Substrate substitution pattern determines both whether backside attack is geometrically possible and whether a stable carbocation can form, which are the two gateway requirements for these mechanisms.
A primary substrate with an open backside path, a strong unhindered nucleophile, and a polar aprotic solvent that doesn't shield the nucleophile is the textbook setup for SN2.
A tertiary substrate in an ionizing polar protic solvent with only a weak nucleophile present is set up to ionize on its own, giving substitution and elimination from the resulting carbocation.
A strong base on a secondary substrate tends to favor elimination, especially with a base that is reasonably hindered, though some competing substitution is still possible.
A strong, minimally basic nucleophile in a polar aprotic solvent favors attacking the carbon directly rather than removing a proton, pushing the reaction toward substitution.
Because azide is a much better nucleophile than base, and the solvent keeps it highly reactive, the reaction favors attacking the carbon over removing a proton.
Forming two separate, more freely moving product pieces (the alkene and, e.g., water) from one substrate is entropically favorable, and that advantage becomes more significant as temperature rises.
SN2 is blocked by the tertiary carbon's sterics, so a strong base reaching an available beta-hydrogen drives E2, and its bulk biases the outcome toward the less hindered, less substituted alkene.
Elimination requires a beta-hydrogen on an adjacent carbon, and methyl carbons have no adjacent carbon whatsoever, so substitution is the only mechanistic option available regardless of base bulk.
Steric crowding doesn't have to come from the reacting carbon alone; a hindered neighboring group plus a bulky base together can tip the balance toward elimination even at a formally primary carbon.

Steric hindrance for SN2 purposes depends on what's crowding the approach path, not strictly on the formal classification of the reacting carbon; a bulky neighbor can make substitution difficult even at a primary center.

Ionizing power and nucleophile/base reactivity are somewhat independent levers; a solvent that strongly favors ionization can tip the balance toward unimolecular pathways even when a competent bimolecular reagent is technically present, partly because that same solvent also dampens the nucleophile's effective reactivity.

Since the bimolecular rate laws depend directly on reagent concentration while the unimolecular ones do not, pushing up reagent concentration makes the bimolecular pathway increasingly competitive, even on a substrate that might otherwise favor ionization.
Both families of mechanism have a hard requirement that this solvent and reagent combination fails to meet: no ionizing power for SN1/E1, and no reactive species at all for SN2/E2.
Even among polar protic solvents, overall polarity/ionizing power can vary; diluting water with a less polar component lowers that ionizing power and slows the rate-determining ionization step.

Some barriers are about rate (how fast something happens) while others are about feasibility (whether it can happen at all); the tertiary SN2 backside-attack problem is of the second, more absolute kind.

Elimination requires the reagent to act as a base, and a species can be an excellent nucleophile while still being a poor base, which is exactly the combination that shuts down the elimination pathway here.

Protic solvents work against bimolecular pathways by caging the nucleophile/base through hydrogen bonding, and simultaneously work in favor of unimolecular pathways by stabilizing developing charge, so both effects push the balance the same direction.

SN2 is blocked at tertiary carbons and SN1/E1 are essentially blocked at primary carbons, but E2 needs neither backside access at the reacting carbon nor carbocation stability, so it tolerates the widest range of substrate types.
alkene-structure: Each alkene carbon has 3 regions of electron density (2 sigma bonds + 1 pi bond counted as part of the double bond group) — sp², trigonal planar, ~120°.
Each ring and each pi bond (in a double bond or triple bond counts twice) contributes one degree of unsaturation — 1 ring + 1 double bond = 2.
Rotating one carbon relative to the other would misalign the parallel p orbitals forming the pi bond, breaking that overlap — this restricted rotation is what gives rise to cis/trans alkene isomers.
Each alkene carbon forms three sigma bonds (to two substituents and the other alkene carbon) plus one pi bond from an unhybridized p orbital, which requires sp2 hybridization with 120° bond angles.
Each pi bond or ring removes two hydrogens relative to the saturated alkane formula CnH2n+2, so one double bond gives CnH2n.
CnH2n+2 is the alkane (fully saturated) formula. Alkenes have one fewer degree of saturation, so they follow CnH2n.
A double bond always consists of one sigma bond (head-on overlap) and one pi bond (side-by-side overlap of p orbitals); you cannot have two sigma bonds between the same two atoms.
The additional pi bond in a double bond pulls the two carbons closer together, shortening the bond compared to a single (sigma-only) bond.
Ethylene has one C-C sigma bond and four C-H sigma bonds (5 total), plus one pi bond that is not counted as a sigma bond.
Rotating one carbon relative to the other would require breaking the pi bond's side-by-side p-orbital overlap, so geometric (cis/trans) isomers are locked in place at room temperature.
Degree of unsaturation = (2(5)+2-10)/2 = (12-10)/2 = 1, consistent with one double bond and no ring.
The suffix -ene specifically designates a double bond in the parent chain, as in propene or 2-butene.
More substituted alkenes are stabilized by additional alkyl groups donating electron density (hyperconjugation) into the pi system, so tetrasubstituted alkenes are typically the most stable.

Cis/trans only works cleanly when it's obvious which groups are 'similar'; when each carbon carries two different substituents, CIP priority rules assign E (opposite, higher priorities) or Z (same side, higher priorities) unambiguously.
DoU = (2×6+2-10)/2 = 2, which could correspond to two double bonds, one ring plus one double bond, or one triple bond.
A triple bond itself counts as two degrees of unsaturation (two pi bonds), so DoU=2 is consistent with one triple bond, two double bonds, two rings, or one ring plus one double bond.
CIP priority is assigned first by atomic number at the point of attachment; chlorine (Z=17) outranks a carbon-based methyl group (Z=6) regardless of what else is in the molecule.
If either alkene carbon has two identical substituents, there is no distinct 'other side' to compare, so no cis/trans isomerism exists; each carbon needs two different groups.
Each sp2 carbon retains one unhybridized p orbital oriented perpendicular to the plane of the three sp2 orbitals; side-by-side overlap of these two p orbitals creates the pi bond.

Pi electrons sit above and below the molecular plane, farther from the nuclei and more accessible to electrophiles, making the C=C pi bond a reactive site compared to the strong, low-energy C-C and C-H sigma bonds in alkanes.
A triple bond contributes two degrees of unsaturation versus one for a double bond, removing two additional hydrogens, so alkynes follow CnH2n-2 while alkenes follow CnH2n.
In the cis isomer, the two methyl groups point to the same side of the double bond and crowd each other, raising the molecule's energy; in trans they point to opposite sides, minimizing steric clash.
DoU = (2×10+2-16)/2 = 3, consistent with, for example, one ring and two double bonds, a common pattern in monoterpenes.
One ring contributes 1 and each of the three pi bonds contributes 1, for a total DoU of 1+3=4, matching benzene's formula C6H6: (2×6+2-6)/2=4.

An sp2 alkene carbon needs its three attached groups and itself to lie in one plane; in small fused or bridged ring systems the bridgehead geometry can't twist into that planar arrangement without severe strain (this limitation is summarized by Bredt's rule).

Placing the ring's two connecting chains on opposite faces of the double bond (trans) in a small ring requires bond angles far from ideal, introducing enormous strain; only larger rings (roughly 8+ membered) can accommodate a stable trans-cycloalkene.

Rotating one carbon 90° relative to the other misaligns the two p orbitals so they can no longer overlap, effectively breaking the pi bond; this costs far more energy (~260 kJ/mol) than is available from ordinary thermal motion.
Because each alkene carbon is sp2 hybridized, its three sigma-bonded groups (including the other alkene carbon) are arranged trigonally in one plane, making the whole six-atom C=C unit planar.
Hydrogenation converts all alkene isomers to the same alkane product, so the isomer that starts out lower in energy (more stable) releases less heat upon hydrogenation.

Alkene stability generally increases with the number of alkyl substituents directly attached to the double-bond carbons, due to increased hyperconjugative and inductive electron donation into the pi system; tetrasubstituted alkenes are the most stable of these options.
addition-reactions: Addition reactions break the reactive pi bond and add two new groups, one to each former alkene carbon.
Alkenes are electron-rich at the pi bond and act as nucleophiles toward an incoming electrophile, forming a carbocation (or similar) intermediate.
Br₂ is polarized by the approaching alkene and forms a bromonium ion intermediate, a classic electrophilic addition across the double bond.
Addition reactions convert the pi bond into two new sigma bonds to the added atoms, removing one degree of unsaturation from the starting alkene.
Addition reactions consume the pi bond, converting an alkene (or alkyne) into a more saturated product, which decreases the degree of unsaturation, not increases it.
H2 doesn't react with alkenes on its own at a useful rate; a transition metal catalyst (commonly Pt, Pd, or Ni) adsorbs H2 and the alkene on its surface, allowing the addition to occur.
Br2 adds across the double bond, putting one bromine on each former alkene carbon, giving the vicinal dihalide 1,2-dibromoethane.
Hydration is the addition of water (formally H and OH) across the pi bond, converting the alkene into an alcohol.
The electron-rich pi bond of the alkene attacks the electrophilic halogen, and both halogen atoms end up added to the former double-bond carbons, making this an electrophilic addition.
Colored Br2 is consumed as it adds across a reactive pi bond, turning colorless; alkanes lack this reactive pi bond and don't decolorize Br2 without light or heat.
Hydrogenation specifically refers to the addition of molecular hydrogen (H2) across a multiple bond, typically with a metal catalyst.
HX adds H to one carbon and the halogen X to the other, converting the alkene directly into an alkyl halide.

The alkene's pi electrons attack one bromine of Br2, displacing bromide and forming a three-membered ring bromonium ion in which bromine bridges both former alkene carbons, before bromide attacks from the opposite face.

Boron, the less electronegative, bulkier atom, adds preferentially to the less hindered (less substituted) carbon, and after oxidation that carbon ends up bearing the OH, giving the anti-Markovnikov alcohol.

Mercury bridges both alkene carbons in a cyclic mercurinium ion; the positive character is delocalized rather than concentrated on one carbon, so water attacks the more substituted carbon (Markovnikov) without a true carbocation able to rearrange.
Since the first bromine already blocks one face as part of the bromonium ion, the incoming bromide ion must attack from the backside, giving net anti addition of the two bromines.
Both the alkene and H2 adsorb onto the same flat metal surface, so both hydrogen atoms are transferred to the same face of the double bond, giving syn addition.
The addition reaction chemically consumes Br2, converting it into a colorless vicinal dibromide, which is why the test solution loses its color as the reaction proceeds.
Hydroboration-oxidation is anti-Markovnikov: boron adds to the less substituted, less hindered carbon due to steric factors (not carbocation stability), and OH ends up there after oxidation.
Acid catalysis protonates the alkene to form a carbocation, which water then attacks, adding H and OH across the former double bond in a process called acid-catalyzed hydration.
Without peroxides, HBr adds through a polar (ionic) mechanism: the alkene is protonated to form the more stable carbocation, which is then captured by bromide, giving the Markovnikov product.

In hydroboration, boron and hydrogen add to the same face of the double bond simultaneously in one transition state, so there's no discrete carbocation intermediate available to undergo a hydride or alkyl shift.
Since the alkene binds flat against the catalyst surface and both hydrogens are transferred from that same surface, they must end up added to the same face, producing syn addition.

Alkanes require light or heat to undergo a slow radical halogenation, whereas alkenes rapidly and visibly decolorize Br2 at room temperature via fast electrophilic addition, making the color change a useful diagnostic test.

In the standard two-step mechanism, the pi bond acts as a nucleophile toward the acidic H of HX, forming the more stable carbocation in the rate-determining first step, after which halide ion rapidly captures that carbocation.

Generating the carbocation requires breaking the pi bond and is the higher-activation-energy step; the subsequent capture of that carbocation by halide ion is fast, so the first step controls the overall rate.

Because a genuine carbocation forms during acid-catalyzed hydration, it is free to rearrange to a more stable carbocation (via a 1,2-hydride or alkyl shift) before water attacks, sometimes giving a product with the OH in an unexpected position.

Because the mercurinium ion delocalizes the positive charge across a three-membered ring rather than placing it entirely on one carbon, there's no free carbocation available to rearrange before water attacks the more substituted carbon.

Additional alkyl groups donate electron density into the pi system (making it a better nucleophile toward electrophiles) and stabilize the developing positive charge in the transition state, so more substituted alkenes typically react faster in electrophilic additions.

The bromonium/chloronium ion intermediate in halogenation blocks one face, forcing backside (anti) attack by the halide, whereas in hydrogenation both H atoms come from the same catalyst surface onto the same (syn) face — different intermediates give different stereochemical outcomes.
markovnikov: Markovnikov’s rule: the electrophile (often H⁺) adds to the carbon with more hydrogens already, placing the nucleophile on the more substituted (more stable-cation) carbon.
Radical mechanisms form the more stable radical at the more substituted carbon, so Br ends up on the less substituted carbon — opposite of the ionic Markovnikov outcome.
In ionic (non-radical) addition, the proton adds to give whichever carbon leads to the more stable carbocation — i.e., the more substituted one — and the nucleophile then attacks that cation.
Markovnikov's original empirical rule: the H of HX ends up on the carbon that already bears more hydrogens, while X ends up on the more substituted carbon.
Vladimir Markovnikov proposed the rule in 1865 based on observed patterns in addition reactions, decades before carbocation intermediates and their stability were used to explain why the rule holds.
Protonation occurs at the terminal CH2 carbon to generate the more stable secondary carbocation, which chloride then captures, giving 2-chloropropane as the Markovnikov product.

Peroxides generate bromine radicals that initiate a radical chain addition mechanism, which adds Br first and gives the opposite (anti-Markovnikov) regiochemistry compared to the normal ionic pathway.

Under radical (peroxide) conditions, bromine adds first to the terminal carbon to generate the more stable secondary radical, placing Br at the end of the chain — the anti-Markovnikov product, 1-bromopropane.
Protonation generates the more stable tertiary carbocation at the central carbon, which water then attacks, giving tert-butanol as the Markovnikov product.

Carbocation stability increases with substitution (methyl less than primary less than secondary less than tertiary) due to hyperconjugation and inductive donation from neighboring alkyl groups, so the reaction favors forming the more substituted, more stable carbocation.

Only HBr undergoes an efficient radical chain addition; the bond energetics for HCl and HI make the necessary radical propagation steps unfavorable, so anti-Markovnikov addition is essentially unique to HBr among the hydrogen halides.
Vladimir Markovnikov, a 19th-century Russian chemist, first described the regiochemical pattern now named after him.

Protonation of the ring double bond occurs at C2 to place the positive charge on C1 (already bearing a methyl group), forming the more stable tertiary carbocation; bromide then attacks C1, so Br and the methyl end up on the same carbon.

Protonating the less substituted alkene carbon generates the more stable tertiary carbocation at the other carbon; iodide then attacks that tertiary center, giving 2-iodo-2-methylbutane as the Markovnikov product.

This mechanistic restatement explains the empirical rule: reaction proceeds through the lower-energy transition state, which is the pathway that forms the more stable (typically more substituted) carbocation.
Protonation at the terminal CH2 carbon generates the more stable carbocation at the internal, more substituted carbon, which halide then attacks, placing X on that more substituted carbon.

Because hydroboration proceeds through steric control (boron adding to the less hindered carbon) rather than carbocation stability, the resulting alcohol has OH on the less substituted carbon — the opposite of the typical Markovnikov outcome.

Water attacks the more substituted carbon of the bridged mercurinium ion, where positive character is greater, giving the same overall Markovnikov regiochemistry as acid-catalyzed hydration, but without carbocation rearrangement.

The radical chain begins when a bromine radical adds to the less hindered terminal carbon, generating the more stable internal (secondary or tertiary) carbon radical, which then abstracts H from HBr — this order is why Br ends up terminal.

Radical addition proceeds by bromine radical adding to generate the most stable carbon radical (paralleling how ionic mechanisms favor the most stable carbocation), which dictates where Br ultimately attaches.

The radical chain mechanism needs peroxides (or similar initiators) to generate the initial bromine radical; absent that, the alkene reacts through the conventional polar mechanism, which is governed by carbocation stability and gives the Markovnikov outcome.

Protonation gives a secondary carbocation adjacent to a carbon bearing three methyl groups; a methyl group can shift over (1,2-shift) to generate a more stable tertiary carbocation, leading to a rearranged chloride product alongside the 'simple' Markovnikov product.

More alkyl groups attached to the cationic carbon donate electron density through hyperconjugation and induction, lowering the energy of the carbocation and the transition state leading to it, which channels the reaction toward the product derived from the more stable intermediate.

Both mechanisms are governed by the same underlying principle — the reaction pathway that generates the lower-energy reactive intermediate (radical or cation) is favored — they just differ in which species (radical vs. cation) and which atom (Br vs. H) adds first.

Peroxides undergo weak O-O bond homolysis to generate alkoxy radicals, which abstract a hydrogen atom from HBr to generate a bromine radical; this bromine radical is what adds to the alkene to begin the chain.

The simple 'more H's' heuristic can fail to clearly distinguish outcomes for more complex or highly substituted alkenes; the mechanistic version — protonate to form the more stable carbocation — is the general and reliable explanation underlying the empirical rule.

The bond dissociation energies involved make each step of the HBr radical chain reasonably exothermic and selective, while the analogous steps for HCl are too exothermic and unselective and for HI are endothermic, so a clean radical chain mechanism practically only works for HBr.

Hydration and halogenation (Br2/Cl2 addition) proceed through cationic or bridged-ion intermediates that follow normal Markovnikov-type (most stable intermediate) selectivity; the radical chain pathway that flips the regiochemistry is essentially unique to peroxide-mediated HBr addition.

The ionic pathway is governed by carbocation stability, favoring Br at the more substituted carbon (C2); the radical pathway is governed by radical stability formed by Br adding first to the terminal carbon (C1), flipping the regiochemistry.

Carbocation stability increases with the number of alkyl groups attached to the cationic carbon because each alkyl group donates electron density via hyperconjugation and the inductive effect, giving the order methyl less than primary less than secondary less than tertiary.
alkynes: sp hybrid orbitals have 50% s-character (vs. 25% for sp³), holding the lone pair closer to the nucleus and stabilizing the conjugate base — more s-character, more acidic.
A triple bond is 1 sigma bond plus 2 pi bonds.
The first HX addition (following Markovnikov) gives a vinyl halide; a second addition of HX to that alkene gives a geminal dihalide, both halogens on the same, more substituted carbon.
Each alkyne carbon forms two sigma bonds (linear, 180°) using sp hybrid orbitals, leaving two unhybridized p orbitals to form the two pi bonds of the triple bond.
sp-hybridized carbons arrange their two sigma bonds linearly, 180° apart, giving alkynes their characteristic straight, rod-like geometry at the triple bond.

Alkyne pi electrons are held closer to the carbon nuclei due to the higher s-character (more electronegative character) of sp carbons, making the alkyne pi bond somewhat less available to electrophiles compared to the more loosely held pi electrons of an alkene.
A triple bond counts as two degrees of unsaturation, removing four hydrogens relative to the saturated alkane (CnH2n+2), giving CnH2n-2.
In a terminal alkyne, such as HC≡C-CH3 (propyne), one sp carbon of the triple bond is bonded to a hydrogen atom rather than to another carbon, placing the triple bond at the very end of the chain.
An internal alkyne, like 2-butyne (CH3-C≡C-CH3), has the triple bond flanked on both sides by carbon substituents, distinguishing it from a terminal alkyne, which has a triple-bond C-H.

Just as with alkenes, Br2 adds across one of the two pi bonds of the triple bond first, converting the alkyne into a dihalogenated alkene; a second equivalent of Br2 would be needed to fully saturate it into a tetrahalide.
The suffix -yne is used specifically to denote a triple bond in the parent chain, as in ethyne (acetylene) or 2-butyne.

A triple bond is composed of exactly one sigma bond (from head-on sp-sp orbital overlap) plus two pi bonds (from two pairs of unhybridized p orbitals); there is never more than one sigma bond between any two directly bonded atoms.

An sp orbital has 50% s character, versus 33% for sp2 and 25% for sp3; more s character means the lone pair sits closer to and is better stabilized by the positively charged nucleus, making the conjugate base (acetylide ion) more stable and the C-H more acidic.

A lower pKa means a stronger acid; water at pKa ~15.7 is far more acidic than even a terminal alkyne C-H (pKa ~25), even though the alkyne C-H is unusually acidic compared to other hydrocarbon C-H bonds.

Since the conjugate acid of amide ion, ammonia (pKa ~38), is a much weaker acid than a terminal alkyne (pKa ~25), sodium amide is a strong enough base to completely deprotonate terminal alkynes to form acetylide ions; hydroxide (conjugate acid water, pKa ~15.7) is not strong enough.

Acetylide ions are strong, relatively unhindered carbanion-like nucleophiles that readily displace halide from primary (unhindered) alkyl halides via SN2, a classic method for extending carbon chains and building larger alkynes.
Markovnikov addition of water places OH on the more substituted alkyne carbon, generating an enol, which rapidly tautomerizes (favoring the more stable keto form) into a ketone.
Boron adds to the less substituted terminal carbon; oxidation replaces boron with OH there, giving an enol with OH on the terminal carbon, which tautomerizes to an aldehyde rather than a ketone.
With an unrestricted (non-poisoned) metal catalyst and excess H2, both pi bonds of the triple bond are hydrogenated in sequence, first to the alkene and then fully to the alkane.

Lindlar's catalyst delivers both hydrogens to the same face of the triple bond (syn addition) and is deliberately poisoned to stop after adding just one equivalent of H2, giving the cis alkene selectively.
