The Na/NH3 dissolving-metal mechanism proceeds through a vinyl radical/anion intermediate that equilibrates to the more stable, less crowded trans geometry before picking up a second electron and proton, giving the trans alkene selectively — complementary to Lindlar's cis selectivity.

Lead and quinoline additives reduce the catalytic activity of Pd just enough that it can still deliver H2 syn across a triple bond but is much less effective at further adsorbing and reducing the resulting alkene, letting the reaction be stopped cleanly at the cis-alkene stage.

Unlike the concerted syn delivery on a catalyst surface, the dissolving-metal mechanism proceeds stepwise through a radical anion intermediate that has time to adopt the thermodynamically preferred, less strained trans-like arrangement before being fully reduced, giving the trans alkene as the major product.

Unless the internal alkyne is symmetrical, Markovnikov addition of water is not perfectly selective for one carbon over the other when both are similarly substituted, so both possible enol/ketone regiochemistries can form, giving a mixture of ketone products.

The first HBr addition follows Markovnikov's rule, putting Br on the more substituted carbon to form a bromoalkene; the second HBr addition again follows Markovnikov's rule on that bromoalkene, placing the second Br on the very same carbon, yielding a geminal dihalide.

Keto-enol tautomerization is a fast, acid- or base-catalyzed equilibrium that overwhelmingly favors the keto form because a C=O pi bond is significantly more stable than a C=C-OH arrangement, so the enol formed transiently from alkyne hydration converts essentially completely to the ketone.

Only a terminal alkyne has a CH-bearing end carbon available for boron's steric preference to place OH there after oxidation, generating a terminal enol that tautomerizes to an aldehyde; internal alkynes lack a terminal position and instead give ketones.

More shared electron pairs (three bonding pairs in a triple bond) pull the bonded atoms closer together and require more energy to break, and the increased s-character of sp orbitals further shortens the sigma bond, making triple bonds the shortest and strongest, followed by double, then single bonds.

sp hybridization uses only one s and one p orbital, leaving two p orbitals unhybridized and oriented perpendicular to each other; each of these forms its own independent pi bond with the matching p orbital on the other sp carbon, giving two distinct, perpendicular pi bonds plus the one sigma bond.

Because both triple-bond carbons of 2-butyne carry identical methyl substituents, it doesn't matter which carbon water's oxygen ends up on — both regiochemical outcomes converge on the same single ketone product (2-butanone), avoiding the mixture problem seen with unsymmetrical internal alkynes.
conjugated-systems: Their p orbitals never meet, so each double bond behaves as though the other were not there.
Every carbon in the run is sp2 and the p orbitals overlap continuously.
The shared carbon is sp, and the two pi systems are perpendicular, so they cannot interact.
Conjugated > isolated > cumulated. Only the conjugated arrangement earns delocalization energy.
A cumulated diene has an sp carbon holding two perpendicular pi systems, and is strained relative to the alternatives.

It pays no rotation penalty, and dimerizes on standing as a result.
It dimerizes at room temperature via a Diels-Alder, and the retro reaction on heating gives it back.
They lower its LUMO, bringing it closer to the diene's HOMO.
They raise its HOMO, narrowing the gap to the dienophile's LUMO.
Mismatching them in this direction brings the interacting orbitals closest in energy.
Two carbonyls flank its double bond, which pulls the LUMO down sharply.
Nothing lowers its LUMO, so the orbital gap to the diene stays wide.
Both bonds form on the same face in one step, so nothing can rotate and the relationship is preserved.
The same suprafacial addition preserves trans just as it preserves cis.
Change the stereochemistry of the starting material and you get a predictably different stereochemistry in the product.
The endo transition state benefits from a secondary orbital interaction, making it faster.
The substituent's pi system interacts favorably with the developing pi system of the diene.
It forms faster, which is a useful corrective to reading kinetic as less hindered.
Heating a suitable cyclohexene sends it back to a diene and a dienophile.
Mentally cutting a six-membered ring at that disconnection is one of the most productive moves in retrosynthesis.
Two double bonds, two pi electrons each. The dienophile brings two more.
One double or triple bond. Four plus two is the [4+2] in the name.
It contributes two pi electrons just as an alkene does, and the extra pi bond survives into the product.
The two terminal carbons form the new sigma bonds, and the central bond becomes the alkene.
Sigma bonds are stronger, so trading two pi bonds for two sigma bonds releases energy.
One transition state, no intermediate, and every consequence of that follows.
The bond arithmetic already favors it; a Lewis acid can lower the dienophile's LUMO further and speed it up.
It can never reach the conformation where both ends point the same way.
uv-vis: A pi to pi-star transition, promoting an electron across the frontier orbital gap.
A bigger gap needs a higher energy photon, and higher energy means shorter wavelength.
Less energy is needed, and lower energy light has a longer wavelength.
More p orbitals give more molecular orbitals over a similar range, so the highest occupied rises and the lowest empty falls.
A single isolated double bond absorbs well below 200 nm, which is inconvenient for ordinary instruments.
Conjugating two double bonds moves the absorption into the accessible range.
Three conjugated double bonds, and the trend continues upward.
Eleven conjugated double bonds put it past 400 nm and into the visible region.
Enough to bring its absorption into the visible, which is why it is colored at all.
In organic UV-Vis it is usually the conjugated pi system.
It removes blue light around 450 nm, and what reaches your eye is the complementary color.
Without a long conjugated system the gap is too wide, so absorption stays in the ultraviolet.
Absorbance equals molar absorptivity times concentration times path length.
A constant for that compound at that wavelength, measuring how strongly it absorbs.
Conventionally 1 cm for a standard cuvette.
The Beer-Lambert relationship makes it the standard way to follow a concentration while a reaction runs.
Conjugated systems absorb strongly, which is part of why the technique is sensitive.
Conjugation narrows the gap, so the conjugated isomer absorbs at the longer wavelength.
It reports on conjugation and amount, but nothing about position or connectivity. Pair it with NMR for that.
Below about 400 nm is ultraviolet, so a compound absorbing past that point can appear colored.
A single C=C absorbs below about 200 nm, which ordinary instruments do not reach comfortably.
The effect is smaller than adding a double bond, but systematic enough that empirical rules exist.
Each technique answers a different question, and this is the one UV-Vis answers sharply.
IR reports on bond vibrations, which are characteristic of particular groups.
It turns the chapter's central claim into a number you can read off an instrument.
Read off the instrument, and proportional to concentration by Beer-Lambert.
Each additional conjugated double bond narrows the gap further and pushes absorption to longer wavelength.
The transition is pi to pi-star, so the empty orbital involved is the pi antibonding one.
Extended conjugation brings its absorption into the visible, which is what makes vision possible.
It answers one question sharply and says little about connectivity, so NMR does the placing.
alcohol-reactions: Hydroxide is a strong base (poor leaving group); alcohols are typically first protonated (or converted to a better leaving group like a tosylate) before substitution/elimination.
Protonation turns the leaving group into neutral H₂O, which is a much weaker base (and thus a far better leaving group) than OH⁻.

TsCl converts the OH into OTs, a weak-base, excellent leaving group, via a mechanism that doesn’t touch the stereocenter’s configuration (unlike acid-catalyzed substitution, which can invert or racemize it).
Tertiary carbocations are stable enough to form, so the reaction proceeds through ionization (loss of water) followed by chloride capture, a classic SN1 pathway.
Primary carbocations are highly unstable, so primary alcohols instead react with HX through SN2, with the protonated alcohol acting as the leaving group while bromide attacks from the backside.
SOCl2 reacts through a chlorosulfite intermediate without generating a free carbocation, avoiding the hydride or alkyl shifts that can occur in purely acid-catalyzed routes.
PCC is an anhydrous, mild oxidant that stops at the aldehyde stage because there is no water present to hydrate the aldehyde into the gem-diol needed for further oxidation.

Strong aqueous Cr(VI) oxidants hydrate the intermediate aldehyde into a gem-diol, which is then readily oxidized further to the carboxylic acid; PCC and Swern conditions are anhydrous and stop at the aldehyde.

Secondary alcohols have only one hydrogen on the carbinol carbon; removing it gives a ketone, which has no further C-H bond to remove, so oxidation stops there regardless of the specific Cr(VI) reagent.
Oxidation by these reagents requires removing a C-H bond from the carbinol carbon; a tertiary carbinol carbon has no such hydrogen, so tertiary alcohols resist this kind of oxidation entirely.

Zaitsev's rule favors the more stable, more substituted alkene; in the E1 mechanism the carbocation loses a proton preferentially toward the more substituted side, forming the more stable double bond.
The OH must first be protonated to become a good leaving group (water), which then departs to generate a carbocation; a base finally removes a beta-proton to form the alkene.

The rate-limiting step is carbocation formation; hyperconjugation and inductive electron donation from additional alkyl groups stabilize more substituted carbocations, lowering the activation energy for their formation.

Because the mechanism passes through a carbocation intermediate, a hydride or alkyl shift can occur before the proton is lost, shifting the position of the resulting double bond or even the carbon skeleton.
Alcohols are weak acids; the reactive Na metal reduces the O-H proton, releasing H2 gas and leaving behind the sodium alkoxide salt.
The alkoxide, not the neutral alcohol, is the nucleophile needed to perform SN2 displacement on the alkyl halide partner, so a strong, non-nucleophilic base like NaH is used first to form it.
Acid catalyzes nucleophilic attack of the alcohol on the protonated carbonyl; after loss of water from the resulting tetrahedral intermediate, the ester is formed. The overall process is reversible.

One OH is protonated and leaves as water to form a carbocation; a neighboring alkyl or hydride group migrates to stabilize the positive charge, and loss of a proton from the resulting species gives the ketone product.
Periodic acid selectively cleaves the carbon-carbon bond between two adjacent hydroxyl groups, converting each carbinol carbon into a carbonyl (an aldehyde or ketone depending on substitution).

The alkyl group attached to the oxygen is electron-donating relative to hydrogen, which destabilizes the alkoxide conjugate base somewhat compared to hydroxide, making most simple alcohols a bit less acidic than water.
The added alkyl groups push electron density onto the already-negative alkoxide oxygen, destabilizing the anion (and hindering its solvation), which raises the pKa relative to methanol.
The O-H of an alcohol is acidic enough to protonate the strongly basic, carbanion-like Grignard reagent, quenching it as an alkane before it can perform any useful addition chemistry.
Like PCC, Swern conditions contain no water, so the aldehyde product cannot be hydrated into the gem-diol that aqueous Cr(VI) systems go on to oxidize; it also avoids toxic chromium reagents.

Tertiary alcohols react almost instantly because their carbocation is highly stabilized, secondary alcohols take several minutes, and primary alcohols show little change at room temperature, so the reaction rate reveals the alcohol's class.
Tertiary alcohols ionize very quickly under these acidic conditions because the resulting carbocation is highly stabilized, so the insoluble alkyl chloride forms almost immediately.

Protecting groups like TMS ethers are easily installed and later removed (for example with mild acid or fluoride), letting chemists carry out reactions elsewhere in a molecule without interference from a free -OH.

PBr3 first converts the OH into a good leaving group, and bromide then displaces it in a single concerted backside attack, giving clean inversion rather than the racemization seen with carbocation intermediates.
Because PBr3 operates through a concerted SN2-type displacement without a free carbocation, bromide must attack from the side opposite the leaving group, inverting the configuration.

Protonation of the OH followed by loss of water generates a planar carbocation that can be attacked by bromide from either face, scrambling the stereochemistry relative to the clean inversion seen with PBr3.

Acid-catalyzed dehydration proceeds through a carbocation intermediate; tert-butanol forms the most stable (tertiary) carbocation most readily, so it reacts fastest, while methanol has no adjacent carbon to form a double bond with at all.
ether-chemistry: Like alcohols, ethers need protonation (acidic conditions) to turn the alkoxide oxygen into a viable leaving group (neutral alcohol) before cleavage.
Protonated ethers at secondary/tertiary centers tend to cleave via SN1 (carbocation pathway), while primary centers favor SN2.

Ethers lack an acidic proton and don’t have a good leaving group under neutral/basic conditions, so they tolerate strongly basic/nucleophilic reagents while still solvating them through the oxygen’s lone pairs.

Alcohols can hydrogen-bond to one another through their O-H groups, which raises their boiling points substantially; ethers lack an O-H bond, so they only experience weaker dipole-dipole and dispersion forces between molecules.
An ether oxygen has lone pairs that can accept a hydrogen bond from an O-H or N-H elsewhere, but since ethers have no O-H or N-H of their own, they cannot donate a hydrogen bond.

Once the ether oxygen is protonated, iodide attacks via SN2 at the less hindered, less sterically crowded methyl carbon rather than the propyl carbon, giving methyl iodide and propanol (which can react further with excess acid).

The tertiary carbon can ionize readily to form a stable carbocation (SN1-like pathway), so iodide captures that carbocation, leaving methanol as the other fragment rather than forming a methyl cation.

The tertiary carbon can ionize to a stable carbocation far more easily than the primary carbon can undergo a slow SN2 displacement, so cleavage occurs preferentially at the tertiary center, releasing the primary alcohol intact.

Breaking the aryl-oxygen bond would require either an unstable aryl cation (no SN1 pathway) or backside attack on a planar, sp2 aromatic carbon (no SN2 pathway), so cleavage instead occurs exclusively at the methyl carbon.

A bulky, basic alkoxide approaching a hindered tertiary carbon strongly favors removing a beta-hydrogen (E2) over performing a backside SN2 attack, so elimination products dominate instead of the desired ether.

Because the alkyl halide is the electrophile undergoing SN2 attack, choosing one that is primary (or otherwise unhindered) avoids competing elimination, regardless of how bulky the alkoxide nucleophile itself is.
The ring of oxygen atoms in a crown ether can wrap around a metal cation of the right size, effectively dissolving otherwise poorly soluble ionic salts in nonpolar solvents.
Crown ethers show size selectivity: 18-crown-6's ring cavity closely matches the ionic radius of K+, giving tighter binding than with the smaller Na+ ion, which fits less snugly.

Normally F- is tightly ion-paired with its counter-cation and poorly solvated in nonpolar media, dampening its reactivity; encapsulating K+ inside the crown ether frees the anion to act as a much more potent, less hindered nucleophile.
Diethyl ether was one of the earliest general anesthetics used in medicine, though it was eventually replaced by safer, less flammable agents.

THF's oxygen lone pairs coordinate to metal cations (helping stabilize organometallic reagents in solution) while its ring is chemically unreactive toward most nucleophiles and bases, making it a versatile, widely used solvent.

Autoxidation at the carbon next to the ether oxygen slowly generates peroxide and hydroperoxide species that can concentrate and detonate, especially when the ether is evaporated or distilled, which is why old ether stocks are handled with caution.

Removing a hydrogen from the carbon next to the ether oxygen gives a radical that is stabilized by overlap with a lone pair on oxygen, making that particular C-H bond especially susceptible to slow radical autoxidation by atmospheric O2.
Ethers lack the O-H and C=O groups that dominate alcohol and carbonyl spectra, so their most diagnostic IR feature is the strong C-O single bond stretch in the 1050-1150 cm-1 region.

With excess strong acid and heat, both C-O bonds of the symmetrical ether are eventually cleaved by iodide via SN2, first releasing ethanol (which itself then reacts further with HI) and ultimately converting both ethyl groups into ethyl iodide.
Adding a proton to the ether oxygen gives it three bonds plus a formal positive charge, a species called an oxonium ion, which makes the adjacent C-O bonds much easier to break.

Reagents like PCC or Jones reagent oxidize by removing the O-H hydrogen along with a C-H hydrogen from the carbinol carbon; since ethers have no O-H to begin with, this pathway simply is not available to them.

Ether solvents donate electron density from their oxygen lone pairs to the electrophilic magnesium center, which helps stabilize and solubilize the highly reactive organomagnesium species; nonpolar hydrocarbons cannot offer this coordination.

Protonating the alkene carbon of a vinyl ether produces a cation stabilized by resonance donation from the adjacent oxygen (an oxocarbenium ion); water then adds and loss of the alcohol gives a carbonyl compound, a much faster pathway than the harsh conditions needed to cleave a saturated dialkyl ether.
THF is a five-membered ring containing one oxygen atom and four carbons, making it a saturated cyclic ether rather than an open-chain one.

Rather than using a standalone 'ether' suffix, the preferred IUPAC approach treats the shorter alkyl-oxygen unit as an alkoxy substituent on the longer parent chain, giving names like methoxyethane for ethyl methyl ether.

The ether oxygen's lone pair can donate into the empty orbital of a Lewis acid like BF3, forming a stable donor-acceptor (Lewis acid-base) adduct, such as the BF3 etherate commonly used as a mild Lewis acid catalyst.

Although ethers cannot donate hydrogen bonds, their oxygen lone pairs can accept hydrogen bonds from water molecules, giving small ethers noticeably greater water solubility than alkanes of similar size.

After the ether oxygen is protonated, the halide ion must still act as the nucleophile (or cation-trapping species) that displaces the alcohol; iodide and bromide are considerably more nucleophilic than chloride, making the overall cleavage much faster and more practical.

A base can attack an ester's carbonyl carbon directly because the resulting tetrahedral intermediate is stabilized by the carbonyl oxygen and can expel a leaving group; an ether has no such electrophilic carbon, so it must first be protonated by strong acid before any C-O bond becomes breakable.
epoxides: The ~60° bond angles in the three-membered ring are far from ideal, so opening the ring relieves substantial strain, driving reactivity.
Basic/neutral conditions favor an SN2-like mechanism — backside attack at the less hindered carbon.

Protonating the epoxide oxygen makes the ring-opening more SN1-like, so the nucleophile attacks the carbon that better stabilizes positive charge — the more substituted one — unlike the SN2-like base-catalyzed case.
Peroxyacids like mCPBA deliver an oxygen atom directly across the carbon-carbon double bond in a single concerted step, converting the alkene into an epoxide.

The peroxyacid transfers its oxygen to both alkene carbons simultaneously from one face in a single concerted step (often pictured as a 'butterfly' transition state), so the new C-O bonds form on the same side of the original double bond.

Syn addition preserves the original cis relationship of the two methyl groups, and the resulting epoxide has an internal mirror plane, making it a single achiral meso compound rather than a mixture of enantiomers.

Syn addition to the trans alkene produces a chiral epoxide (no internal mirror plane); because the peroxyacid can approach either face of the planar alkene with equal likelihood, both enantiomers form in equal amounts, giving a racemic mixture.

In both the basic and acidic mechanisms, the nucleophile approaches from the side opposite the breaking C-O bond, so the carbon under attack is inverted even though the overall regiochemistry (which carbon is attacked) differs between the two conditions.
Water attacks the protonated epoxide from the face opposite the ring oxygen (backside attack), so the two new OH groups end up anti to each other, giving the trans diol rather than the cis one.

Hydride is a strong nucleophile that reacts via an SN2-like pathway, so like other strong nucleophiles it attacks the less sterically hindered carbon, which ends up bonded to the delivered hydrogen while the OH remains on the more substituted carbon.
Grignard reagents are strong, basic carbon nucleophiles that react with epoxides under essentially basic-type conditions, favoring backside SN2 attack at the more accessible, less hindered carbon.

Under acidic conditions the protonated epoxide is opened by bromide acting as the nucleophile at one carbon, while the oxygen (now an OH after losing its proton) remains on the adjacent carbon, giving a halohydrin.

Protonation of the epoxide oxygen gives the C-O bonds partial cationic character, concentrated at the carbon that would form the more stable carbocation; even a weak nucleophile like methanol is then directed to that more substituted carbon.

Under basic or neutral conditions the epoxide is not protonated, so the strong methoxide nucleophile simply performs a straightforward SN2 attack at the more sterically accessible, less hindered carbon.
An epoxide, or oxirane, is defined by this specific three-membered ring of two carbons and one oxygen, which is what gives it its characteristic angle strain and heightened reactivity.

The epoxide's three-membered ring has bond angles far smaller than the ideal tetrahedral angle, storing substantial strain energy; breaking a C-O bond releases that strain, which strongly drives the ring-opening reaction forward.

Under acid, protonation weakens the C-O bonds and shifts positive character toward whichever carbon can better stabilize it (the more substituted one), directing even weak nucleophiles there; under base, the unprotonated, still-strained ring is simply attacked wherever the strong nucleophile can approach most easily, favoring the less hindered carbon.

Protonating the epoxide oxygen makes the ring vastly more electrophilic, so weak nucleophiles that would otherwise be unreactive can now attack; without that activation, only strong, good nucleophiles can open the strained but un-activated ring at a useful rate.

Amines are good, strongly basic nucleophiles, so like other strong nucleophiles they attack the less sterically hindered carbon of the epoxide via an SN2-like pathway, generating a beta-amino alcohol.

A meso epoxide has two carbons that are enantiotopic to each other; an achiral nucleophile has no way to distinguish between them, so it attacks each one with equal probability, producing equal amounts of both resulting enantiomers.

Protonation of the epoxide oxygen gives the more substituted carbon significant carbocation-like character in the transition state, so water (even though it is a weak nucleophile) is directed there preferentially, just as with other acid-catalyzed epoxide openings.

The highly strained bond angles of the oxirane ring store considerable potential energy; opening the ring to form a less strained, acyclic product is thermodynamically favorable and is the underlying reason epoxides react so readily compared to ordinary ethers.

An unstrained ether's C-O bond is simply too strong and the oxygen too poor a leaving group for hydroxide to displace at room temperature, but the epoxide's ring strain dramatically lowers the barrier for the same kind of backside nucleophilic attack.

The reaction is usually described as borderline or concerted, with the nucleophile beginning to attack as the C-O bond breaks rather than waiting for a fully independent, freely rotating carbocation to form first; this is why some stereochemical and regiochemical control is retained even under acidic conditions.

A neutral ether oxygen is a poor leaving group, but once protonated it becomes a much better one (similar to protonating an alcohol); this protonation also pulls electron density away from the ring carbons, making them more attractive targets for even weak nucleophiles.

The three-membered epoxide ring forces C-O-C and C-C-O bond angles down to roughly 60 degrees, well below the ideal ~109.5 degrees for sp3 atoms, storing substantial strain energy that is released upon ring-opening; six-membered cyclic ethers have nearly ideal bond angles and little such strain.

Thiolate is a strong, highly polarizable nucleophile, so it follows the same basic-conditions pattern as other strong nucleophiles, attacking the less sterically hindered carbon via an SN2-like pathway to give a beta-hydroxy sulfide.

Because both new C-O bonds form in a single step without any intermediate that could allow rotation about the former double bond, the spatial relationship of the substituents on the alkene is carried over faithfully into the epoxide product.

If a nucleophilic group like an alcohol is positioned correctly within the same molecule, it can attack the strained epoxide ring intramolecularly, closing a new ring and forming a cyclic ether, a key step used to build many natural polyether frameworks.

The severe angle strain in the three-membered ring distorts the hybridization and bonding at the ring carbons, making the C-O bonds considerably easier to cleave by nucleophilic attack than the analogous bonds in an unstrained, open-chain ether.
aldehydes-ketones: The carbonyl carbon has 3 regions of electron density (trigonal planar) — sp², just like an alkene carbon.
Extra alkyl groups add steric bulk (hindering attack) and donate electron density (reducing the carbonyl’s electrophilicity) compared to aldehydes.
An aldehyde has only one electron-donating alkyl group (vs. two for a ketone) and less steric bulk, leaving its carbonyl carbon more electron-poor and more reactive toward nucleophiles.

Ketones take the suffix -one (e.g., propan-2-one, acetone), while aldehydes use -al. The position of the carbonyl is indicated by a locant for ketones but not needed for aldehydes since the carbonyl must be terminal.
Formaldehyde is the simplest aldehyde, with two hydrogens bonded to the carbonyl carbon instead of one H and one R group. This makes it especially small and electrophilic.
Acetone is the everyday name for propan-2-one, the simplest ketone, commonly used as a solvent and nail polish remover.
Oxygen is more electronegative than carbon, so it pulls electron density from the C=O bond toward itself, leaving the carbonyl carbon electron-poor and susceptible to nucleophilic attack.

Aldehydes have a C-H bond on the carbonyl carbon that allows them to be oxidized to a carboxylic acid, reducing the diamine silver complex to metallic Ag(0). Ketones lack that hydrogen and resist oxidation.

Aldehydes and ketones lack an O-H (or N-H) group, so they cannot hydrogen-bond with themselves, giving them lower boiling points than comparably sized alcohols, even though the polar C=O allows dipole-dipole attraction.

Benzophenone has two bulky, electron-donating aryl groups that sterically block approach of a nucleophile and electronically stabilize the carbonyl carbon through resonance, making it one of the least electrophilic common carbonyls.

The aromatic ring can donate electron density into the carbonyl through resonance, partially stabilizing the positive charge on the carbonyl carbon and making aromatic aldehydes somewhat less electrophilic than simple aliphatic aldehydes.

The carbonyl C=O stretch is a strong, diagnostic IR absorption typically found between about 1700 and 1750 cm-1 for non-conjugated aldehydes and ketones; conjugation with a ring or double bond shifts it to slightly lower wavenumber.

The aldehyde C-H is strongly deshielded by the adjacent electron-withdrawing carbonyl, pushing its signal far downfield to roughly 9-10 ppm, a distinctive marker used to confirm the presence of an aldehyde.

Electrophilicity decreases as more alkyl groups are attached to the carbonyl carbon, since alkyl groups are electron-donating (inductively) and bulkier. Formaldehyde (two H's) is most electrophilic, acetone (two methyls) is least.

Oxidation of an aldehyde to a carboxylic acid requires removing the hydrogen on the carbonyl carbon. Ketones have two carbon substituents on that carbon instead of a hydrogen, so this oxidation pathway is unavailable to them.

Water can add reversibly across the carbonyl to form a geminal diol (two OH groups on one carbon). For most ketones and aldehydes this equilibrium favors the carbonyl form, but for very electrophilic carbonyls like formaldehyde, the hydrate can dominate.

Formaldehyde's minimal steric hindrance and strongly electrophilic carbonyl carbon allow water to add efficiently, shifting the hydration equilibrium far toward the diol, unlike bulkier or less electrophilic carbonyls where the free carbonyl dominates.

Keto-enol tautomerism requires an alpha carbon bearing at least one hydrogen adjacent to the carbonyl. Formaldehyde has no carbon atom alpha to the carbonyl (only hydrogens on the carbonyl carbon itself), so it cannot tautomerize to an enol.

Sodium borohydride (NaBH4) is a milder, more selective hydride donor than lithium aluminum hydride, commonly used to reduce aldehydes and ketones to alcohols while leaving less reactive carbonyls such as esters largely untouched.
sp2 hybridization gives a trigonal planar geometry around the carbonyl carbon, with bond angles of approximately 120 degrees between the three attached groups.

Although acetone cannot hydrogen-bond with itself as a pure liquid, its carbonyl oxygen can accept hydrogen bonds from water, and its small size allows it to mix completely with water in all proportions.

Acetone (propan-2-one) is the simplest ketone because a ketone's carbonyl carbon must be bonded to two other carbons; a three-carbon chain is the minimum needed to place the carbonyl in the middle position.
When another group outranks the ketone in IUPAC priority (such as a carboxylic acid), the ketone oxygen is named as a substituent using 'oxo-' with a locant, rather than using the -one suffix.

The polarized C=O bond creates a substantial molecular dipole in aldehydes and ketones, leading to stronger dipole-dipole intermolecular forces and higher boiling points than nonpolar alkanes of similar size.
Cyclohexanone has a six-membered carbon ring with one ring carbon replaced by a carbonyl (C=O), making it a common cyclic ketone used in industry and as a synthetic intermediate.

Tollens' reagent selectively oxidizes aldehydes (which have an oxidizable C-H on the carbonyl carbon), depositing metallic silver, while ketones generally give no reaction, making it useful for distinguishing the two.

As the incoming nucleophile approaches the planar sp2 carbonyl carbon to form a tetrahedral intermediate, larger substituents (two alkyl/aryl groups in ketones vs. one in aldehydes) crowd that approach and raise the energy of the transition state, slowing the reaction.

The aromatic pi system can conjugate with the carbonyl, delocalizing electron density toward the carbonyl carbon through resonance and reducing (though not eliminating) its electrophilicity relative to a simple alkyl aldehyde.

In the standard IUPAC seniority order of functional groups, aldehydes rank higher than ketones, so when both are present the molecule is named as an '-al' with the ketone indicated by an 'oxo-' substituent prefix and locant.

Glyceraldehyde is an aldotriose (aldehyde at C1) while dihydroxyacetone is a ketotriose (ketone at C2); both share the same molecular formula but differ in the position and type of the carbonyl group.
nucleophilic-addition: The carbonyl carbon is δ+ due to oxygen’s electronegativity, making it the site of nucleophilic attack.
The nucleophile forms a new bond to carbon while the C=O pi electrons shift entirely onto oxygen, giving a tetrahedral alkoxide intermediate.
The carbonyl carbon becomes sp³ and tetrahedral, bearing the new nucleophile bond and a negatively charged oxygen (alkoxide), which is then typically protonated.

For simple nucleophilic addition (not substitution), the nucleophile's attack on the electrophilic, sp2 carbonyl carbon to form the tetrahedral alkoxide intermediate is typically the slow, rate-determining step; the final proton transfer is usually fast.

Protonating the carbonyl oxygen makes the molecule an oxocarbenium-like species, pulling even more electron density away from the carbonyl carbon and making it a much stronger electrophile, which speeds up nucleophile attack, especially useful for weak nucleophiles like alcohols.

The nucleophile approaches at roughly 107 degrees relative to the C=O axis (the Bürgi-Dunitz angle) to minimize repulsion with the forming oxygen lone pair, trajectory that leads smoothly to the tetrahedral geometry of the product.
Cyanide adds to the carbonyl carbon, and after protonation of the resulting alkoxide, the product is a cyanohydrin, which has both a hydroxyl group and a nitrile group on the same carbon.
A primary amine first adds to give a hemiaminal (carbinolamine), which then loses water to form a C=N double bond, known as an imine or Schiff base.

A secondary amine's nitrogen, after addition, only has one hydrogen. When water leaves, the nitrogen cannot also lose its one remaining hydrogen to form a neutral C=N (that would leave nitrogen positively charged/unstable), so instead a proton is removed from the alpha carbon, forming a conjugated carbon-carbon/nitrogen double bond system: the enamine.

Grignard reagents are strongly basic/nucleophilic and react irreversibly with carbonyls to form a magnesium alkoxide salt. This intermediate is stable until an aqueous acid workup protonates it, releasing the neutral alcohol product.

Reversibility in carbonyl addition depends on whether the newly added group can leave again. An alkoxide (from an organometallic addition) is a strong base and terrible leaving group, so once the strongly nucleophilic carbanion adds, it essentially never leaves, making the reaction irreversible under normal conditions.

Hydration of carbonyls is a classic reversible nucleophilic addition. Highly electrophilic, unhindered carbonyls (like formaldehyde or chloral) favor the hydrate, while typical ketones favor the free carbonyl form at equilibrium.

A negatively charged nucleophile like hydroxide has more electron density available to donate than a neutral nucleophile like water, making it significantly more reactive in attacking an electrophilic carbonyl carbon.
An electron-withdrawing group nearby pulls electron density away from the carbonyl carbon inductively, intensifying its partial positive charge and making it a better target for a nucleophile.

The three strongly electron-withdrawing chlorine atoms on the adjacent carbon pull electron density away inductively, greatly increasing the electrophilicity of the carbonyl carbon and favoring nucleophilic addition (chloral hydrate forms readily as a stable solid, unlike most simple hydrates).
The carbonyl carbon starts as sp2 and planar (bonded to three groups). After the nucleophile adds and the pi bond breaks, that carbon becomes sp3 with four substituents arranged tetrahedrally.
As the nucleophile forms a new sigma bond to carbon, the C=O pi bond breaks and its electron pair moves entirely onto the oxygen, generating a negatively charged alkoxide intermediate.

When one equivalent of alcohol adds to a ketone's carbonyl carbon, the product bears both an -OH and an -OR group on the same carbon, which is defined as a hemiacetal (specifically a hemiketal when derived from a ketone).

A planar sp2 carbonyl carbon is equally accessible to the nucleophile from either face (top or bottom) in the absence of a chiral catalyst or existing stereocenter nearby, so both possible stereochemical outcomes form in equal amounts, giving a racemic mixture.

Having two carbon substituents instead of one both physically blocks nucleophile approach (sterics) and donates more electron density into the carbonyl carbon (electronics), both factors working together to slow nucleophilic addition in ketones relative to aldehydes.

Esters, acid chlorides, and amides have an additional electronegative group (OR, Cl, NR2) on the carbonyl carbon that can leave after the tetrahedral intermediate forms, regenerating the C=O and substituting the nucleophile for the leaving group. Aldehydes and ketones have only H or alkyl/aryl groups (poor leaving groups), so the tetrahedral intermediate persists as the final addition product.

Hydride (H-) attacks the electrophilic carbonyl carbon just like other nucleophiles, forming a tetrahedral alkoxide intermediate that is then protonated (often during an aqueous workup) to give the alcohol product.

Hydride delivered from a reactive metal hydride is an extremely strong, essentially irreversible nucleophile toward carbonyls, a neutral amine is a good but more moderate nucleophile that forms reversible addition products first, and neutral water is comparatively weak, needing acid or base assistance to react efficiently.

While iodide is a great leaving group and decent nucleophile in substitution chemistry, its addition to a carbonyl is not thermodynamically favorable here; there's little driving force, and any adduct would readily revert, so iodide addition to simple carbonyls is not a standard useful reaction.

Because alcohols are weak, neutral nucleophiles, catalysis helps either by activating the electrophile (acid protonates the carbonyl oxygen) or by activating the nucleophile (base removes the alcohol's proton to generate a more reactive alkoxide).

Regardless of the final multistep outcome, the first mechanistic event when any amine reacts with a carbonyl is nucleophilic addition of the nitrogen lone pair to the electrophilic carbonyl carbon, forming a tetrahedral intermediate (hemiaminal) before any subsequent dehydration or reduction steps.

The alkoxide intermediate carries a negative charge on oxygen and is a strong base; an aqueous or mildly acidic workup simply transfers a proton onto that oxygen to give the stable, neutral alcohol final product.

As any nucleophile approaches the carbonyl carbon to form the crowded tetrahedral intermediate, a bulkier nucleophile experiences greater steric strain with the existing substituents on that carbon, slowing the reaction relative to a smaller nucleophile.

Protonation places a full positive charge on oxygen, which is stabilized by resonance delocalization onto the adjacent carbon, greatly enhancing that carbon's electrophilicity and priming it for nucleophilic attack by the alcohol.

Unhindered aldehydes combine low steric bulk with high electrophilicity, both of which favor fast nucleophilic addition, whereas bulky diaryl ketones are both sterically hindered and electronically stabilized by resonance, making them poor substrates for addition.
acetals: The first alcohol gives a hemiacetal; a second equivalent (after loss of water) gives the full acetal with two OR groups on the former carbonyl carbon.
Acetal formation/hydrolysis is acid-catalyzed and reversible — acetals are stable to base, making them useful as protecting groups, but hydrolyze back to the carbonyl in aqueous acid.

Converting a reactive carbonyl into a stable acetal lets other parts of a molecule be modified under basic/non-acidic conditions without the carbonyl interfering, then mild aqueous acid hydrolyzes the acetal back.

Acetal formation requires two separate additions of alcohol: the first gives a hemiacetal, and the second, after loss of water, replaces the hemiacetal's OH group with a second OR group to give the full acetal.

A hemiacetal is the product of adding just one equivalent of alcohol to an aldehyde or ketone; that carbon now carries one OH (from the original carbonyl oxygen, now protonated) and one OR (from the added alcohol).

Acetal hydrolysis requires protonation of one of the alkoxy oxygens to kick off the reverse mechanism (loss of alcohol, formation of an oxocarbenium ion, then addition of water); this only proceeds efficiently under acidic aqueous conditions.

Masking a reactive carbonyl as an acetal lets chemists run reactions elsewhere in the molecule (such as Grignard additions or reductions) that would otherwise also attack the carbonyl; afterward, brief treatment with dilute aqueous acid cleanly regenerates the original aldehyde or ketone.

Although modern IUPAC usage often groups both under 'acetal,' the traditional and still widely used term 'ketal' specifically refers to the double-alkoxy product derived from a ketone rather than an aldehyde.

Protonation of the hemiacetal's hydroxyl allows water to leave, generating a cation on the carbon that is stabilized by resonance donation from the remaining oxygen's lone pair, forming the key oxocarbenium intermediate that the second alcohol then attacks.

Ethylene glycol's two OH groups are positioned to both add intramolecularly to the same carbonyl carbon, closing a five-membered ring containing two oxygens (a 1,3-dioxolane), a very common cyclic acetal protecting group.

Because acetal formation is reversible, Le Chatelier's principle applies: increasing alcohol concentration or physically removing the water byproduct shifts the equilibrium in favor of acetal formation rather than staying as the hemiacetal or reverting to the carbonyl.

Only one hydroxyl group from within the glucose chain adds to the aldehyde carbon, giving a ring carbon with one OH and one OR (the ring oxygen) attached, the classic structure of a cyclic hemiacetal, not a full acetal.

When the open-chain aldose or ketose cyclizes, the original carbonyl carbon becomes a new stereocenter bearing both an OH and a ring oxygen; this carbon is specifically called the anomeric carbon, and its two possible configurations are the alpha and beta anomers.

Because the cyclic hemiacetal is in equilibrium with the open-chain carbonyl form, the ring can open and re-close repeatedly, randomizing which face the new hydroxyl ends up on and gradually establishing an equilibrium mixture of alpha and beta anomers, changing the observed optical rotation over time.

The same structural features that make aldehydes generally more reactive toward nucleophilic addition overall (less steric hindrance, greater electrophilicity) also apply to acetal formation, so aldehydes convert to acetals more readily and under milder conditions than most ketones.

Because Grignard reagents react readily with ketones but an acetal is essentially inert to strongly basic/nucleophilic organometallic reagents, temporarily converting the ketone into an acetal shields it during the Grignard step; mild aqueous acid afterward cleanly unmasks the ketone again.

Sulfur is a weaker base than oxygen and less able to stabilize a positive charge through resonance in the way needed for the acid-catalyzed hydrolysis mechanism, so thioacetals (such as dithianes) are notably more robust toward aqueous acid than their oxygen analogs and require special reagents (like Hg2+ salts) to remove.

Acetal formation (and its reverse, hydrolysis) proceeds through cationic intermediates that require acid catalysis; a strong base like NaOH does not activate the carbonyl for this pathway and acetals are, in fact, stable to basic conditions rather than promoted by them.

In acetal hydrolysis, one OR group leaves (after protonation) to form an oxocarbenium ion, and it is water (present in the aqueous acid medium) that then adds to that cation; losing a proton and losing the second equivalent of alcohol regenerates the free carbonyl.

In most open-chain cases, hemiacetals are typically in a facile equilibrium with the open carbonyl plus alcohol and are often not isolable (except in special cases like intramolecular cyclic sugar hemiacetals), whereas once a full acetal forms it is quite stable under neutral/basic conditions and can be isolated and purified.

Cyclic acetals undergo the same acid-catalyzed hydrolysis mechanism as acyclic ones: protonation, ring-opening to an oxocarbenium/hydroxy species, and addition of water, ultimately releasing the original carbonyl compound along with the diol that had formed the ring.

The defining structural feature of an acetal is that a single carbon bears two C-O bonds (both as -OR groups), which allows acid-catalyzed hydrolysis through a stabilized oxocarbenium intermediate; ordinary ethers have only one oxygen per carbon and lack this pathway, making them far more resistant to aqueous acid.

The entire usefulness of an acetal as a protecting group rests on its selective vulnerability: stable enough to survive basic/nucleophilic/reducing conditions elsewhere in a synthesis, yet cleanly removable with mild aqueous acid when the free carbonyl is needed again.

Counting atoms: carbonyl (C=O) plus two R-OH gives the acetal (C with two OR groups) plus H2O; the oxygen originally present as the carbonyl ends up, together with two hydrogens from the alcohols, as the water byproduct.

Acetal formation is not a redox process: no electrons are transferred to or from an external oxidizing/reducing agent. The carbon still has two oxygen-based substituents before and after (one C=O becomes two C-O), so its formal oxidation level is unchanged even though its hybridization shifts from sp2 to sp3.

Converting the anomeric hemiacetal hydroxyl into an -OR group by reaction with a second alcohol produces a glycoside, which is structurally a full acetal; glycosides are locked in one anomeric configuration and, unlike free sugars, no longer show mutarotation or act as reducing sugars.

Acetal formation/hydrolysis is a reversible, acid-catalyzed equilibrium. By Le Chatelier's principle, a large excess of water (one of the products of hydrolysis, consumed during formation) will push the equilibrium back toward hydrolysis, regenerating the carbonyl and alcohol.

Many carbohydrates exist predominantly as cyclic structures because an internal hydroxyl group on the same molecule is well positioned to add to the carbonyl carbon, forming a ring; with one more external alcohol this can further extend to a full (intramolecular/intermolecular combined) acetal, as in a glycoside.

The ring size of a cyclic acetal depends on the spacing between the diol's two hydroxyl groups: a 1,2-diol like ethylene glycol gives a five-membered dioxolane, while a 1,3-diol like 1,3-propanediol gives a six-membered dioxane when both oxygens bond to the same carbonyl carbon.

Esters have a carbonyl carbon that remains electrophilic and can undergo nucleophilic acyl substitution even under basic or strongly nucleophilic conditions. Acetals have no carbonyl at all (the carbon is fully sp3 and surrounded by two ether-like oxygens), so they are essentially unreactive toward bases and nucleophiles, which is precisely why they make good protecting groups used alongside such reagents.

carboxylic-acids: The carboxylate anion spreads its negative charge equally over two equivalent oxygens via resonance, which is far more stabilizing than an alkoxide’s localized charge.
Most simple carboxylic acids have pKa values around 4–5, far more acidic than alcohols (pKa ~16–18).

The two resonance structures of a carboxylate are equivalent, so the true structure is a symmetric hybrid with the charge (and bond order) shared equally between both oxygens, confirmed by equal C–O bond lengths.
The carboxyl group (C double bonded to O, single bonded to OH) is the defining group of carboxylic acids.
Carboxylic acids are named with the suffix -oic acid added to the parent chain name, e.g. ethanoic acid.
The O-H proton donates a hydrogen bond while the carbonyl oxygen (and the hydroxyl oxygen) can accept one, which is why carboxylic acids dimerize strongly.
Formic acid, HCOOH, is the one-carbon carboxylic acid found in ant stings and formic acid solutions.
Most carboxylic acids have pKa around 4-5, meaning they are only partially ionized in water, unlike strong mineral acids which ionize essentially completely.
Each added electronegative chlorine withdraws electron density inductively, further stabilizing the negative charge on the conjugate base, so acidity increases with each additional chlorine.

Inductive electron withdrawal is transmitted through sigma bonds and falls off quickly with distance, so a halogen closer to the carboxyl group stabilizes the conjugate base more than one farther away.

The nitro group is a strong electron-withdrawing group that stabilizes the negative charge on the carboxylate through both induction and resonance, increasing acidity relative to unsubstituted benzoic acid.

Two carboxylic acid molecules can hydrogen bond to each other reciprocally (each O-H donating to the other's carbonyl oxygen), forming a stable cyclic dimer, especially pronounced without a polar solvent to compete for hydrogen bonding.

Water solubility depends on the balance between the polar, hydrogen-bonding carboxyl group and the nonpolar alkyl chain; as the chain grows, the hydrophobic character increasingly dominates and solubility drops.
Each carboxylic acid molecule can both donate and accept two hydrogen bonds in a dimer, giving a stronger net intermolecular attraction than a single alcohol O-H can provide.

Carboxylic acids (pKa about 4-5) are acidic enough to protonate bicarbonate (pKa of carbonic acid about 6.4), releasing CO2 gas; this bubbling test is used to distinguish carboxylic acids from weaker acids like phenols.

Phenol (pKa about 10) is not acidic enough to protonate bicarbonate significantly, so it does not produce a noticeable bubbling reaction, unlike carboxylic acids; this difference is a classic diagnostic test.

Beta-keto acids can lose CO2 readily on mild heating because the reaction proceeds through a favorable six-membered cyclic transition state that directly generates the more stable ketone enol, which then tautomerizes.

The Grignard carbanion adds to the electrophilic carbon of CO2 to give a magnesium carboxylate, which is protonated on acidic workup to give the carboxylic acid; this is a classic way to build a carboxylic acid while adding one carbon.
Strong oxidants like hot KMnO4 or Jones reagent fully oxidize a primary alcohol through the aldehyde stage to the carboxylic acid, whereas PCC is a mild oxidant that stops cleanly at the aldehyde.
SOCl2 (or PCl3/PCl5) reacts with the carboxylic acid's OH group, converting it into a much better leaving group and producing the reactive acyl chloride along with SO2 and HCl gas.
LiAlH4 is a strong enough hydride donor to reduce carboxylic acids completely past the aldehyde stage to the primary alcohol; it does not stop partway.
NaBH4 is too mild a hydride source to reduce the relatively unreactive carboxylic acid carbonyl efficiently; LiAlH4 (a stronger hydride donor) is needed for that reduction.
Unlike other carboxylic acids, formic acid's carboxyl carbon bears a hydrogen instead of an alkyl or aryl group, giving it mild reducing properties reminiscent of an aldehyde.

The carboxyl carbon is doubly bonded to one oxygen and singly bonded to the other oxygen and to the R group, giving three sigma bonds plus one pi bond -- the sp2, trigonal planar geometry typical of carbonyl carbons.

The three highly electronegative fluorines withdraw electron density inductively, strongly stabilizing the conjugate base and dropping the pKa to around 0.3, far more acidic than acetic acid's pKa of about 4.76.

Once the first carboxyl group loses its proton to become negatively charged, pulling a second positive proton away from the nearby second carboxyl group is both electrostatically harder and the inductive withdrawal helping acidity is reduced, so Ka2 is substantially smaller than Ka1.
Carboxylic acids dimerize through two simultaneous hydrogen bonds, giving a stronger net intermolecular attraction than the single hydrogen bond an alcohol typically forms, raising the boiling point.
Removing the first proton changes the electronic environment (the molecule becomes anionic), so the second -COOH ionizes with a different, typically higher, pKa than the first.

Only the carboxyl group is polar and hydrogen-bonds with water; as the hydrocarbon chain lengthens, the hydrophobic surface area grows faster than the one polar group can compensate for, so solubility declines.
Carboxylic acids are acidic enough to be fully deprotonated by a strong base like NaOH, giving the sodium carboxylate salt and water in a straightforward neutralization.
esters-amides: Amide resonance delocalizes nitrogen’s lone pair strongly into the carbonyl, making amides far less electrophilic and far more hydrolytically stable than esters.
Nitrogen’s lone pair donates into the carbonyl more than an ester oxygen does, giving the amide C=O more single-bond character and a lower, weaker stretching frequency.
Amides with N–H bonds can hydrogen-bond extensively (donor and acceptor), giving them notably higher melting/boiling points than comparable esters, which lack an O–H/N–H donor.
Fischer esterification is the acid-catalyzed condensation of a carboxylic acid with an alcohol, releasing water and forming an ester; it is an equilibrium reaction.

Because the amine is a base and the carboxylic acid is an acid, a simple acid-base proton transfer forming the carboxylate salt happens faster than nucleophilic attack on the carbonyl; forming the amide usually requires heating to drive off water or first converting the acid to a more reactive derivative (such as an acyl chloride).
Many small esters (such as those found in bananas, apples, and pineapples) have characteristic fruity smells, which is why they are widely used as flavoring and fragrance agents.
Ester names follow the pattern 'alkyl acid-oate,' where the alkyl group names the alcohol-derived R group and the '-oate' part names the acid-derived acyl portion.

Delocalization of the nitrogen lone pair into the carbonyl pi system gives the C-N bond partial double-bond character, making it shorter and stronger than a typical single bond, and restricting rotation around it much like a true double bond.

In transesterification, a new alcohol attacks the ester's carbonyl carbon and displaces the original alkoxide leaving group, swapping one ester for another (commonly used, for example, in making biodiesel from vegetable oil).

Saponification is the hydroxide-mediated hydrolysis of esters, classically triglycerides, yielding glycerol and fatty acid carboxylate salts, which are soaps; this reaction is effectively irreversible.

Because Fischer esterification is acid-catalyzed and both the forward (esterification) and reverse (acid-catalyzed hydrolysis) reactions are accessible, the reaction reaches equilibrium and excess alcohol or removal of water is often used to push the equilibrium toward the ester.
LiAlH4 reduces the ester carbonyl all the way to a primary alcohol while releasing the original alkoxy group as its own (separate) alcohol, so two different alcohols are produced overall.

Reduction of an amide's C=O by LiAlH4 proceeds with loss of the oxygen (rather than the nitrogen), converting the carbonyl carbon into a CH2 group attached to nitrogen and giving an amine, unlike ester reduction which gives alcohols.

At room temperature, the amine simply deprotonates the acid to form an ammonium carboxylate salt; converting this salt to the amide typically requires strong heating to drive off water, or using a more reactive acyl derivative.

Resonance donation of the nitrogen lone pair toward the carbonyl oxygen gives the amide significant C=N double bond character and delocalizes the electron density, so the nitrogen is a much weaker base than an ordinary amine nitrogen.
Because the amide nitrogen's lone pair is tied up in resonance with the carbonyl, it is a much poorer proton acceptor (weaker base) than the lone pair on a simple, non-delocalized amine nitrogen.
Without any N-H or O-H bond, a tertiary amide has no hydrogen to donate, but its carbonyl oxygen (made more electron-rich by nitrogen resonance donation) remains an excellent hydrogen bond acceptor.

Even without an N-H donor, the amide carbonyl is highly polarized by nitrogen lone pair donation, giving tertiary amides large dipole-dipole attractions and correspondingly high boiling points relative to their size.
Polyesters are condensation polymers in which a dicarboxylic acid (or its derivative) repeatedly reacts with a diol, forming many ester linkages along the polymer backbone.
Nylon is made by repeatedly forming amide bonds between a dicarboxylic acid (or its derivative) and a diamine, making it a polyamide.
A peptide bond forms when the carboxyl group of one amino acid condenses with the amino group of another, producing the same C(=O)-N bond found in any amide.
Waxes are esters formed from long-chain carboxylic acids (fatty acids) and long-chain alcohols, giving them a waxy, water-repellent character.

The first equivalent of Grignard reagent displaces the alkoxide to give a ketone, which is even more reactive than the ester and is immediately attacked by a second equivalent of Grignard reagent, giving (after workup) a tertiary alcohol.
Esters have no O-H or N-H bond, so they cannot donate a hydrogen bond; they can only accept hydrogen bonds through their carbonyl (and ether-like) oxygens.
A lactone forms when a hydroxyl group and a carboxyl group within the same molecule condense intramolecularly, producing a ring containing an ester linkage.
A lactam is the nitrogen analog of a lactone: an intramolecular condensation between an amine and a carboxyl group within the same molecule forms a ring containing an amide linkage.
Saponification specifically refers to the hydroxide-driven hydrolysis of esters (classically fats and oils) into glycerol and carboxylate salts (soap).

Without an O-H to donate, ester molecules can only engage in weaker dipole-dipole interactions with each other, while carboxylic acids form doubly hydrogen-bonded dimers, giving acids a notably higher boiling point for comparable size.

The major resonance contributor moves the nitrogen lone pair toward the oxygen, leaving partial positive character on carbon and nitrogen and partial negative character on oxygen -- this is why amide carbonyls are strongly polarized and why their IR stretch shifts to a lower wavenumber.
The ester functional group, -C(=O)-O-R, has a carbonyl oxygen double bonded to carbon and a separate ether-like oxygen singly bonded to carbon and to the R group.
acyl-substitution: Acyl substitution goes through a tetrahedral intermediate (addition step) that then expels a leaving group, regenerating the carbonyl — net substitution rather than simple addition.
Chloride is a much weaker base than an amine/amide nitrogen, making acyl chlorides far more reactive electrophiles than amides in acyl substitution.

Reactivity tracks how good the leaving group is and how much the heteroatom lone pair is tied up in resonance with the carbonyl: Cl⁻ is an excellent leaving group with little resonance donation (most reactive), while amide nitrogen donates strongly into the carbonyl and is a poor leaving group (least reactive).

Nucleophilic acyl substitution proceeds by the nucleophile first adding to the carbonyl carbon, then a leaving group being eliminated to restore the carbonyl, an addition-elimination sequence distinct from simple substitution at sp3 carbon.
Nucleophilic acyl substitution begins with nucleophilic addition to the sp2 carbonyl carbon, producing a tetrahedral alkoxide intermediate, before any leaving group departs.

The mechanism is addition first, then elimination: the nucleophile adds to the carbonyl carbon to form a tetrahedral intermediate, and only afterward does the leaving group depart to restore the carbonyl.

Reactivity tracks how good each group's substituent is as a leaving group and how poorly it donates electron density into the carbonyl by resonance; chloride is the best leaving group and poorest resonance donor, while nitrogen in an amide is the worst leaving group and best resonance donor, giving this overall order.

Weaker bases are more stable as free anions (or neutral species) and are less prone to holding onto a bonding pair of electrons, which is exactly why chloride (a very weak base) leaves far more readily than an amide nitrogen (effectively a strong base, as NH2-/RNH-) leaves.

Nitrogen's lone pair donates into the carbonyl pi system more effectively than oxygen or chlorine can, which both lowers the carbonyl's electrophilicity and means that once a tetrahedral intermediate forms, nitrogen (as a strongly basic amide anion) is reluctant to leave.

Chlorine's lone pairs are in a larger, poorly overlapping orbital, so they donate little electron density into the carbonyl by resonance, leaving the carbon highly electrophilic; additionally chloride ion, being a very weak base, departs easily once the tetrahedral intermediate forms.

Carboxylate is a moderately basic, resonance-stabilized anion, but chloride is an even weaker base and therefore a better leaving group, which is part of why acyl chlorides outrank anhydrides in reactivity.

Water acts as the nucleophile, attacking the highly electrophilic acyl chloride carbonyl; after the tetrahedral intermediate collapses and chloride leaves, loss of a proton gives the carboxylic acid and HCl.
The alcohol's oxygen attacks the acyl chloride carbonyl; after chloride departs and a proton is lost (often assisted by a base or excess alcohol), the product is an ester plus HCl.

One amine equivalent attacks the carbonyl to displace a carboxylate leaving group and form the amide; because carboxylic acid is a stronger acid than the amide's conjugate acid, a second amine equivalent is typically consumed neutralizing the liberated carboxylic acid.

The alcohol attacks one of the anhydride's two carbonyl carbons; the other acyl-oxygen half departs as a carboxylate (which is then protonated), so the overall products are an ester and a carboxylic acid.

Going from a reactive derivative to a less reactive one replaces a good leaving group with a worse one in an energetically downhill step; the reverse would require a leaving group (such as an amide nitrogen) that is both basic and a poor leaving group to depart, which is very unfavorable.

This would require nitrogen (a strongly basic, poor leaving group) to depart, which is extremely unfavorable; amides are the least reactive acyl derivative and are not readily converted into more reactive derivatives like esters by simple nucleophilic substitution.

Protonating the carbonyl oxygen pulls electron density away from the carbon through the resulting resonance-stabilized cation, making the carbon much more attractive to a comparatively weak nucleophile such as water, which otherwise would react too slowly.

In Fischer esterification, the leaving group would have to be hydroxide (a poor leaving group), so acid catalysis is needed to make departure possible and the reaction is a slow equilibrium; with an acyl chloride, chloride is already an excellent leaving group, so the reaction proceeds quickly without a catalyst and is essentially irreversible.

Nitrogen is less electronegative and holds its lone pair less tightly than oxygen, making amines generally better nucleophiles than comparably substituted alcohols, which in turn are typically better nucleophiles than water.

The first Grignard equivalent adds to the ester carbonyl and the tetrahedral intermediate collapses, expelling the alkoxide leaving group to give a ketone; because the ketone is even more electrophilic than the starting ester, a second equivalent of Grignard reagent immediately adds to it.

The ketone intermediate generated from the first addition is actually more reactive toward the Grignard reagent than the original ester was, so under normal conditions with excess Grignard reagent the reaction proceeds on to give a tertiary alcohol rather than stopping at the ketone.

When the nucleophile's electron pair adds to the carbon, the carbon-oxygen pi bond breaks and its electrons move fully onto the oxygen, giving a negatively charged alkoxide oxygen in the tetrahedral intermediate.

A pi bond to oxygen is strong and energetically favorable to reform; the tetrahedral alkoxide intermediate is generally higher in energy than either the starting carbonyl compound or the product, so it collapses to restore the stable carbonyl as soon as a leaving group can depart.

Classic SN2 substitution occurs at an sp3 carbon with backside attack displacing a leaving group in one step; the carbonyl carbon in acyl substitution is sp2 and planar, so the nucleophile must add to one face to form a new sp3 tetrahedral intermediate before a leaving group can depart in a separate step.

Unlike nucleophilic addition (which destroys the carbonyl pi bond permanently), acyl substitution regenerates the carbonyl in the final product; only the group attached via the leaving position has been swapped out.

Thionyl chloride or phosphorus chlorides convert the poor -OH leaving group of a carboxylic acid into the excellent -Cl leaving group, producing the highly reactive acyl chloride used in many subsequent nucleophilic acyl substitution reactions.

Once hydroxide attacks and the carboxylate anion is formed, its negative charge (stabilized by resonance) makes it far too unreactive an electrophile to be attacked again by the departed alkoxide, effectively trapping the reaction as products; acid-catalyzed hydrolysis, by contrast, gives a neutral carboxylic acid that remains in equilibrium with the ester under the same conditions.

A carboxylate leaving group (departing from an anhydride) is a better leaving group than an alkoxide (departing from an ester), and the second carbonyl group in an anhydride also inductively withdraws electron density, both of which make anhydrides more reactive than esters.

Hydroxide is a poor leaving group, so direct substitution at a carboxylic acid's carbonyl is slow; additionally, with basic nucleophiles such as amines, simple acid-base proton transfer (forming a salt) usually outcompetes attack on the carbonyl, which is why carboxylic acids are often first converted to a more reactive derivative (like an acyl chloride) before substitution.
alpha-hydrogens: Removing an alpha H gives a carbanion that resonance-delocalizes onto the carbonyl oxygen, forming a stabilized enolate — this is why alpha H’s (pKa ~20) are far more acidic than typical C–H bonds (pKa ~50).
The enolate resonance structures place negative charge either on the alpha carbon (carbanion form) or the oxygen (enolate form, more stable).
Deprotonating the central CH₂ gives an anion that can delocalize into either flanking carbonyl, doubling the resonance stabilization compared to a mono-ketone’s enolate.

The carbon directly attached to the carbonyl carbon is called the alpha carbon, so hydrogens on it are alpha hydrogens. The carbonyl carbon itself has no H in ketones and usually one in aldehydes, but that H is not called 'alpha.'

Alpha hydrogens are unusually acidic compared to ordinary C-H bonds because the resulting carbanion can be stabilized by resonance delocalization into the adjacent carbonyl, something an alkyl carbanion cannot do.

LDA is a strong, bulky, non-nucleophilic base that removes alpha protons quickly and cleanly without attacking the carbonyl carbon itself, driving deprotonation essentially to completion at low temperature.

Keto-enol tautomers differ only in the position of a proton and a double bond: the keto form has C=O and a C-H at the alpha carbon, while the enol form has C=C-OH. They are neutral isomers, not charged species.

An enolate is formed by removing an alpha C-H, not an O-H; a simple ketone or ester typically has no O-H to remove in the first place. The resulting negative charge is then delocalized onto oxygen by resonance.

The 'alpha carbon' on the aryl side of PhCHO is part of the aromatic ring; removing a ring C-H there would destroy aromaticity and is not the kind of alpha-deprotonation relevant to enolate chemistry, so PhCHO's only true alpha hydrogens would have to come from an alkyl substituent, which it lacks.

Even though both deprotonations are stabilized somewhat by electronegative oxygen, the alcohol O-H is still considerably more acidic, so only a weak-to-moderate base is needed there, while alpha C-H deprotonation needs a much stronger base such as an amide base.

Oxygen is more electronegative than carbon, so it stabilizes negative charge better, making the oxygen-centered resonance form the greater contributor even though many enolate reactions proceed through the carbon end as the nucleophile.
Each additional carbonyl provides another resonance pathway to delocalize the negative charge of the resulting anion, so flanking a CH2 with two carbonyls instead of one lowers its pKa substantially.

Ethyl acetoacetate's central CH2 sits between a ketone and an ester carbonyl, giving it two stabilizing resonance pathways and a much lower pKa than acetone's single-carbonyl-stabilized alpha H, while a vinylic C-H has essentially no special stabilization and is among the least acidic C-H bonds listed.

In an ester, resonance donation from the alkoxy oxygen competes with the carbonyl's ability to stabilize an adjacent negative charge, making ester groups somewhat less effective than ketone carbonyls at lowering alpha C-H pKa, which is why malonates (two esters) are less acidic than 1,3-diketones (two ketones).

Nitriles, like carbonyls, have a pi system into which a negative charge on the adjacent carbon can be delocalized, so alpha hydrogens next to a nitrile are likewise more acidic than ordinary alkane C-H bonds, though typically less so than those next to a ketone.

LDA is sterically bulky and essentially irreversible under these conditions, so it preferentially removes the most kinetically accessible (least hindered, often less substituted) alpha proton, favoring the kinetic enolate rather than the more stable, more substituted thermodynamic enolate.

Under strongly basic, low-temperature, irreversible conditions, the faster-formed (kinetic) enolate dominates; under conditions allowing equilibration (weaker base, higher temperature, excess ketone), the more stable, typically more substituted thermodynamic enolate dominates instead.

The same resonance donation from the ester's -OR oxygen that makes ester carbonyls less electrophilic toward nucleophiles also makes them somewhat less effective at stabilizing an adjacent carbanion than a ketone carbonyl is.

Carboxylic acids have two acidic sites, but the O-H is dramatically more acidic because its conjugate base (carboxylate) is stabilized by two equivalent resonance structures with the negative charge shared between both oxygens; a much stronger base is needed to reach the alpha carbon, and the carboxylate must usually be protected or already formed first.

The carbonyl in cyclohexanone is flanked by two different alpha carbons, C2 and C6; adding a methyl at C2 still leaves one alpha hydrogen there (C2 becomes a stereocenter upon enolate formation consideration) while C6 still has two, so enolization can occur on either side.

Like a carbonyl, the nitro group has resonance forms that can accept and stabilize a developing negative charge on the adjacent carbon, making nitroalkane alpha hydrogens strongly acidic despite nitro not being a classic carbonyl-type carbon.

A nitrile does provide meaningful resonance stabilization of an adjacent carbanion (just generally less than a carbonyl), so a beta-ketonitrile's alpha C-H is typically considerably more acidic than a simple ketone's (often in the pKa 9-13 range), not merely equal to it.

Acid-base equilibria favor the side with the weaker acid and weaker base; since a 1,3-diketone is more acidic than triethylammonium, its deprotonation is favorable, but a simple ketone is less acidic than triethylammonium, so that deprotonation is unfavorable and only a small equilibrium concentration of enolate forms.

Because a 1,3-diketone's pKa (~9-11) is well below water's pKa (~15.7), hydroxide readily and nearly completely deprotonates it; a monoketone's pKa (~20) is well above water's pKa, so hydroxide deprotonates it to only a tiny, unfavorable extent, illustrating why base strength must be matched to the acidity of the specific alpha hydrogens involved.

In enones, conjugation extends the resonance-stabilized pi system out to the gamma carbon, so gamma-deprotonation can generate an extended enolate whose negative charge is delocalized across oxygen, the alpha carbon, and the gamma carbon, a reactivity pattern beyond simple alpha-carbon enolates.

Adding the substrate to excess strong, bulky, non-equilibrating base at low temperature ensures deprotonation is fast, irreversible, and governed by steric accessibility, favoring the kinetic (less substituted) enolate rather than allowing the system to equilibrate toward the more stable, more substituted thermodynamic enolate.

Enolate formation requires removing an actual hydrogen from the alpha carbon; if that specific carbon has been substituted until it bears no hydrogens (as in a ketone with a fully branched alpha carbon), there is no alpha C-H to remove at that position, regardless of what is going on elsewhere in the molecule.

Only the sp3 CH3 carbon attached to the carbonyl is the true alpha carbon capable of forming a resonance-stabilized enolate; the ring carbon on the other side of the carbonyl is aromatic and its hydrogens are not involved in this kind of carbonyl-stabilized deprotonation.

Cyclic 1,3-diketones such as 1,3-cyclohexanedione are known to be notably more acidic than their open-chain counterparts, partly because the enol tautomer is particularly stable and well-conjugated in the ring, pulling the equilibrium and making the corresponding proton unusually easy to remove.

Nitrogen is a better pi-donor than oxygen, so amide resonance (donation of the nitrogen lone pair into the carbonyl) is even stronger than the ester case, making amide carbonyls notably less effective at stabilizing an adjacent alpha carbanion, which is why amide alpha C-H bonds are less acidic (pKa often above 30) than ketone alpha C-H bonds.
aldol: The aldol reaction is an enolate (nucleophile, from one carbonyl’s alpha carbon) attacking the electrophilic carbonyl carbon of a second molecule, forming a new C–C bond and a beta-hydroxy carbonyl.
Base- or acid-promoted loss of water from the beta-hydroxy group, conjugated with the carbonyl, gives the thermodynamically favorable α,β-unsaturated (enone) product.

With two different carbonyls that can each form enolates and each act as electrophiles, an uncontrolled mixed aldol gives up to four possible products — selectivity requires strategies like using one component in excess or pre-forming one enolate completely before adding the other carbonyl.

Base removes an alpha hydrogen to generate a resonance-stabilized enolate, and it is the nucleophilic alpha carbon of that enolate that attacks the electrophilic carbonyl carbon of a second molecule of aldehyde or ketone.

The new C-C bond forms between the alpha carbon of one molecule and the carbonyl carbon of the other; after protonation, that carbonyl carbon now bears an -OH group that is beta (two carbons away) to the remaining carbonyl group, giving a beta-hydroxy carbonyl compound.

Both the enolate (or enol) formation step and the C-C bond-forming addition step are equilibria; the aldol product can revert to starting materials (a retro-aldol), which is part of why the overall process is often driven toward completion by subsequent dehydration.

The beta-hydroxy group is positioned so that E1cb (base) or E1 (acid)-type elimination across the alpha-beta bond is favorable, expelling water and forming a conjugated, thermodynamically stabilized alpha,beta-unsaturated carbonyl, commonly called an aldol condensation product.

Conjugation between the new alkene and the carbonyl group extends pi overlap and lowers the overall energy of the product, providing a thermodynamic driving force for elimination of water even though the beta-hydroxy ketone itself is a stable, isolable compound.

In acid-catalyzed mechanisms, the carbonyl oxygen is protonated first, which both activates the carbonyl carbon toward nucleophilic attack and increases the acidity of the adjacent alpha hydrogens, facilitating enol formation in the next step.

When both partners possess alpha hydrogens and comparable reactivity, enolates of either compound can form and attack either carbonyl, giving a mixture of self-addition and cross-addition products that is difficult to control and separate without deliberate strategy.

Because the alpha-hydrogen-free partner cannot form its own enolate, it can only act as the electrophile, while the other carbonyl compound's enolate is the only nucleophile available, greatly simplifying the reaction to essentially one major crossed product.

As with most ring-forming reactions, five- and six-membered rings form fastest and most favorably due to good orbital alignment and minimal strain, so intramolecular aldol (and aldol condensation) reactions are typically designed to close five- or six-membered rings.

Acetone's enolate attacks the carbonyl carbon of a second acetone molecule; after protonation, the product is a beta-hydroxy ketone known as diacetone alcohol, which can later be dehydrated (with acid and heat) to the conjugated enone mesityl oxide.

The same steric and electronic factors that make aldehydes more reactive toward nucleophiles in general (less crowding, less alkyl-group electron donation stabilizing the carbonyl) also make them better electrophilic partners in aldol addition.

By using excess strong base to exclusively deprotonate the first compound before the second carbonyl compound is even present, the chemist avoids having two competing enolates form simultaneously, which otherwise leads to an uncontrolled mixture of self- and cross-aldol products.
